The places on the dry slope are 1 and 2: place 1 is high up and cooler, while place 2 is at the foot and very hot.

yechim.doska: Desert = hot + very little precipitation → place 2
yechim.ovoz: A desert forms where it is hot and there is very little precipitation — that is place 2.
The correct answer is B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A correctly found the dry slope but did not take into account that place 1 is high up and cool.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C chose a wet place under the clouds — there is a lot of precipitation there, so it cannot be a desert.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D looked only for a hot place, but place 4 is at the foot of the wet slope — there is a lot of precipitation there.

variantlar.maslahat: Recall the two conditions a desert needs and find the slope where it does not rain.

kunikma: Know specific negative and positive effects of a volcanic eruption on the environment (air, soil, plant and animal life)
usul: Recall what comes out during a volcanic eruption — lava, ash, and gases (water vapor, carbon dioxide, sulfur gases) — and work out how each of them affects the air, the soil, and living things.

variantlar.savol: Which of the following correctly describes an effect of a volcanic eruption on the environment?
javoblar: Volcanic gases are made mostly of pure oxygen and clean the air.
Volcanic ash stays only inside the crater and does not spread to the surrounding area.
Ash and sulfur gases released into the atmosphere pollute the air and cause acid rain.
Where lava has flowed, the soil stays dead forever and plants never grow there again.

yechim.doska: A volcano releases: lava, ash, gases
yechim.ovoz: When a volcano erupts, lava, ash, and various gases come out.
Most of the gases are water vapor, carbon dioxide, and sulfur gases, not oxygen.
Sulfur gases combine with moisture in the air to form acid rain, and the ash pollutes the air.

yechim.doska: Wind carries ash hundreds of km; lava weathers and over time gives fertile soil
yechim.ovoz: Wind carries ash very far, and over time lava weathers and turns into fertile soil — so B and D are wrong.
The correct answer is C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A did not know what volcanic gases are made of; they contain almost no oxygen and instead contain poisonous gases.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought ash is heavy and stays where it falls; fine ash is carried very far by the wind.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought short-term damage is permanent; over time lava weathers and plants grow there again.

variantlar.maslahat: Recall which gases come out of a volcano and what they form with water in the air.

variantlar.savol: Despite the danger, many farmers live and farm at the foot of extinct volcanoes or volcanoes that erupt from time to time. What is the main reason for this?
javoblar: The soil formed from volcanic ash and weathered lava is rich in minerals and fertile.
Near a volcano the air is always cool and it rains a lot.
The heat of the lava protects crops from frost in winter.
Insect pests do not live near volcanoes at all.

yechim.doska: Volcanic ash and lava — rich in minerals
yechim.ovoz: Volcanic ash and lava are rich in elements that plants need, such as potassium, phosphorus, and magnesium.
When they weather over time, they form very fertile soil.
That is why large harvests are grown at the foot of volcanoes, and people live there despite the danger.

yechim.doska: This is a positive effect of a volcano on the environment
yechim.ovoz: This is a positive, long-term effect of a volcanic eruption on the environment.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) the soil is fertile
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought the climate near a volcano is always cool and wet; climate depends on the region, not on the volcano.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C imagined that lava is always flowing and warming the surroundings; between eruptions the lava cools and hardens.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D made an unfounded generalization; insects live at the foot of volcanoes as usual.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about how the makeup of the soil changes when volcanic ash and lava weather.

kunikma: Know that organic waste (from living things) breaks down quickly through the action of microorganisms, while metal, glass, and plastic break down very slowly
usul: Decide whether the waste comes from a living thing (a plant or an animal) or is an artificial/mineral material: bacteria and fungi break down organic substances quickly.

variantlar.savol: The following items were buried in a landfill. Which of them breaks down (rots) the fastest?

yechim.ovoz: Bacteria and fungi in the soil break down organic substances.

yechim.doska: Apple peel — organic matter from a plant
yechim.ovoz: Apple peel comes from a plant, and it rots within a few weeks.

yechim.doska: Aluminum, plastic, glass — tens to hundreds of years
yechim.ovoz: An aluminum can, a plastic bag, and glass are hardly broken down by microorganisms at all; they last for decades or even hundreds of years.
The correct answer is B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought thin metal wears away quickly; aluminum does not rust and lasts a very long time.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C wrongly thought that something light and thin rots quickly; plastic does not break down for hundreds of years.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought glass breaks down quickly because it is brittle; even when broken, pieces of glass hardly break down in nature.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about which waste bacteria and fungi can break down as “food.”

variantlar.savol: Which of the following items lasts the LONGEST in nature without breaking down?

yechim.ovoz: A newspaper is made from wood, cotton fabric from cotton fiber, and a banana peel comes from a plant — these are organic materials.

yechim.doska: Banana peel — weeks; newspaper — months; cotton fabric — months
yechim.ovoz: A banana peel breaks down in a few weeks, and a newspaper and cotton fabric in a few months.

yechim.doska: Glass — a mineral material, microbes do not break it down
yechim.ovoz: Glass is a mineral material made from sand; microorganisms cannot break it down, and it lasts for thousands of years.
The correct answer is D.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought paper is an artificial material; paper is made from wood fiber and breaks down fairly quickly.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought fabric lasts a long time because it is strong; cotton is a natural fiber and it rots.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C did not notice the word “longest” in the question and chose the item that breaks down fastest.

variantlar.maslahat: Find the item that does not come from a living thing.

kunikma: Know that when the temperature of a substance changes, the speed of its molecules changes (temperature is a measure of the average speed of the molecules)
usul: Recall that molecules move faster when the temperature rises and slower when it falls; heating or cooling does not change the size, mass, or number of molecules.

variantlar.savol: A closed plastic bottle of air was put in a freezer, and the temperature of the air dropped. What happens to the air molecules in the bottle?

yechim.doska: Temperature — a measure of molecular motion
yechim.ovoz: The temperature of a substance shows how fast its molecules are moving.
When the air cools, the molecules start moving more slowly.

yechim.doska: Size and number do not change
yechim.ovoz: The molecules themselves do not get smaller, and because the bottle is closed, their number does not change either.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) they move more slowly
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B took the contraction of an object in the cold to mean that the molecules get smaller; in fact, the distance between the molecules decreases.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought the air “decreases” in the cold; in a closed bottle the number of molecules does not change.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D got the relationship between temperature and molecular speed backwards.

variantlar.maslahat: Recall how the speed of molecules changes when the temperature drops.

variantlar.savol: The water in a kettle was heated, and its temperature rose. Which property of the water molecules increases?
javoblar: the average speed of the molecules

yechim.doska: Heating → energy is given to the molecules
yechim.ovoz: When we heat water, we give energy to its molecules.
Thanks to this energy, the molecules move faster on average, and that is why the temperature rises.

yechim.doska: Size, number, mass — do not change
yechim.ovoz: The molecules do not get bigger, their mass does not change, and heating does not increase their number.
The correct answer is C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A took the expansion of a heated object to mean that the molecules get bigger; in fact, the distance between the molecules increases.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought heating creates new molecules.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D wrongly thought a molecule that gains energy gets heavier; the mass of a molecule does not change when it is heated.

variantlar.maslahat: Recall that sugar or tea spreads faster in hot water, and think about how this is connected with the motion of molecules.

kunikma: Apply the knowledge that in sexual reproduction offspring receive genetic material from both parents to a specific situation
usul: Recall that in sexual reproduction a new organism develops from a zygote formed when the father's sex cell joins with the mother's egg cell: offspring receive half of their genetic material from the father and half from the mother, regardless of their sex or birth order.

variantlar.savol: Malika and her younger brother Jasur are children of the same parents. Which statement about their genetic material is correct?
javoblar: Jasur received genetic material only from his father, and Malika only from her mother.
Both received genetic material only from their mother, because they were born to their mother.
Because Malika is the older child, she received more of her genetic material from her father.
Both received genetic material from both their father and their mother.

yechim.ovoz: Humans reproduce sexually: the father's sex cell joins with the mother's egg cell to form a zygote.

yechim.doska: Half of the zygote's chromosomes come from the father, half from the mother
yechim.ovoz: Half of the chromosomes in the zygote come from the father and the other half from the mother, and the child develops from this zygote.

yechim.doska: Sons and daughters — the same rule; birth order does not matter
yechim.ovoz: Neither whether the child is a boy or a girl nor the order in which the child is born changes this rule.

yechim.doska: Answer: D) Both received it from both their father and their mother
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is D.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A had heard that a boy gets his Y chromosome from his father and wrongly generalized that all genetic material is divided by sex.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought that because a baby develops inside the mother, it also gets its genetic material only from the mother.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C wrongly thought that birth order affects how genetic material is shared out.

variantlar.maslahat: Recall which two sex cells join to form each child.

variantlar.savol: A cow on a farm gave birth to two calves at once: one male and one female. Both calves have the same father, a bull. Which statement about the calves' genetic material is correct?
javoblar: Both calves received genetic material from both the bull and the cow.
The male calf received genetic material only from the bull, and the female calf only from the cow.
Both calves received genetic material only from the cow.
Both calves received genetic material only from the bull.

yechim.doska: The cow is a mammal and reproduces sexually
yechim.ovoz: Cows and bulls, like humans, reproduce sexually.

yechim.doska: Each calf: the bull's sex cell + the cow's egg cell
yechim.ovoz: Each calf developed from a zygote formed when a sex cell from the bull joined with an egg cell from the cow.

yechim.doska: Genetic material: half from the father (bull), half from the mother (cow)
yechim.ovoz: So each calf gets half of its genetic material from the bull and half from the cow; whether it is male or female makes no difference.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) Both calves received it from both the bull and the cow
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B wrongly thought that offspring get their genetic material from the parent of the same sex.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought that because the calf was born from the cow, its genetic material also comes only from the cow.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D relied on the mistaken idea that only the father passes on hereditary traits.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about which cells joined for the calf to start developing.

kunikma: Use the arrangement of rock layers to determine the relative age of the fossils in them
usul: Sedimentary layers build up one on top of another: in undisturbed (not overturned) layers, the lower layer formed first and the upper layer formed later. The size, number, or similarity of fossils does not tell you their age.

variantlar.savol:
The picture shows rock layers containing fossils, as seen in a cliff by a river. The layers have not been disturbed: layer 1 is at the top and layer 5 is at the bottom.
Which statement about the age of the fossils is most likely to be correct?
javoblar: The fossils in layer 2 are older than those in layer 5, because they are larger.
The fossils in layers 1 and 2 are the same age, because they look alike.
The fossils in layer 5 are the oldest, because this layer is at the bottom.
The fossils in layer 3 are the youngest, because they look like modern fish.

yechim.doska: Sediments build up layer by layer: each new layer on top of the old one
yechim.ovoz: Sediments collect layer by layer at the bottom of a body of water, and each new layer settles on top of the previous one.

yechim.doska: Lower layer — formed first, upper layer — formed later
yechim.ovoz: So in undisturbed layers, the lower a layer is, the older it is.

yechim.doska: Layer 5 is at the bottom → its fossils are the oldest
yechim.ovoz: Layer 5 is at the very bottom, so the fossils in it are the oldest.

yechim.doska: Size and similarity do not tell age
yechim.ovoz: A fossil's size or its similarity to another fossil does not show its age, and layer 3 is in the middle.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) the fossils in layer 5 are the oldest
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A linked a fossil's size with its age, but the age of a layer depends on its position.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought that similar organisms lived at the same time; similar species can live in different periods, and the layers formed at different times.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D ignored the position of the layer: layer 3 is in the middle with two more layers above it, so it cannot be the youngest.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about the order in which the layers build up — from the bottom up or from the top down.

variantlar.savol:
The picture shows rock layers exposed when a mountain road was cut. The layers have not been disturbed: layer P is at the top and layer S is at the bottom.
The fossils in which layer are most likely to be the youngest (formed most recently)?
javoblar: In layer S, because it has the most fossils.
In layer R, because its fossils are the smallest.
In layer Q, because this layer is the thickest.
In layer P, because this layer is at the top.

yechim.doska: Each new layer settles on top of the previous one
yechim.ovoz: Sedimentary layers build up one after another, each on top of the last.
So in undisturbed layers, the top one formed last, that is, it is the youngest.

yechim.doska: P is at the top → its fossils are the youngest
yechim.ovoz: Layer P is at the top, so the fossils in it are the youngest.

yechim.doska: Number and size of fossils, thickness of a layer — do not tell age
yechim.ovoz: How many fossils there are, how small they are, or how thick the layer is does not determine its age.

yechim.doska: Answer: D) the fossils in layer P
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is D.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought that if there are many fossils, those organisms lived recently; in fact, layer S is at the bottom and is the oldest.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B mistook small fossils for “young” organisms; an organism's size has nothing to do with the age of the layer.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought the thickest layer is the newest; thickness only shows how long or how fast sediment built up.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about which layer could have settled last, on top of the others.

kunikma: Choose the correct experiment to show that water a plant takes from the soil passes through the plant and evaporates into the air through the leaves (transpiration)
usul: The experiment must show exactly the process being tested: you should observe water passing through a living plant with its roots in soil and going out into the air, while other sources of water (evaporation from the soil or from water in a container) are ruled out.

variantlar.savol:
Nilufar has a houseplant growing in a pot. She wants to do an experiment to show that water the plant takes from the soil passes through the plant and goes out into the air.
Which experiment shows this?
javoblar: Wrap one of the plant's leafy shoots in a clear plastic bag, tie the bag closed, and water the plant; after a few hours, drops of water appear inside the bag.
Put a glass of water next to the pot; after a few days, there is less water in the glass.
Pick one leaf off the plant and put it in a plastic bag; a little moisture appears inside the bag.
Put a cut shoot of the plant in water with ink added; the leaf veins turn blue.

yechim.doska: Need to show: soil → plant → air
yechim.ovoz: The experiment must show that water goes from the soil into the plant and then out into the air.

yechim.doska: Water in a glass — evaporates by itself, nothing to do with the plant
yechim.ovoz: Water in a glass evaporates even without a plant, so this experiment tells us nothing about the plant.

yechim.doska: Picked leaf and cut shoot — separated from roots and soil
yechim.ovoz: A picked leaf cannot take water from the soil, and the ink experiment only shows water rising upward, not going out into the air.

yechim.doska: Shoot of a living plant in a bag → drops = water vapor from the leaves
yechim.ovoz: The drops in the bag wrapped around a shoot of a watered living plant form from water vapor given off by the leaves; this process is called transpiration.
The correct answer is A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B mistook water evaporating from the glass by itself for water evaporated by the plant.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought a picked leaf keeps taking water from the soil; it has been separated from the plant and only gives off the little moisture it contains.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D confused water rising up the stem with water going out into the air.

variantlar.maslahat: In which experiment can you see water passing through a living plant and going out into the air?

variantlar.savol:
Aziz wants to prove that water absorbed from the soil by a plant's roots goes out into the air through the leaves. He has a potted plant and a large glass bell jar.
Which experiment shows this most convincingly?
javoblar: Water the pot and place the whole plant, pot and all, under the glass bell jar; drops of water appear on the walls of the jar.
Put the pot on a sunny windowsill; after two days, the soil dries out.
Water the pot, cover the surface of the soil tightly with plastic film, then place the plant and its pot under the bell jar; drops of water appear on the walls of the jar.
Place a pot that contains soil but no plant under the bell jar; drops appear on the walls of the jar.

yechim.doska: Need to prove: water goes out into the air through the leaves
yechim.ovoz: We need to be sure that the drops inside the jar came only from the leaves.
Uncovered wet soil also gives off water vapor by itself, so the drops in option A could also come from the soil.

yechim.doska: Soil covered with film → vapor only from the plant
yechim.ovoz: In option C, the soil is covered with film, so the drops in the jar can only form from water given off by the plant's leaves.

yechim.doska: B and D — the plant plays no part
yechim.ovoz: In B, we only see the soil drying out, and in D there is no plant at all; they prove nothing about leaves.
The correct answer is C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A did not take into account that wet soil also evaporates water: the drops could come from the leaves and also from the soil.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B linked the soil drying out with the plant's activity, but soil also dries out by itself in the sun.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought an experiment without a plant could also tell us something about leaves; it only shows evaporation from the soil.

variantlar.maslahat: How can you be sure that the drops came from the leaves and not from the soil?

kunikma: Know that people with diabetes need to limit foods and drinks that are high in sugar and raise blood sugar quickly
usul: In diabetes, the body cannot control the amount of sugar (glucose) in the blood well, because there is not enough insulin or it does not work properly; so find the product among the options that contains the most sugar.

variantlar.savol: Dilnoza's grandfather has diabetes. Which of the following should he be especially careful about eating or drinking?

yechim.doska: Diabetes → blood sugar rises above normal
yechim.ovoz: In diabetes, the amount of sugar, that is glucose, in the blood can become very high.

yechim.doska: High-sugar product → blood sugar rises quickly
yechim.ovoz: Foods and drinks with a lot of sugar raise blood sugar quickly.

yechim.doska: Meat, egg — mainly protein; cucumber — a low-sugar vegetable
yechim.ovoz: Chicken and eggs contain mainly protein, and cucumber has very little sugar.

yechim.doska: Sweet fizzy drink — very high in sugar
yechim.ovoz: A sweet fizzy drink, however, has a lot of sugar dissolved in it.

yechim.doska: Answer: B) a sweet fizzy drink
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought all filling foods are dangerous in diabetes; meat is made up mainly of protein.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C did not know what cucumber contains; it is mostly water and has very little sugar.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D confused an egg with sweets; an egg contains mainly protein and fat.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about which product contains the most sugar.

variantlar.savol: A doctor diagnosed Sardor with diabetes. Which of the following should Sardor be careful about eating?

yechim.doska: In diabetes, blood sugar must be kept under control
yechim.ovoz: In diabetes, the most important thing is that blood sugar does not rise sharply.

yechim.doska: Jam = fruit + a lot of sugar
yechim.ovoz: Jam is made by boiling fruit together with a great deal of sugar.

yechim.doska: Cabbage — a vegetable; cheese and fish — high in protein
yechim.ovoz: Cabbage salad has little sugar, and cheese and fish are made up mainly of protein and fat.
The correct answer is D.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought all plant foods are sweet; cabbage has very little sugar.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought cheese, which is made from milk, is a sweet food; cheese is made up mainly of protein and fat.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C wrongly thought protein-rich fish raises blood sugar.

variantlar.maslahat: Which product is made using a lot of sugar?

kunikma: Use the process of photosynthesis to justify why planting trees reduces the amount of carbon dioxide in the air
usul: In photosynthesis, green plants absorb carbon dioxide from the air and, together with water, make organic substances from it and release oxygen; choose the answer that explains the proposal specifically by the absorption of carbon dioxide.

variantlar.savol:
Because the number of cars in our city has grown, the amount of carbon dioxide in the air is increasing. The mayor proposed planting more trees along the streets.
Which statement about the mayor's proposal is correct and correctly justified?
javoblar: The proposal is right, because trees release oxygen, and oxygen destroys the carbon dioxide in the air.
The proposal is wrong, because trees absorb oxygen from the air and release carbon dioxide.
The proposal is right, because trees absorb carbon dioxide from the air during photosynthesis.
The proposal is wrong, because trees do not affect carbon dioxide; they only give shade.

yechim.ovoz: In photosynthesis, green leaves use light to make organic substances from carbon dioxide and water and release oxygen.
So as trees grow, they absorb carbon dioxide from the air.
Oxygen does not destroy carbon dioxide, so an explanation based only on oxygen is wrong.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) The proposal is right: $CO_2$ is absorbed in photosynthesis
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A remembered only that oxygen is released and wrongly thought that oxygen “destroys” carbon dioxide.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B confused photosynthesis with respiration; a growing tree absorbs more carbon dioxide in photosynthesis than it releases in respiration.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D did not know the role of plants in gas exchange.

variantlar.maslahat: Which gas does a plant take from the air for photosynthesis?

variantlar.savol:
Because of a cement plant and a large highway nearby, the amount of carbon dioxide in the air in a district has increased. Ecologists proposed planting a large wooded area around the plant.
Once the trees have grown, how will they affect the amount of carbon dioxide in the air, and why?
javoblar: They will reduce it, because trees absorb carbon dioxide in photosynthesis and make organic substances.
They will reduce it, because the oxygen released by the trees combines with carbon dioxide and gets rid of it.
They will increase it, because trees release only carbon dioxide when they respire.
They will have no effect, because only seas and oceans can absorb carbon dioxide.

yechim.ovoz: In photosynthesis, green plants make organic substances from carbon dioxide and water.

yechim.doska: The trees absorb $CO_2$ → less $CO_2$ in the air
yechim.ovoz: More trees mean more photosynthesis, so more carbon dioxide is absorbed from the air.

yechim.doska: $O_2$ and $CO_2$ do not cancel each other out
yechim.ovoz: Oxygen does not combine with carbon dioxide and get rid of it; this explanation is wrong.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) They will reduce it: $CO_2$ is absorbed in photosynthesis
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B explained the correct result with the wrong reason: oxygen does not get rid of carbon dioxide.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C considered only respiration and forgot about photosynthesis.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D knew that oceans absorb carbon dioxide but forgot the role of land plants.

variantlar.maslahat: What do trees take from the air for photosynthesis?

kunikma: Understand that mechanical action (hitting, crushing, crumpling) only changes the shape of an object, while the atoms of the substance do not change
usul: A change of shape is a physical change: the shape of the object changes, but the atoms do not split, flatten, disappear, or turn into atoms of another element; only their arrangement can change.

variantlar.savol: A craftsman hammered a copper wire into a flat strip. Which statement about the copper atoms in the wire is correct?
javoblar: The copper atoms broke into tiny pieces.
Some of the copper atoms turned into atoms of another element.
The copper atoms did not change; they are still the same copper atoms.

yechim.doska: Hammering → the shape of the wire changes
yechim.ovoz: When the wire is hammered, only its shape changes: it becomes a flat strip.

yechim.doska: No new substance formed → physical change
yechim.ovoz: The strip is still made of copper and no new substance was formed, so this is a physical change.

yechim.doska: Atoms do not split, flatten, or turn into other atoms
yechim.ovoz: With this kind of action, atoms do not split, flatten, or turn into atoms of another element; only their arrangement changes.

yechim.doska: Answer: D) The copper atoms did not change
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is D.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A transferred a property of the whole object (being flat) to the individual atoms.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought a hard blow breaks atoms; ordinary mechanical action cannot split atoms.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C confused a physical change with a chemical one, and even with one element changing into another.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about what substance the strip is made of after it is formed.

variantlar.savol: Malika crumpled the aluminum foil from a chocolate bar into a small ball. Which statement about the aluminum atoms in the foil is correct?
javoblar: The aluminum atoms were crushed and became smaller.
The aluminum atoms did not change; they are still aluminum atoms.
Some of the aluminum atoms disappeared.
The aluminum atoms joined together into larger atoms.

yechim.doska: Crumpling → the shape of the foil changes
yechim.ovoz: When the foil is crumpled, it takes the shape of a ball; that is, only its shape changes.

yechim.doska: The ball is still aluminum → physical change
yechim.ovoz: The ball is made of the same aluminum; no new substance was formed.

yechim.doska: The number and type of atoms do not change
yechim.ovoz: Atoms do not disappear, shrink, or join together into other atoms; they only change their arrangement.

yechim.doska: Answer: B) The aluminum atoms did not change
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought that because the whole piece of foil got smaller, the atoms got smaller too.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought there was less substance because the ball looks smaller; the mass does not change.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D wrongly imagined that squeezing fuses atoms together.

variantlar.maslahat: What substance is the ball made of, and did its mass change?

kunikma: Identify metals from physical properties in a table (state, appearance, electrical conductivity)
usul: Metals conduct electricity well and have a characteristic metallic luster — check both features together. A shiny substance that does not conduct electricity is not a metal; a colorless or colored solution that conducts electricity is not a metal either; a metal can be liquid at room temperature (mercury).

The table gives some physical properties of five substances (K, L, M, N, P). Two of them are metals.
Which two substances are metals?

variantlar.maslahat: Check whether each substance has both features typical of a metal.

The correct answer is A.

kunikma: Know that burning needs oxygen, and know how to put out a fire by cutting it off from the air
usul: Burning needs three conditions: a fuel, oxygen (air), and a high enough temperature. Putting out a fire removes one of these conditions; if a fire is covered, oxygen from the air cannot reach it.

variantlar.savol:
In the kitchen, the oil in a pot got too hot and caught fire. Mother covered the pot tightly with a lid, and the fire went out.
Why did the fire go out?
javoblar: The lid soaked up the burning oil.
The lid stopped oxygen in the air from reaching the fire.
The lid pressed down on the flame and made it smaller.
The lid instantly cooled the oil to room temperature.

yechim.doska: Conditions for burning: fuel + oxygen + high temperature
yechim.ovoz: Burning needs a fuel, oxygen, and a high temperature.

yechim.doska: The lid is on → no fresh air reaches the fire
yechim.ovoz: When the lid is on, no air can get into the pot, and the little oxygen inside is quickly used up.
Once the oxygen runs out, burning cannot continue and the fire goes out.

yechim.doska: Never pour water on burning oil!
yechim.ovoz: Remember: never pour water on burning oil — the oil will splatter and the fire will get worse; cover it instead.

yechim.doska: Answer: B) Oxygen was cut off
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought the lid absorbs the oil; a metal lid does not soak up anything.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought the flame getting smaller was the cause; in fact, it is a result of the lack of oxygen.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought cooling was the main cause; a lid cannot instantly cool hot oil.

variantlar.maslahat: Which of the three conditions needed for burning is removed when the lid is put on?

variantlar.savol:
Hikers made a campfire in the mountains. Before leaving, they covered the fire with a thick layer of dry sand, and the fire went out.
Why did the sand put out the fire?
javoblar: The sand broke down the burning wood chemically.
The sand itself burned and took away the heat of the fire.
The weight of the sand crushed the flame and made it lower.
The sand cut the burning wood off from the air and kept oxygen from reaching it.

yechim.ovoz: Any burning needs oxygen from the air.

yechim.doska: The layer of sand separates the wood from the air
yechim.ovoz: A thick layer of sand cuts the embers and wood off from the air.

yechim.doska: Oxygen cannot reach it → burning stops
yechim.ovoz: Once oxygen stops coming in, burning stops and the fire goes out.

yechim.doska: Sand does not burn and does not react with wood
yechim.ovoz: Sand does not burn itself and does not break down the wood chemically.

yechim.doska: Answer: D) It kept oxygen from reaching the wood
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is D.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought sand reacts with wood; sand hardly reacts at all under burning conditions.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought sand is a fuel; sand does not burn.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought the flame getting smaller was the main cause; the real cause is the lack of oxygen.

variantlar.maslahat: After the campfire is covered, what stops reaching it from the air?

kunikma: Explain how the expansion of water when it freezes causes solids (rocks, containers, asphalt) to crack
usul: Think about which property can create a force large enough to widen a crack: when water freezes, its volume increases by about 9% and it pushes hard on the sides of a crack or a container; when freezing and thawing repeat many times, the crack gets bigger and bigger.

variantlar.savol:
One winter night, Aziz left a glass jar full of water with a tightly closed lid out in the yard. During the night the air temperature dropped to $-8$ °C. In the morning the jar had cracked.
Which property of water was most responsible for the jar cracking?
javoblar: Water's volume decreases when it cools

yechim.ovoz: Because the temperature was below zero, the water in the jar froze.

yechim.doska: When water freezes, its volume increases by ~9%
yechim.ovoz: When water turns into ice, its volume increases by about nine percent.

yechim.doska: Jar full and closed → ice pushes on the walls
yechim.ovoz: Because the jar was full and closed, there was no room for the expanding ice, so it pushed on the glass walls with great force and the jar cracked.

yechim.doska: Boiling — at 100 °C; dissolving — does not crack glass
yechim.ovoz: No boiling happened here, and water's ability to dissolve substances cannot crack glass.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) Water expands when it freezes
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A picked the best-known property of water, but water does not boil on a cold night.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought the jar cracked because water's volume decreases as it cools; if the volume decreased, the pressure on the walls would not increase — and in fact, the volume increases when water freezes.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D remembered that water dissolves things, but glass does not dissolve in water overnight.

variantlar.maslahat: How does the volume of water change when it turns into ice?

variantlar.savol:
In the fall, small cracks appeared in the asphalt of a mountain road, and rainwater got into them. Throughout the winter, the temperature was below 0 °C at night and above 0 °C during the day. By spring, the cracks had become much wider, and the asphalt began to break into pieces.
Which property of water was most responsible for this?
javoblar: Water is less dense than asphalt
Water is a poor conductor of heat

yechim.doska: Night < 0 °C → water in the cracks freezes
yechim.ovoz: At night the temperature is below zero, and the water in the cracks freezes.

yechim.doska: Freezing increases volume by ~9% → the sides of the crack are pushed apart
yechim.ovoz: When the water freezes, its volume increases by about nine percent, and it pushes the sides of the crack apart and widens it.

yechim.doska: Day > 0 °C → the ice melts, and water gets in even deeper
yechim.ovoz: During the day the ice melts, and the water gets even deeper into the widened crack.

yechim.doska: Freezing and thawing repeat many times → the asphalt breaks up
yechim.ovoz: This process repeats many times over the winter, the cracks grow, and the asphalt breaks into pieces.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) Water expands when it freezes
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought the difference in density was the cause; a difference in density does not create a force that widens cracks.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C remembered water's thermal properties, but they do not break asphalt apart.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought dissolving was the cause; asphalt hardly dissolves in water at all — it is broken up by the expansion of ice.

variantlar.maslahat: What happens to the water in a crack when the temperature keeps changing around zero?

kunikma: Determine and justify whether an object floats or sinks in a liquid by comparing the densities of the object and the liquid
usul: If an object's density is less than the liquid's density, the object floats in the liquid; if it is greater, the object sinks. Compare the densities, not the object's mass or how “light” or “heavy” it is.

variantlar.savol:
An object has a density of $0.8$ g/cm³. There are two liquids:
Liquid 1: density $1.0$ g/cm³
Liquid 2: density $0.7$ g/cm³
In which liquid does the object float, and why?
javoblar: In liquid 2, because the object's density is greater than the density of this liquid.
In liquid 1, because the object's mass is less than the mass of the liquid.
It floats in both liquids, because the object's density is less than 1 g/cm³.
In liquid 1, because the object's density is less than the density of this liquid.

yechim.ovoz: For an object to float in a liquid, its density must be less than the density of the liquid.
Zero point eight is less than one, so the object floats in the first liquid.
Zero point eight is greater than zero point seven, so the object sinks in the second liquid.

yechim.doska: Answer: D) In liquid 1, because the object's density is less
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is D.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A remembered the condition for floating backwards: an object with a greater density sinks.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B found the right liquid but compared mass instead of density — this is the wrong reason.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought you always have to compare with the density of water (1 g/cm³) and did not look at the densities of the given liquids.

variantlar.maslahat: Compare the object's density with the density of each liquid separately.

variantlar.savol:
An object has a density of $1.2$ g/cm³. There are two liquids:
Liquid P: density $1.0$ g/cm³
Liquid Q: density $1.4$ g/cm³
In which liquid does the object float, and why?
javoblar: In liquid Q, because the object's density is less than the density of liquid Q.
In liquid P, because liquid P is lighter and lifts the object easily.
In liquid P, because the object's density is greater than the density of liquid P.
It does not float in either, because the object's density is greater than the density of water.

yechim.ovoz: An object floats only if its density is less than the density of the liquid.
One point two is greater than one, so the object sinks in liquid P.
One point two is less than one point four, so the object floats in liquid Q.
The correct answer is A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought that “a light liquid lifts an object”; in fact, a denser liquid pushes up on an object more strongly.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C remembered the condition for floating backwards: an object denser than the liquid sinks.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D compared only with water and did not take into account that liquid Q has a greater density.

variantlar.maslahat: Compare the object's density with the density of each liquid separately.

kunikma: Know that water at a height has potential energy
usul: An object (or water) raised to some height above the ground has potential energy: the higher it is and the greater its mass, the greater its potential energy ($E_p = mgh$). A moving object has kinetic energy.

variantlar.savol:
The picture shows water flowing down from a tank mounted on a tall stand and turning a wheel.
What kind of energy does the water in the tank have? Write the type of energy in 1–2 words.
variantlar.javob: potential energy|potential|gravitational potential energy|gravitational potential|energy of position

yechim.doska: The water in the tank is raised high above the ground
yechim.ovoz: The tank stands on a tall stand, so the water in it is well above the ground.

yechim.doska: An object raised to a height → potential energy ($E_p = mgh$)
yechim.ovoz: Any object raised to a height has potential energy, equal to the product of its mass, the acceleration due to gravity, and its height.

yechim.doska: The water in the tank is almost still → not kinetic energy
yechim.ovoz: The water in the tank is hardly moving, so we are not talking about kinetic energy here.
The answer is potential energy.

xatolar.umumiy: Many students write “kinetic energy” because they think about the water moving later, even though the water in the tank is still; others write an amount, such as “a lot of energy,” instead of a type of energy.

variantlar.maslahat: Recall what type of energy an object has when it is raised high above the ground.

kunikma: Know that the potential energy of falling water turns into kinetic energy
usul: When water falls from a height, its height decreases and its speed increases: potential energy turns into kinetic energy, the energy of motion ($E_k = \frac{mv^2}{2}$). Water that has reached the bottom and is hitting a wheel or turbine has mainly kinetic energy.

variantlar.savol:
The picture shows water flowing down from a tank mounted on a tall stand and turning a wheel.
What kind of energy does the water have after it has come down, just before it hits the blades of the wheel? Write the type of energy in 1–2 words.
variantlar.javob: kinetic energy|kinetic|energy of motion|kinetic and potential energy|kinetic and potential

yechim.doska: In the tank: water is high up → potential energy
yechim.ovoz: In the tank, the water had potential energy because it was high up.
As the water falls, its height decreases and its speed increases.
So the potential energy turns into the energy of motion, that is, kinetic energy.

yechim.doska: Just before hitting the blades — high speed → kinetic energy
yechim.ovoz: Just before it hits the wheel, the water is moving fast and has kinetic energy.
The answer is kinetic energy.

xatolar.umumiy: Many students repeat the situation in the tank and write “potential energy,” not taking into account that energy is converted as the water falls; some give vague answers such as “mechanical” or “water energy.”

variantlar.maslahat: Think about how the speed of the water changes as it falls.

kunikma: Justify how to make a wheel or turbine spin faster by increasing the energy of the water flow (drop height, flow rate)
usul: The wheel is turned by the kinetic energy of the water hitting it: the greater the height the water falls from and the more water hits it each second, the more energy the wheel receives. Check whether each change increases or decreases these quantities.

variantlar.savol:
The picture shows water flowing down from a tank mounted on a tall stand and turning a wheel.
Which of the following changes should be made to the system so that the wheel spins faster?

Make the outlet hole at the bottom of the tank narrower
Reduce the number of blades on the wheel
Mount the tank on a taller stand

yechim.doska: The wheel is turned by the kinetic energy of the water
yechim.ovoz: The wheel is turned by the kinetic energy of the water hitting it.

yechim.doska: Water falling from higher up → greater speed → more energy
yechim.ovoz: The higher the water falls from, the greater its potential energy, and the faster it moves at the bottom.

yechim.doska: Lowering the tank and narrowing the hole → less energy
yechim.ovoz: Lowering the tank reduces the drop height, and narrowing the hole reduces the amount of water flowing.

yechim.doska: Fewer blades → less water is caught
yechim.ovoz: With fewer blades, the wheel captures less of the water's energy.

yechim.doska: Answer: D) Raise the tank higher
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is D.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought water comes out of a narrow hole “more strongly”; in that case, less water falls each second and the wheel receives less energy.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought that with fewer blades the wheel turns more easily; in fact, there are fewer blades to catch the water.

variantlar.maslahat: What increases the energy of the water hitting the wheel?

kunikma: Know that the holes in volcanic rocks form when gas bubbles are trapped as lava hardens
usul: Lava (magma that has reached the Earth's surface) contains dissolved gases; as the lava cools and hardens, the released gases are trapped as bubbles, and once the rock has hardened, the spaces they occupied remain as empty holes.

variantlar.savol:
Pumice is a very light rock formed from lava erupted by a volcano. It has so many tiny holes that pieces of it often float on water.
How did these holes form?
javoblar: Gas bubbles inside the lava were trapped as it hardened.
River water washed over the rock for many years and opened up holes.
Tiny animals living in the rock dug burrows.
After the lava hardened, the crystals inside it fell out.

yechim.ovoz: Lava contains dissolved gases such as water vapor and carbon dioxide.

yechim.doska: Lava reaches the surface → gases come out as bubbles
yechim.ovoz: When lava reaches the surface, the pressure drops and the gases start to come out, forming bubbles.

yechim.doska: Lava hardens quickly → bubbles are trapped
yechim.ovoz: Because the lava cools and hardens quickly, the bubbles do not have time to escape, and the spaces they leave become empty holes.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) Gas bubbles were trapped
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B confused weathering (the action of water) with the way volcanic rock forms; water washing over rock does not create tiny bubble-like holes inside it.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought the holes were made by living things; no animal can live in hot lava.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought the holes form when crystals fall out; the holes in pumice are traces of round gas bubbles.

variantlar.maslahat: Recall what appears when you open a bottle of fizzy drink — something similar happens in lava.

variantlar.savol:
A piece of basalt taken from a hardened lava flow on the slope of a volcano has many round holes in it.
How did these holes form?
javoblar: Hailstones fell on the lava while it was still soft and left marks.
Sand grains blown by the wind drilled through the rock.
Gases released from the liquid lava formed bubbles, and when the lava hardened, the spaces left by the bubbles stayed empty.
As the rock cooled and hardened, water in it froze, then melted and drained away.

yechim.ovoz: Liquid lava contains dissolved gases.

yechim.doska: The gases come out and form bubbles
yechim.ovoz: As the lava flows and cools, the gases come out and form bubbles inside it.

yechim.doska: Lava hardens → the spaces left by bubbles remain as holes
yechim.ovoz: When the lava hardens, the bubbles are trapped inside, and round holes can be seen in the rock.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) The spaces left by gas bubbles stayed empty
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought the holes were marks left by things falling on the surface; hail falling on hot lava would melt immediately, and there are holes inside the rock too.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought wind erosion caused the holes; wind smooths the surface but does not create round bubbles inside the rock.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought freezing was the cause; the temperature of hardening lava is very high, so water cannot freeze in it.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about what substance could be inside liquid lava before it hardens.

kunikma: Justify how fossils (of the same land organisms) serve as evidence that the continents were once joined
usul: Ask yourself whether the organism could cross the ocean on its own: if fossils of the same age from an organism that cannot fly and cannot swim in the sea are found on two continents, the continents were joined at that time.

variantlar.savol:
Mesosaurus was a reptile that lived about 280 million years ago and was about 1 meter long. Scientists think it lived in the shallow waters of lakes and coasts and could not swim across a wide, open ocean.
Its fossils have been found in rocks of the same age in South America and Africa, which are now separated by the Atlantic Ocean.
What conclusion can be drawn from this observation?
javoblar: When Mesosaurus lived, these two continents were joined to each other.
Mesosaurs swam across the Atlantic Ocean and migrated to the other continent.
Mesosaurs appeared separately on the two continents, independently of each other.
Ocean waves carried Mesosaurus fossils from one continent to the other.

yechim.doska: Mesosaurus: lived in shallow water, could not swim across the ocean
yechim.ovoz: First, let's pick out the key information in the problem: this animal could not cross a wide ocean.

yechim.doska: Fossils: South America + Africa, rocks of the same age
yechim.ovoz: Even so, its fossils have been found on two continents that are separated by an ocean today.

yechim.doska: Crossing the ocean ✗  ⇒  the continents were joined
yechim.ovoz: If the animal could not cross the ocean, then at that time there was no ocean between the two continents; they were one connected landmass.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) the continents were joined
yechim.ovoz: So the correct conclusion is option A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B ignored the important information in the problem: it "could not swim across a wide, open ocean."
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought that the same species could appear separately in two places; a species appears in only one place and then spreads.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought the fossils were moved later; in fact, on both continents they lie inside rocks of the same age, which means the animal lived in those places.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about how the animal could have gotten from one continent to the other.

variantlar.savol:
Malika, a scientist, is testing the idea that two continents now separated by an ocean were once a single landmass.
Which of the following observations supports this idea MOST STRONGLY?
javoblar: Swallows of the same species build nests on both continents today.
Fish of the same species live in the waters near the coasts of both continents.
Fossils of the same land plant, whose heavy seeds are not carried far by wind or water, have been found in rocks of the same age on both continents.
Active volcanoes and earthquakes occur on both continents.

yechim.doska: Condition for evidence: the organism must not be able to cross the ocean on its own
yechim.ovoz: Only organisms that cannot cross an ocean can prove that the continents were joined.

yechim.doska: A: birds fly ✗;  B: fish swim ✗
yechim.ovoz: Swallows can fly and fish can swim from one continent to another, so they are not evidence.

yechim.doska: D: volcanoes are found in many places ✗
yechim.ovoz: Volcanoes and earthquakes also occur in many regions that were never joined to each other.

yechim.doska: C: land plant with heavy seeds, fossils of the same age ✓
yechim.ovoz: If fossils of a plant whose seeds cannot cross the ocean are found on both continents, then the continents were joined at that time.
The correct answer is option C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A did not consider that birds can fly across the ocean; besides, this is a present-day observation, not ancient evidence.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B did not take into account that fish swim freely in ocean water and can move between continents.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought volcanoes showed that the continents were similar, but volcanoes exist in many parts of the world and do not prove the continents were joined.

variantlar.maslahat: Find the organism that cannot cross the ocean by itself.

kunikma: Apply the advantage of terrace (stepped) farming on mountain slopes in protecting soil from erosion
usul: Remember that on sloping land, rainwater flows quickly and washes the soil away; terraces divide the slope into horizontal steps, slowing the flow of water and letting it soak into the soil.

variantlar.savol:
The picture shows an orchard laid out in terraces (steps) on a mountain slope in the Fergana Valley.
What is the MAIN advantage of this method?
javoblar: The steps shade the plants from sunlight and protect them from scorching.
On the steps, plants can grow without any watering at all.
Rainwater flows slowly on the steps and soaks into the soil, so the soil is not washed away.
The steps always keep the soil fertile, even without fertilizer.

yechim.doska: Sloping hillside: rainwater flows fast → soil is washed away (erosion)
yechim.ovoz: On ordinary sloping land, rainwater runs downhill quickly and carries away the fertile topsoil.
A terrace divides the slope into flat steps, and each step holds back water.

yechim.doska: Water flow slows down and soaks into the soil → less erosion
yechim.ovoz: Because the water flows slowly, it soaks into the soil and the soil is not washed away.
So the main advantage is option C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought that terraces shade the plants; in fact, the steps do not block the light.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B stretched the idea that "water is held back" too far; a terrace saves water, but it does not completely remove the need for watering.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D confused protecting the soil with making the soil fertile; a terrace does not add minerals by itself.

variantlar.maslahat: Imagine what happens to the soil on sloping land after heavy rain.

variantlar.savol:
Jasur's grandfather planted almond trees on two mountain slopes with the same steepness. He left slope 1 as it was, and on slope 2 he built terraces (steps) (see the picture).
After heavy spring downpours, which statement about the two slopes is correct?
javoblar: Less soil is washed off slope 1, because water runs off it quickly.
Less soil is washed off slope 2, because on the steps the water slows down and soaks into the soil.
The same amount of soil is washed off both, because they are equally steep.
More soil is washed off slope 2, because water collects on the steps.

yechim.doska: Same steepness; the difference is the terraces
yechim.ovoz: The two slopes differ in only one way: slope 2 has steps.

yechim.doska: Slope 1: water flows fast → carries soil away
yechim.ovoz: On a slope without terraces, water speeds up and washes away the topsoil.

yechim.doska: Slope 2: water slows down on the steps → soaks into the soil
yechim.ovoz: On the steps, water flows with stops and starts, much of it soaks into the soil, and the soil is not washed away.
So the correct answer is option B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought that fast-flowing water is helpful; in fact, fast-flowing water washes away more soil.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C looked only at the overall steepness and did not consider that terraces slow down the flow of water.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought that water collected on the steps washes the soil away; still water does not carry soil away, it soaks into it.

variantlar.maslahat: Compare where water flows faster and what fast-flowing water does to the soil.

kunikma: Read a graph of how the pulse (breathing rate) changes after exercise and choose the conclusion that matches the data
usul: Check each option against the graph separately: read values at exact points, and count the time it takes to rise and to fall in minutes.

variantlar.savol:
Malika's resting pulse is 75 beats per minute. She ran for 2 minutes, then measured her pulse every minute and drew a graph. The shaded part is the running time.
What conclusion can be drawn from the results?
javoblar: Her pulse increased by 130 beats per minute.
After she stopped running, her pulse returned to its starting value in 4 minutes.
At minute 3, her pulse was 90 beats per minute.
Her pulse took less time to fall than it took to rise.

yechim.ovoz: We read from the graph: at the start the pulse is 75, and at the end of the run it is 130 beats.
So the pulse increased by 55 beats, not by 130; this took 2 minutes.
The point at minute three is at 110, and 90 belongs to minute four.
The pulse dropped back to 75 at minute six, that is, 4 minutes after the run ended; this is longer than the time it took to rise.
So the correct conclusion is option B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A took the highest value (130) as the change; in fact, the change is $130 - 75 = 55$ beats.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C read the points shifted by one minute: 90 beats corresponds to minute 4, while at minute 3 it is 110.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D compared the times incorrectly: the rise lasted 2 minutes, and the fall lasted 4 minutes.

variantlar.maslahat: Compare the number in each option with the matching point on the graph.

His breathing rate took more time to rise than it took to fall.
At minute 3, his breathing rate was 28 breaths per minute.
After the exercise ended, his breathing rate returned to its starting value in less than 5 minutes.

yechim.ovoz: We read from the graph: 16 at the start and 34 breaths at the end of the exercise.
So the breathing rate increased by 18, and this took 1 minute.
Twenty-eight belongs to minute two, and at minute three it is 22 breaths.

yechim.doska: Back to 16 at minute 5:  $5 - 1 = 4$ minutes $< 5$ minutes
yechim.ovoz: At minute five it returned to 16, that is, 4 minutes after the exercise, which is less than 5 minutes.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B compared the times the wrong way around: the rise lasted 1 minute, and the fall lasted 4 minutes.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C read the point from one minute earlier: 28 is the value at minute 2.

kunikma: Know that life on Earth first appeared in water in the form of single-celled organisms
usul: Remember the order in which life developed in Earth's history: simple single-celled organisms first appeared in water, and organisms moved onto land much later.

variantlar.savol: Which of the following groups of organisms appeared EARLIEST in Earth's history?
javoblar: Flowering plants that grow on land
Single-celled organisms that live in water

yechim.ovoz: Life on Earth first appeared in water and moved onto land much later.

yechim.doska: The very first: single-celled organisms (in water)
yechim.ovoz: The oldest living organisms were simple single-celled organisms that lived in water.
Reptiles, mammals, and flowering plants appeared hundreds of millions of years after them.
So the correct answer is option D.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought flowering plants were the oldest because plants appeared before animals; flowering plants appeared relatively recently.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought of reptiles as "ancient" animals, but for a long time before them there were only organisms that lived in water.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C did not know the order in which animals appeared; mammals appeared even later than reptiles.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about how the first organisms were built and where they could have lived.

variantlar.savol:
Scientists have found the oldest traces of life on Earth: layered rock structures formed by single-celled organisms billions of years ago.
Where did these first organisms live?
javoblar: In a dry desert, among the sand
In water, in shallow seas and lakes
In the soil of high mountains
In the air, on dust particles

yechim.doska: Oldest traces of life: single-celled organisms
yechim.ovoz: As the problem says, the oldest organisms were single-celled.

yechim.doska: At that time there was no life on land
yechim.ovoz: In that period there were no plants or animals on land; even soil had not yet formed.

yechim.doska: Environment of the first life: water
yechim.ovoz: The first organisms appeared and lived in water, and such rock structures formed in shallow water.
So the correct answer is option B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought the organisms lived on land because the rocks were found on land; the rock layers formed under water long ago.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought soil had always existed; soil formed after life appeared on land.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought an organism could live permanently in the air; no organism spends its entire life in the air.

variantlar.maslahat: Imagine what the land was like when life first appeared.

kunikma: Apply the idea of competition between crops and weeds for water, minerals, and light to explain a situation
usul: Remember what plants need to grow (water, minerals, light), and think about how plants growing in the same place share these limited resources.

variantlar.savol:
Nilufar planted tomato seedlings in her garden plot. A few weeks later, weeds grew up among the seedlings.
Why is it important to pull out the weeds?
javoblar: The weeds eat the tomato fruits.
The weeds compete with the tomatoes for water and minerals in the soil and for sunlight.
The weeds add too many minerals to the soil and poison the tomatoes.
The weeds take in all the air that the tomatoes need.

yechim.doska: A plant needs: water, minerals, light
yechim.ovoz: Every green plant needs water, minerals, and sunlight to grow.
Weeds also take up water and minerals from the same soil and block light with their leaves.

yechim.doska: Limited resources → competition → tomatoes get less
yechim.ovoz: Because resources are limited, there is competition between them, and less is left for the tomatoes.
So the correct answer is option B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought plants feed like animals; green plants do not eat other plants.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought weeds add minerals to the soil; in fact, they take minerals from the soil.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought the gases in the air could run out in an open field; there is enough air in a field, and the limited resources are water, minerals, and light.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about which things both the tomatoes and the weeds need in order to grow.

variantlar.savol:
Jasur, a farmer, regularly pulled the weeds in one part of his cotton field but not in the other part. All other conditions were the same. In the fall, the part where the weeds were not pulled gave a much smaller cotton harvest.
Which is the BEST explanation for this?
javoblar: The weeds took the chlorophyll from the cotton plants' leaves.
The weeds ate the cotton bolls.
The harvest increased in the weeded part because the soil there got warmer.
The weeds competed with the cotton plants for water, minerals, and light, leaving fewer resources for the cotton.

yechim.ovoz: In the experiment, the two parts differ only in the weeds, so that is where the cause lies.

yechim.doska: Cotton and weeds: water, minerals, light
yechim.ovoz: Both the cotton and the weeds need the same resources.

yechim.doska: Competition → fewer resources for cotton → smaller harvest
yechim.ovoz: They competed for these resources, the cotton got less, and the harvest decreased.
So the best explanation is option D.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought chlorophyll can pass from one plant to another; each plant makes its own chlorophyll.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B confused weeds with pest animals; plants do not eat other plants.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C made up a cause that is not stated in the problem; according to the problem, all other conditions were the same.

variantlar.maslahat: Pay attention to how the two parts in the experiment differed.

kunikma: Know that even a single-celled organism carries out life processes such as excretion, respiration, and reproduction, in addition to feeding
usul: Recall the life processes common to all living organisms, and use the organism's structure (does it have chloroplasts, lungs, roots?) to choose the process that fits it.

variantlar.savol:
The picture shows a single-celled organism, the common amoeba. To live, the amoeba feeds: it takes in food and digests it.
Which other life process MUST the amoeba carry out to live?

Removing excess water and waste substances from the cell (excretion)
Absorbing water from the soil through roots

yechim.doska: Amoeba: nucleus, food vacuole, contractile vacuole, pseudopod
yechim.ovoz: Let's look at the parts of the amoeba in the picture: it has no chloroplasts, lungs, or roots.
It has no chloroplasts, so it does not photosynthesize; it is a single cell, so it cannot have lungs or roots.

yechim.doska: Contractile vacuole → removes excess water and waste
yechim.ovoz: Every living organism must get rid of waste substances; in the amoeba, this is done by the contractile vacuole and the cell surface.
So the correct answer is option C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought all single-celled organisms photosynthesize; the amoeba has no chloroplasts and feeds on ready-made food.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B linked respiration only with lungs; the amoeba takes in oxygen through the whole surface of its cell.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D confused the amoeba with a plant; only plants have roots.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about which part in the picture serves to remove something from the cell.

variantlar.savol:
The picture shows a single-celled fungus, a yeast cell (used to make bread dough rise). To live, yeast absorbs sugar as food through its cell surface and gets energy from it.
Which other life process MUST yeast carry out so that the species does not die out?
