kunikma: Know the chemical formula of a common substance from its name
usul: From the name of the substance, determine which elements it contains and how many atoms of each element there are (pay attention to parts of the name such as “(II)” and “di-” and to valence), then choose the formula that matches that composition.

variantlar.savol: What is the chemical formula of carbon monoxide, carbon(II) oxide?

yechim.doska: Carbon(II) oxide: elements — C and O
yechim.ovoz: From the name, we know the substance is made of carbon and oxygen.

yechim.doska: (II) — the valence of carbon is 2, and oxygen's is also 2
yechim.ovoz: The Roman numeral two shows the valence of carbon; oxygen always has a valence of two.
Since the valences are equal, there is one oxygen atom for each carbon atom.
So the formula of carbon monoxide is C O.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B confused carbon(II) oxide with carbon dioxide, which is carbon(IV) oxide.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C put the subscript on the wrong atom; this composition does not match a carbon valence of two.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D focused on the word “oxygen” in the oxide's name and chose just an oxygen molecule, which contains no carbon.

variantlar.maslahat: Remember that the Roman numeral in the name shows the valence of carbon.

variantlar.savol: What is the chemical formula of table salt, sodium chloride?

yechim.doska: Sodium chloride: elements — Na (sodium) and Cl (chlorine)
yechim.ovoz: From the name, we find that the substance is made of sodium and chlorine.

yechim.doska: Sodium has a valence of 1; in a chloride, chlorine has a valence of 1
yechim.ovoz: Sodium is a metal with a valence of one, and chlorine has a valence of one in chlorides.
The valences are equal, so there is one chlorine atom for each sodium atom.
So the formula of table salt is N a C l.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought sodium has a valence of two; sodium has a valence of one, so one chlorine atom is enough.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B put a subscript on sodium; when the valences are equal, no subscript is needed.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C confused the symbol for sodium with potassium (K); Na is sodium, K is potassium.

variantlar.maslahat: Compare the valences of sodium and chlorine.

kunikma: Recognize an organelle in a drawing of a plant cell by its appearance and identify its function
usul: First identify the part marked X by its shape and position (nucleus — round, with a nucleolus inside; chloroplast — oval and green; vacuole — large, filled with cell sap; cell wall — thick outer layer), then recall the function of that organelle.

variantlar.savol:
The picture shows a plant cell.
What is the function of the part of the cell marked X?
javoblar: It controls the cell's processes and stores hereditary information.
It stores cell sap — water and dissolved substances.
It uses energy from sunlight to make organic substances.
It gives the cell strength and keeps its shape.

yechim.doska: X — a round body with a dark nucleolus inside
yechim.ovoz: The part marked X is round, with a small dark body inside it — the nucleolus.
A round structure with a nucleolus is the cell nucleus.
The nucleus contains chromosomes, which carry hereditary information.

yechim.doska: The nucleus controls the life processes in the cell
yechim.ovoz: That is why the nucleus is considered the cell's control center.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) It controls the cell's processes and stores hereditary information.
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought X was the vacuole; the vacuole is the largest space in the middle of the cell and has no nucleolus.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C confused X with a chloroplast; chloroplasts are small, oval, and green, with no nucleolus inside.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought X was the cell wall; the wall is the thick outer layer of the cell, while X is inside it.

variantlar.maslahat: Pay attention to the dark body inside the part marked X.

variantlar.savol:
The picture shows a plant cell.
What is the function of the part of the cell marked X?
javoblar: It controls the cell's processes and stores hereditary information.
It gives the cell strength and keeps its shape.
It stores cell sap — water and dissolved substances.
It uses energy from sunlight to make organic substances.

yechim.doska: X — a small oval body; the cell has many such bodies
yechim.ovoz: The part marked X is small and oval, and there are several of them in the cell.

yechim.doska: This is a chloroplast (a green plastid)
yechim.ovoz: Such small bodies with layers inside are chloroplasts.

yechim.doska: A chloroplast contains chlorophyll, which absorbs light
yechim.ovoz: The green pigment in the chloroplast, chlorophyll, absorbs sunlight.

yechim.doska: Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
yechim.ovoz: Using light energy, the chloroplast makes an organic substance, glucose, from carbon dioxide and water.

yechim.doska: Answer: D) It uses energy from sunlight to make organic substances.
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is D.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A confused X with the nucleus; there is only one nucleus, it is larger, and it has a nucleolus inside.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought X was the cell wall because it lies close to it; the wall is the thick layer that surrounds the whole cell.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought X was the vacuole; the vacuole is the largest part, in the middle of the cell.

variantlar.maslahat: Notice how many of these small oval bodies the cell has, and that they are found only in plants.

kunikma: Identify organs that perform the same function (gas exchange) in different organisms
usul: First determine the function of the given organ (the lungs): gas exchange — taking in oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide. Then recall which organ performs this function in the other organism.

variantlar.savol: An earthworm has no lungs. Which of its organs performs a function similar to that of human lungs?

yechim.doska: Function of the lungs — gas exchange: $\mathrm{O_2}$ in, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ out
yechim.ovoz: In humans, oxygen passes into the blood through the lungs, and carbon dioxide is removed from it.

yechim.doska: An earthworm has no special breathing organ
yechim.ovoz: An earthworm has neither lungs nor gills.

yechim.doska: Its skin is thin and always moist, with many blood vessels underneath
yechim.ovoz: An earthworm's skin is kept moist by mucus, and blood capillaries are densely packed beneath it.

yechim.doska: Oxygen passes into the blood through the moist skin → the skin breathes
yechim.ovoz: Gases pass into the blood through the moist skin, which means the earthworm breathes through its whole body surface.
So in the earthworm, the skin does the job of the lungs.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A confused the intestine passing nutrients into the blood with gas exchange; the intestine is a digestive organ.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C confused the nervous system, which controls breathing, with a breathing organ.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought of “removing unneeded substances from the body” and confused releasing carbon dioxide with excretion.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about why earthworms come to the surface after rain and why their skin is always moist.

variantlar.savol: Which structure of a grasshopper performs a function similar to that of a bird's lungs?

yechim.doska: Function of the lungs — gas exchange: taking in $\mathrm{O_2}$, releasing $\mathrm{CO_2}$
yechim.ovoz: In a bird, the lungs take oxygen from the air and release carbon dioxide.
Insects such as grasshoppers have no lungs.

yechim.doska: Small openings on the sides of the body (spiracles) → tracheae
yechim.ovoz: Air enters through the breathing openings on the sides of the body into branching tubes called tracheae.

yechim.doska: The tracheae deliver oxygen directly to the cells
yechim.ovoz: The tracheae branch throughout the whole body, delivering oxygen to the tissues and carrying carbon dioxide away.
So in the grasshopper, the tracheae do the job of a bird's lungs.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought Malpighian tubules are breathing organs; they are the excretory organs of insects.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought the wings breathe because they work with air; wings are used for flying.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D confused transporting gases with gas exchange; an insect's heart pumps hemolymph and does not carry out gas exchange.

variantlar.maslahat: Recall where the tiny openings on the sides of an insect's body lead.

kunikma: Know the overall equation of cellular respiration (starting substances and products)
usul: In respiration, the cell breaks down glucose using oxygen to get energy, and carbon dioxide and water are formed as products. Remember that the photosynthesis equation is the reverse of this, and do not confuse them.

variantlar.savol: Which of the following equations correctly represents cellular respiration?
javoblar: carbon dioxide + water + energy → glucose + oxygen
glucose + carbon dioxide → oxygen + water + energy
glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
oxygen + water → glucose + carbon dioxide + energy

yechim.doska: Respiration — breaking down glucose using oxygen
yechim.ovoz: To get energy, the cell breaks down glucose in the presence of oxygen.
So glucose and oxygen must be on the left side of the equation.
As a result, carbon dioxide, water, and energy that the cell uses are produced.

yechim.doska: A — the photosynthesis equation (the reverse process)
yechim.ovoz: The equation in option A represents photosynthesis, which is the reverse of respiration.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
yechim.ovoz: So the respiration equation is option C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A confused respiration with photosynthesis; this equation shows how green plants make organic substances.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B swapped oxygen and carbon dioxide: in respiration oxygen is used up, and carbon dioxide is released.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought glucose is produced in respiration; in fact, glucose is used up in respiration.

variantlar.maslahat: Remember which gas we take in and which gas we breathe out.

variantlar.savol: Which two substances are used up (react) in cellular respiration?

yechim.doska: Respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
yechim.ovoz: First, let's write the overall equation of respiration.

yechim.doska: Left side — substances that are used up
yechim.ovoz: The substances to the left of the arrow react, that is, they are used up.
So the cell uses up glucose and oxygen.

yechim.doska: Carbon dioxide and water are products
yechim.ovoz: Carbon dioxide and water, on the other hand, are produced by the process.
So the correct answer is A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B wrote the substances used up in photosynthesis; in respiration, carbon dioxide and water are produced.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought carbon dioxide is used up; in respiration it is released.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D got oxygen right but forgot the energy source, glucose; water is produced in respiration.

variantlar.maslahat: Recall which substance the cell gets its energy from and which gas it needs to do this.

kunikma: Recognize a neutralization reaction, in which an acid and a base react and the color of an indicator changes
usul: An indicator shows by its color whether a solution is acidic or alkaline. If the color changes when a base is added to an acid (or an acid to a base), they have neutralized each other — this is a neutralization reaction.

variantlar.savol:
Dilnoza added a few drops of phenolphthalein to limewater (calcium hydroxide solution), and the solution turned deep pink. Then she added hydrochloric acid drop by drop, and the pink color disappeared.
What process took place?

yechim.doska: Phenolphthalein is pink in an alkaline solution
yechim.ovoz: Phenolphthalein turns pink in an alkali, so limewater is an alkali.
Dilnoza added an acid to an alkali.
An acid and a base react to form a salt and water; the alkali is used up, and the solution becomes neutral.

yechim.doska: The alkali is used up → phenolphthalein becomes colorless
yechim.ovoz: Because no alkali is left, the indicator became colorless.
So this is a neutralization reaction.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B took the disappearing color to mean the substance had dissolved; melting is when a solid turns into a liquid on heating.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought the color “flew away”; in evaporation a liquid turns into a gas, and the color of the indicator does not change.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D called every chemical change rusting; rusting is the corrosion of iron caused by moisture and oxygen.

variantlar.maslahat: Compare the kind of solution in which phenolphthalein is pink with the substance Dilnoza added.

variantlar.savol:
When a person has too much acid in the stomach, a doctor recommends taking a medicine containing magnesium hydroxide. This medicine reacts with the excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach and reduces its effect.
What process takes place?

yechim.ovoz: The stomach contents are acidic; they contain hydrochloric acid.
The medicine contains a base, magnesium hydroxide.
The base reacts with the acid to form a salt, magnesium chloride, and water.
The reaction of an acid with a base to form a salt and water is called neutralization.
So the medicine neutralizes the acid.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A took the phrase that the acid “disappears” to mean it evaporates; acid in the stomach does not evaporate, it takes part in a chemical reaction.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought every chemical reaction is combustion; combustion is a substance combining with oxygen, giving off flame and heat.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D chose a method for separating mixtures; distillation is purifying a liquid by evaporating it and then cooling it, and it is not a chemical reaction.

variantlar.maslahat: Determine whether the substance in the medicine is an acid or a base.

kunikma: Use data from a graph to draw a conclusion about how the amount of carbon dioxide affects the rate of photosynthesis, and justify it scientifically
usul: Compare the two lines at the same light intensity: is the rate higher when there is more carbon dioxide? Then explain this using the fact that carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis.

variantlar.savol:
Kamola studied how light intensity and the amount of carbon dioxide affect the rate of photosynthesis. She placed two identical plants in closed glass containers: the air in the first container had 0.10% carbon dioxide, and the air in the second had 0.04%. She measured the rate of photosynthesis in each plant at different light intensities and showed the results on a graph.
Does an increase in the amount of carbon dioxide affect the rate of photosynthesis? Choose the answer that matches the graph and is correctly justified.
javoblar: No, it does not: both lines rise as light increases, so only light determines the rate.
Yes, it does: when there is more carbon dioxide, photosynthesis slows down, because this gas is harmful to the plant.
Yes, it does: at the same light intensity, photosynthesis is faster in the container with more carbon dioxide, because carbon dioxide is a raw material needed for photosynthesis.
No, it does not: in weak light the two lines are close together, so the difference is due to chance.

yechim.ovoz: Let's take the same light intensity, for example three units: in the container with more carbon dioxide the rate is about 1.1, and in the one with less it is about 0.5.

yechim.doska: At every light intensity, the 0.10% line is higher
yechim.ovoz: Across the whole graph, the line for more carbon dioxide is on top.

yechim.doska: Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
yechim.ovoz: Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis; it is used up to make glucose.
That is why photosynthesis goes faster when there is more carbon dioxide.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) Yes, it does: … carbon dioxide is a raw material needed for photosynthesis
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A looked only at the shape of the lines and did not compare the difference between the two lines at the same light intensity.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B read the graph the wrong way round and thought carbon dioxide is a harmful gas; for a plant, it is a raw material for photosynthesis.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D looked only at the start of the graph; as light increases, the gap between the lines clearly gets bigger.

variantlar.maslahat: Pick one light intensity on the graph and compare the values of the two lines.

variantlar.savol:
Jasur did an experiment with the water plant elodea. He put two identical elodea shoots in containers of water: he added a little baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) to the water in the first container and left plain water in the second. At different light intensities, he counted the oxygen bubbles released by each shoot in 1 minute and showed the results on a graph.
According to the graph, how does adding soda to the water affect the rate of photosynthesis, and why?
javoblar: It has no effect, because soda only changes the taste of the water.
It slows it down, because fewer bubbles are released in the water with soda.
It speeds it up, because soda gives the plant extra light energy.
It speeds it up, because soda is a source of carbon dioxide in the water, and carbon dioxide is needed for photosynthesis.

yechim.doska: The bubbles are oxygen released in photosynthesis
yechim.ovoz: The more bubbles there are, the faster photosynthesis is going.

yechim.doska: Light 3 units: with soda ≈ 26, in plain water ≈ 11
yechim.ovoz: At the same light intensity, for example three units, there are about twenty-six bubbles in the water with soda and about eleven in plain water.

yechim.doska: The container with soda always has more bubbles → faster photosynthesis
yechim.ovoz: At every light intensity, the line for the water with soda is higher.

yechim.doska: Soda (sodium bicarbonate) provides carbon dioxide to the water
yechim.ovoz: In water, baking soda is a source of carbon dioxide that the plant can use, and carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis.

yechim.doska: Answer: D) It speeds it up … carbon dioxide is needed for photosynthesis
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is D.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A did not look at the graph; the graph shows there are many more bubbles in the water with soda.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B mixed up the lines on the graph and read it the wrong way round.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C drew the right conclusion but gave the wrong reason: soda does not provide light energy; it is a source of carbon dioxide.

variantlar.maslahat: Recall which substances are needed for photosynthesis and think about which one soda provides.

kunikma: Decide how to measure the quantity being studied in an experiment (magnet strength), distinguishing the variable being changed from the result being measured
usul: Separate the factor being changed in the experiment (for example, the type of magnet or the number of turns) from the result being measured: the strength of a magnet is measured by its effect, that is, by the result of what it does.

variantlar.savol:
Jasur wants to compare the strength of different electromagnets. Each electromagnet has a different number of turns of wire. He lowers each electromagnet into a box of iron nails and then lifts it.
In this experiment, how is the strength of an electromagnet determined?
javoblar: by the number of turns on the electromagnet
by the number of nails the electromagnet can lift
by the length of the electromagnet's wire
by the length of the nails

yechim.doska: Factor being changed: number of turns
yechim.ovoz: Jasur's electromagnets differ from one another in the number of turns — this is the factor he is changing.

yechim.doska: Result being measured: how strongly the magnet attracts
yechim.ovoz: What we need is a result that shows how strong the electromagnet is.
The stronger the electromagnet, the more nails it can lift.
So we determine strength by counting the number of nails lifted.

yechim.doska: Answer: B) by the number of nails the electromagnet can lift
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A confused the factor being changed in the experiment with the result being measured; the number of turns affects the strength, but it is not a measure of strength.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C chose another quantity related to how the electromagnet is built; the length of the wire does not show how strongly the magnet attracts.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D chose the size of the nails; the same nails are used for all the electromagnets, so they do not show the strength.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about how a strong and a weak electromagnet would give different results in the experiment.

variantlar.savol:
Aziz wants to test the strength of different permanent magnets. His magnets have different sizes, shapes, and masses. He slowly moves each magnet toward a steel ball resting on a table and measures the distance at the moment the ball starts to move toward the magnet.
In this experiment, how is the strength of a magnet determined?
javoblar: by the size of the magnet
by the mass of the magnet
by the distance between the magnet and the ball when the ball starts to move
by the mass of the steel ball

yechim.doska: The magnets differ in size, shape, and mass
yechim.ovoz: These features describe the magnets themselves, but they do not directly show how strong they are.

yechim.doska: Result being measured: the distance at which the ball moves
yechim.ovoz: For each magnet, Aziz measures the distance at which the ball starts to move.

yechim.doska: A strong magnet attracts the ball from farther away
yechim.ovoz: The stronger the magnet, the greater the distance from which it can move the ball.

yechim.doska: Strength = distance at which the ball starts to move (greater distance → stronger magnet)
yechim.ovoz: So the strength of the magnet is determined by this distance.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) by the distance when the ball starts to move
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought a big magnet is always strong; a small magnet can also be strong, and strength is determined by the result of the experiment.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought a heavier magnet is stronger; mass does not show a magnet's strength.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D chose a property of the ball, which is the same for all the magnets; it does not distinguish between the magnets.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about what you could measure in the experiment that would show a difference between a strong and a weak magnet.

kunikma: Choose the right experiment (investigation) plan to find out whether a trait is inherited (a difference between varieties) or the result of growing conditions or ripening
usul: Choose a plan in which both samples being tested are grown under the same conditions, only one factor differs, and the result can be observed; plans in which two factors change at once or there is no comparison do not answer the question.

variantlar.savol:
Dilnoza and Bobur bought yellow and red tomatoes at the bazaar. They know that traits such as fruit color are passed from parents to offspring (are inherited).
Dilnoza said, “These are two different varieties — yellow tomatoes stay yellow even when they are ripe.”
Bobur said, “It's the same variety; the yellow tomatoes just aren't fully ripe yet. If they stayed on the vine, they would turn red.”
Which experiment would help find out who is right?
javoblar: Plant only seeds from the red tomato and see what color its fruit is
Plant seeds from the yellow and the red tomatoes under the same conditions, leave the fruit on the vine without picking it until it is fully ripe, and observe its color
Plant the yellow tomato seeds in a sunny spot and the red tomato seeds in a shady spot, and compare the color of the fruit
Cut both tomatoes open, count the seeds inside, and compare

yechim.doska: Question: is the yellow color a trait of the variety or a sign of unripeness?
yechim.ovoz: First, let's decide what we are testing: does a yellow tomato stay yellow even when it is fully ripe?

yechim.doska: Yellow seeds ↔ red seeds, same conditions
yechim.ovoz: To do this, we plant both kinds of seeds and give them the same soil, water, and light.

yechim.doska: The fruit stays on the vine until fully ripe → its color is observed
yechim.ovoz: We do not pick the fruit early; we wait until it is fully ripe and look at its color.

yechim.doska: If it stays yellow, Dilnoza is right; if it turns red, Bobur is right
yechim.ovoz: The result shows who is right: if the ripe fruit stays yellow, it is a different variety; if it turns red, it was just unripe.

yechim.doska: Answer: B) Plant seeds from the yellow and the red tomatoes under the same conditions, leave the fruit on the vine without picking it until it is fully ripe, and observe its color
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought it was enough to check that a red tomato produces red fruit; but the argument is about the yellow tomato, and without planting it the question cannot be answered.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C understood that both kinds of seeds must be planted but made the conditions different; then you cannot tell whether the color difference comes from the variety or from the light.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought it was enough to measure any difference between the tomatoes; the number of seeds does not show what color the fruit turns when it ripens.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about whether both kinds of tomatoes must take part in the experiment and whether their conditions must be the same.

variantlar.savol:
Malika and Jasur saw sunflowers growing in two neighboring fields: the sunflowers in the first field were about 2 m tall, and those in the second were about 1 m tall.
Malika said, “These are two different varieties — height is an inherited trait.”
Jasur said, “It's the same variety; the fields just have different soil and watering.”
Which experiment would help find out who is right?
javoblar: Plant seeds from the tall sunflowers in fertile soil and seeds from the short sunflowers in poor soil, and compare their heights
Measure the heights of the sunflowers in both fields again a month later
Plant only seeds from the tall sunflowers and see whether even taller plants grow
Take seeds from both fields, plant them in the same soil at the same time, water them the same way, and compare their heights once they are fully grown

yechim.doska: Question: is the height difference inherited or caused by conditions?
yechim.ovoz: First, let's state the question to be tested: do the sunflowers differ because of their variety or because of their conditions?
In the experiment, only one thing should differ: which field the seeds came from.

yechim.doska: Soil, water, planting time — the same
yechim.ovoz: We keep all the other conditions the same; otherwise the result cannot be explained.

yechim.doska: Again 2 m and 1 m → Malika is right; same height → Jasur is right
yechim.ovoz: If the difference remains even under the same conditions, the varieties are different; if the difference disappears, the cause was the conditions.

yechim.doska: Answer: D) Take seeds from both fields, plant them in the same soil at the same time, water them the same way, and compare their heights once they are fully grown
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option D.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A correctly chose to plant both kinds of seeds but also made the soil different; now you cannot separate whether the height difference comes from the variety or from the soil.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought measuring again would give new information; but the conditions stay the same, so the cause cannot be determined.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought an experiment with one kind of seed was enough; for comparison, seeds from the short sunflowers must also be planted under the same conditions.

variantlar.maslahat: Remember how many factors should change in a fair test.

kunikma: Correctly classify substances by composition into elements, compounds, and mixtures
usul: For each substance, ask: is it made of one kind of atom (element), is it a single pure substance in which different elements are chemically bonded (compound), or is it simply several substances mixed together (mixture)? Then choose the option in which all the groups are correct.

variantlar.savol:
Sort the following six substances into elements, compounds, and mixtures:
copper, oxygen, distilled water, carbon dioxide, air, tea with sugar.
In which option are all the substances grouped correctly?
javoblar: Elements: copper, oxygen, air; compounds: distilled water, carbon dioxide; mixtures: tea with sugar
Elements: copper; compounds: oxygen, distilled water, carbon dioxide; mixtures: air, tea with sugar
Elements: copper, oxygen; compounds: distilled water, carbon dioxide; mixtures: air, tea with sugar
Elements: copper, oxygen; compounds: distilled water, carbon dioxide, tea with sugar; mixtures: air

yechim.doska: Element — one kind of atom: Cu, $O_2$
yechim.ovoz: Copper and oxygen are each made of only one kind of atom, so they are elements, that is, simple substances.
Water is formed from hydrogen and oxygen chemically bonded together, and carbon dioxide from carbon and oxygen — these are compounds.

yechim.doska: Mixtures: air ($N_2$, $O_2$, Ar, $CO_2$...), tea with sugar
yechim.ovoz: Air is a mixture of several gases, and tea with sugar is a mixture of water, sugar, and substances from the tea.

yechim.doska: Find the option in which all three groups are correct
yechim.ovoz: Now let's compare the options: only one of them has all six substances in the right place.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) Elements: copper, oxygen; compounds: distilled water, carbon dioxide; mixtures: air, tea with sugar
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought air is a single substance (an element); in fact, air is a mixture of gases such as nitrogen, oxygen, argon, and carbon dioxide.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought oxygen is a compound because its molecule has two atoms ($O_2$); but both atoms are oxygen, so it is a simple substance.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought a new substance formed because the sugar dissolved and could no longer be seen; a solution is a mixture, and the water and sugar in it can be separated by evaporation.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about whether air and solutions are single pure substances or several substances mixed together.

variantlar.savol:
Sort the following six substances into elements, compounds, and mixtures:
aluminum, nitrogen, baking soda, methane, steel, milk.
In which option are all the substances grouped correctly?
javoblar: Elements: aluminum, nitrogen; compounds: baking soda, methane; mixtures: steel, milk
Elements: aluminum, nitrogen, steel; compounds: baking soda, methane; mixtures: milk
Elements: aluminum; compounds: nitrogen, baking soda, methane; mixtures: steel, milk
Elements: aluminum, nitrogen, methane; compounds: baking soda; mixtures: steel, milk

yechim.ovoz: Aluminum and nitrogen are each made of only one kind of atom — they are elements.
Baking soda and methane are pure substances formed when several elements combine chemically — they are compounds.

yechim.doska: Mixtures: steel (Fe + C), milk (water, fat, protein, sugar...)
yechim.ovoz: Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon, and milk is a mixture of many substances.
We choose the only option in which all six substances are placed correctly.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) Elements: aluminum, nitrogen; compounds: baking soda, methane; mixtures: steel, milk
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought steel is an element because it is a metal; in fact, steel is an alloy of iron and carbon (sometimes with other metals too), that is, a mixture.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought nitrogen is a compound because it is a gas and its molecule is $N_2$; but it is a simple substance made only of nitrogen atoms.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought methane is an element like nitrogen because it is a gas; methane ($CH_4$) is a compound made of carbon and hydrogen.

variantlar.maslahat: Check whether a metal alloy can be a single element.

kunikma: Distinguish a chemical process that absorbs energy (endothermic) from processes that release energy (exothermic)
usul: For each process, decide whether heat or light is released (exothermic) or whether energy must be supplied continuously from outside for the process to keep going (endothermic).

variantlar.savol: In which of the following chemical processes is energy ABSORBED?
javoblar: the oxidation of glucose in cells (respiration)
breaking down limestone into quicklime and carbon dioxide by strong heating

yechim.doska: Exothermic: energy is released; endothermic: energy is absorbed
yechim.ovoz: Reactions that release energy are called exothermic, and those that absorb energy are called endothermic.

yechim.doska: Burning, slaking lime, respiration → heat is released
yechim.ovoz: When a match burns, when lime is slaked, and when glucose is oxidized in a cell, heat is released — these are exothermic.
Limestone, however, breaks down only while it is heated strongly and continuously: if the heating stops, the reaction stops too.

yechim.doska: Energy is absorbed → limestone breaks down
yechim.ovoz: So the process that absorbs energy is the breakdown of limestone.

yechim.doska: Answer: D) breaking down limestone into quicklime and carbon dioxide by strong heating
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option D.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A saw that a match has to be struck to burn and thought energy is absorbed; in fact, once started, burning gives off heat and light on its own.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought the water “cools” the lime when it is slaked; in fact, this reaction releases so much heat that the mixture gets hot.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought that in respiration the body “takes in” food, so energy is absorbed; in fact, when glucose is oxidized, energy is released and the cell uses it.

variantlar.maslahat: Which process cannot continue unless it is heated nonstop?

variantlar.savol: In which of the following chemical processes is energy ABSORBED?
javoblar: a magnesium ribbon burning with a bright flame
splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using an electric current
an acid solution and an alkali solution neutralizing each other
natural gas burning on a gas stove

yechim.ovoz: First, let's recall the two kinds of processes: those that release energy and those that absorb energy.

yechim.doska: Burning magnesium, burning gas, neutralization → heat is released
yechim.ovoz: When magnesium and natural gas burn, and when an acid is neutralized by an alkali, heat is released.
To split water, however, an electric current must be supplied all the time: if the current is cut off, the splitting stops.

yechim.doska: Energy is absorbed → water is split
yechim.ovoz: So the process that absorbs energy is the splitting of water by an electric current.

yechim.doska: Answer: B) splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using an electric current
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A took the bright flame to mean “a lot of energy is being used”; in fact, flame and light are signs of energy being released.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought energy is absorbed because the color and appearance do not change; in neutralization the solution warms up, which means heat is released.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D saw that a spark is needed to light the stove and thought energy is absorbed; in fact, burning gas releases heat, and we cook food with that heat.

variantlar.maslahat: Which process stops immediately unless energy is supplied from outside?

kunikma: Determine how the density of a substance changes when it changes state between liquid and gas
usul: Density $\rho = m/V$: draw your conclusion keeping in mind that mass is conserved when the state changes, while volume changes.

variantlar.savol:
The water in a kettle boiled and turned into water vapor.
How does the DENSITY of the substance change when liquid water turns into vapor?

yechim.ovoz: Density is the ratio of mass to volume.
When water turns into vapor, the mass is conserved, but the distance between molecules increases many times, so the volume becomes larger.
The mass is the same and the volume is larger, so the density of the vapor is much less than that of water.
So the correct answer is option B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought vapor “rises and is stronger”; in fact, the same mass takes up a much larger volume, so the density gets smaller.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought the density does not change because the substance is still water; density depends on the state of the substance.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D imagined the process happening in two stages; when a liquid turns into vapor, the density only decreases.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about which of mass and volume changes in the density formula.

variantlar.savol:
In winter, water vapor touching a cold windowpane turned into water droplets (condensed).
How does the DENSITY of the substance change when vapor turns into liquid water?

yechim.ovoz: Let's recall density in terms of mass and volume.
In condensation, the mass is conserved, the molecules pack closely together, and the volume becomes much smaller.
The mass is the same and the volume is smaller, so the density increases.
So the correct answer is option A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B reversed the direction of the process: this is vapor turning into liquid, and the molecules move closer together.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought the density stays the same because the substance is still water; density depends on the state, and liquid water is much denser than vapor.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D imagined condensation as a two-stage process; when vapor turns into liquid, the density only increases.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about what happens to the volume when vapor turns into liquid, then look at the density formula.

kunikma: Apply the conservation of mass of a substance in a closed system during a change of state (liquid ↔ gas)
usul: Mass depends on the number and kind of molecules in a substance: if these do not change in a closed container, the mass does not change even when the state changes.

variantlar.savol:
A small amount of alcohol in a tightly sealed glass container turned completely into vapor when heated. Nothing escaped from the container.
How does the MASS of the alcohol change when it turns from liquid into vapor?

yechim.doska: The container is closed → the number of molecules does not change
yechim.ovoz: The container is tightly sealed, so no alcohol molecules escape and no new molecules are added.

yechim.doska: A change of state is a physical change
yechim.ovoz: In evaporation, the molecules only move farther apart; the molecules themselves do not change.
That is why the mass does not change.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) It does not change
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought the mass increases because the vapor takes up more space; an increase in volume does not mean an increase in mass.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought the mass decreases because a gas is “light”; the container is closed, so not a single molecule is lost.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D confused evaporation with a change in mass; in a closed container the mass always stays the same.

variantlar.maslahat: Does the number of alcohol molecules in the closed container change?

variantlar.savol:
Hot water vapor in a tightly sealed container turned completely into water droplets when it was cooled. Nothing escaped from the container.
How does the MASS of the substance change when vapor turns into liquid?

yechim.doska: The container is closed → the number of molecules stays the same
yechim.ovoz: The container is closed; no molecules escaped and none were added.
When vapor turns into water, the molecules only move closer together.
So the mass does not change — what changes are the volume and the density.

yechim.doska: Answer: D) It does not change
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option D.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought the mass increases because a liquid seems “heavier”; the density increases, but the mass stays the same.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought the mass decreases because the volume gets smaller; volume and mass are different quantities.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought the mass keeps changing during condensation; in a closed container the mass is always conserved.

variantlar.maslahat: Mass depends on the number of molecules: has that number changed?

kunikma: Use the arrangement of molecules to determine how the volume of a substance changes when it changes state between liquid and gas
usul: In a gas, the distance between molecules is many times greater than in a liquid: going from liquid → gas, the volume increases; going from gas → liquid, it decreases.

variantlar.savol:
A small amount of ether was drawn into a syringe, and its tip was sealed. When the syringe was dipped in warm water, the ether turned into vapor and the plunger was pushed out.
How does the VOLUME of the ether change when it turns from liquid into vapor?

yechim.ovoz: In a liquid, the molecules are very close to one another.

yechim.doska: Gas: the distance between molecules is large
yechim.ovoz: In a gas, the distance between molecules is many times greater than the molecules themselves.
That is why the vapor takes up a lot of space and pushes the plunger — the volume increases.
So the correct answer is option A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought the volume gets smaller because the vapor becomes invisible; in fact, vapor takes up a volume many times larger than the liquid.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought the volume does not change because the mass does not change; the mass is conserved, but the volume increases.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D added the shrinking of vapor as it cools to this process; while turning into vapor, the volume only increases.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about why the plunger was pushed out.

variantlar.savol:
Hot water vapor in a bathroom touched a cold mirror and turned into water droplets.
How does the VOLUME of this substance change when vapor turns into liquid water?

yechim.ovoz: In vapor, there are large spaces between the molecules.
In condensation, the molecules move closer together and become closely packed.
That is why the volume decreases sharply: vapor that filled a whole room produces just a few drops of water.
So the correct answer is option B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought a liquid takes up more space because it is “heavier” than vapor; in fact, water takes up much less space than vapor.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought the volume is conserved because the mass is conserved; the mass is conserved, but the volume gets smaller.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought condensation happens in two stages; when vapor turns into liquid, the volume only decreases.

variantlar.maslahat: How does the distance between molecules change during condensation?

kunikma: Apply the idea that during a change of state (liquid ↔ gas) the size of molecules does not change; only the distance between them changes
usul: A change of state is a physical change: the molecules themselves do not change; only the distance between them and their speed of motion change.

variantlar.savol:
Water in an open saucer evaporated within a few hours.
How does the SIZE of the water MOLECULES change when water evaporates and turns into a gas?
javoblar: The size of the molecules does not change
The molecules break apart into separate atoms

yechim.ovoz: No new substance forms in evaporation: the vapor is still the same water.

yechim.doska: $H_2O$ molecules in both the liquid and the vapor
yechim.ovoz: Both liquid water and water vapor contain the same $H_2O$ molecules.

yechim.doska: What changes: the distance between molecules and their motion
yechim.ovoz: It is not the molecules themselves that change, but the distance between them and their motion.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) The size of the molecules does not change
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought each molecule swells and gets bigger because the vapor takes up a large volume; the volume grows because the distance between molecules increases.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought the molecules become tiny because the vapor is invisible; the size of molecules does not depend on the state.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought evaporation is a chemical change; the vapor contains the same $H_2O$ molecules, and they do not break apart.

variantlar.maslahat: Does the volume grow because the molecules get bigger or because the distance between them increases?

variantlar.savol:
Drops formed from the water vapor in the air on the outside of a glass holding a cold drink.
How does the SIZE of the water MOLECULES change when water vapor turns into liquid water?
javoblar: The size of the molecules does not change
The molecules join together to form one big new molecule

yechim.ovoz: No new substance forms when vapor turns into water.

yechim.doska: $H_2O$ in both the vapor and the drop
yechim.ovoz: Both the vapor and the drops contain the same $H_2O$ molecules.

yechim.doska: What changes: distance and speed, not size
yechim.ovoz: The molecules only move closer together; their size stays the same.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) The size of the molecules does not change
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought each molecule is squeezed and gets smaller because the volume decreases; the volume decreases because the molecules move closer together.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought the molecules of a liquid are bigger because a liquid is “denser and heavier”; the size of a molecule does not depend on the state.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought condensation forms a new substance; the drops also contain separate $H_2O$ molecules.

variantlar.maslahat: When the state changes, does the molecule itself change, or only how the molecules are arranged?

kunikma: Determine how the speed of molecules changes with temperature during a change of state that involves heating or cooling
usul: The speed of molecules depends on temperature: when the temperature rises, the speed increases; when it falls, the speed decreases. In a gas, molecules move more freely than in a liquid.

variantlar.savol:
Water at 20 °C in a kettle was heated, boiled at 100 °C, and turned into vapor.
How does the SPEED of the water MOLECULES change during this process?

yechim.ovoz: Heat was supplied to the water, and its temperature rose from twenty degrees to one hundred degrees.
The higher the temperature, the faster the molecules move.

yechim.doska: In vapor, molecules fly about freely and quickly
yechim.ovoz: Molecules that have turned into vapor move far apart and move freely and quickly.
So the correct answer is option A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought gas molecules “float around” and so are slow; when the temperature rises, molecules move faster.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought the speed stays the same because the molecules themselves do not change; their size does not change, but their speed depends on temperature.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D imagined that the molecules stop after turning into vapor; as the temperature rises, the molecules move faster and faster.

variantlar.maslahat: Recall how temperature and the motion of molecules are related.

variantlar.savol:
Water vapor at 100 °C coming from a pot touched a cold lid, turned into water droplets, and the droplets cooled to 30 °C.
How does the SPEED of the water MOLECULES change during this process?

yechim.ovoz: The vapor gave off heat to the lid and cooled; its temperature dropped from one hundred degrees to thirty degrees.
When the temperature falls, the motion of the molecules slows down.

yechim.doska: In a drop, molecules are close together and slower
yechim.ovoz: In a liquid drop, the molecules are close to one another and move more slowly than in vapor.
So the correct answer is option B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought that because a liquid is denser, the molecules collide more often and so move faster; the speed decreases because the temperature fell.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought only the state changes while the motion of the molecules stays the same; when the temperature falls, the molecules slow down.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought the molecules first speed up during cooling; the temperature only fell, so the speed also only decreases.

variantlar.maslahat: What happens to the motion of molecules during cooling?

kunikma: Apply the idea that thermal insulation (wrapping) slows heat transfer to determine and explain which piece of ice melts faster
usul: Heat always flows from a warmer object to a colder one. A wrapping does not give off heat; it only slows the flow of heat, so heat reaches unwrapped ice faster from the warm air.

variantlar.savol:
On a hot summer day at a teahouse, Aziz put two identical pieces of ice on identical saucers. Ice 1 was left uncovered, and ice 2 was wrapped in a thick wool scarf.
Which piece of ice will melt first, and why?
javoblar: Ice 2, because the wool scarf warms the ice
Ice 1, because heat passes to it more easily from the warm air around it, while the scarf slows the flow of heat to ice 2
Ice 2, because the scarf soaks up the cold from the ice
Both melt at the same time, because the air temperature is the same for both

yechim.ovoz: Heat always flows from a warmer object to a colder one: from the air to the ice.

yechim.doska: Ice 1: the air touches it directly
yechim.ovoz: Warm air touches the uncovered ice directly, and heat flows in quickly.

yechim.doska: Ice 2: wool is a poor conductor of heat
yechim.ovoz: The air between the wool fibers conducts heat poorly, so heat reaches the wrapped ice slowly.
So the first piece of ice, which is uncovered, melts first.

yechim.doska: Answer: B) Ice 1, because heat passes to it more easily from the warm air around it, while the scarf slows the flow of heat to ice 2
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought the scarf warms the ice because wool clothes keep us warm; in fact, wool does not produce heat itself; it only slows the flow of heat.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought “cold” flows; in fact, heat flows from the warm air to the ice, and the scarf blocks this flow.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D considered only the air temperature and ignored the fact that the wrapping affects heat transfer.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about whether the wrapping produces heat or only blocks the flow of heat.

variantlar.savol:
Nilufar took two identical bottles of frozen water to a cotton field. She wrapped bottle 1 in several layers of newspaper, left bottle 2 uncovered, and put both in the shade. The air temperature was 38 °C.
In which bottle will the ice melt first, and why?
javoblar: In bottle 1, because the newspaper warms the bottle and melts the ice faster
In bottle 1, because the newspaper cannot hold in the cold and lets it out
In bottle 2, because the warm air touches it directly; the layers of newspaper slow the flow of heat to bottle 1
Both melt at the same time, because both bottles are in the same 38 °C air

yechim.ovoz: Heat flows from the warm air to the cold ice.

yechim.doska: Bottle 2: the air touches it directly
yechim.ovoz: Warm air touches the uncovered bottle directly, and heat flows in quickly.

yechim.doska: Bottle 1: the newspaper layers and the air between them conduct heat poorly
yechim.ovoz: The newspaper and the air between its layers slow the flow of heat.

yechim.doska: The ice in bottle 2 melts faster
yechim.ovoz: So the ice in the second bottle, which is uncovered, melts first.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) In bottle 2, because the warm air touches it directly; the layers of newspaper slow the flow of heat to bottle 1
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought the wrapping “warms”; the newspaper does not produce heat itself; it slows the flow of heat from the warm air.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought “cold” moves; in fact, heat flows from the air to the ice, and the newspaper reduces this flow.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D looked only at the air temperature and did not take into account that the wrapping slows the flow of heat.

kunikma: Determine the path and direction of a light ray in a periscope as it reflects off two plane mirrors and travels from an object to the eye
usul: Light comes from the object to the eye (it does not come out of the eye). The ray hits the upper mirror, reflects off the 45° mirror downward, then reflects off the lower mirror toward the eye; it cannot travel in a straight line through the wall.

yechim.ovoz: For us to see an object, light coming from it or reflected by it must reach our eyes.

yechim.doska: The wall blocks the light → no straight path
yechim.ovoz: A ray cannot travel in a straight line from the tree to the eye through the wall, so mirrors are needed.

yechim.doska: Upper mirror: horizontal → down; lower mirror: down → to the eye
yechim.ovoz: The ray reflects off the upper mirror and goes down, then reflects off the lower mirror and reaches Jasur's eye.

yechim.doska: Arrows from the tree toward the eye
yechim.ovoz: The picture in which both the path and the arrows are drawn this way is picture 3.
So the correct answer is option C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought that to see, light goes out from the eye to the object; the path is right, but the direction is reversed — light comes from the tree to the eye.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought the light arrives in a straight line without the mirrors; such a ray would be blocked by the opaque wall.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D got the direction of reflection from the lower mirror wrong; the ray reflected from the 45° mirror goes to the wall, not to the eye.

variantlar.maslahat: Where does the light come from: the eye or the tree?

variantlar.savol:
Jasur is looking at a tree behind a fence through the periscope shown in the picture. The periscope has two plane mirrors.
Which path does the light take so that Jasur can see the tree?

javoblar: tree → straight through the fence → Jasur's eye

yechim.doska: Light comes from the source to the eye
yechim.ovoz: Sunlight reflected from the tree must reach Jasur's eye.

yechim.doska: The tree is high up → the light hits mirror 1 first
yechim.ovoz: The tree is taller than the fence; its light enters the upper opening of the periscope and hits mirror 1.

yechim.doska: Mirror 1 → down → mirror 2 → to the eye
yechim.ovoz: The light reflected from mirror 1 goes down, then reflects off mirror 2 and reaches Jasur's eye.

yechim.doska: Answer: D) tree → mirror 1 → mirror 2 → Jasur's eye
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option D.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought that to see, light comes out of the eye; the order of the mirrors is right, but light comes from the tree to the eye.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B mixed up the order of the mirrors; the tree is high up, so its light hits the upper mirror, mirror 1, first.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C did not understand what the mirrors do; the opaque fence blocks light traveling in a straight line.

variantlar.maslahat: Which end of the periscope is the tree closer to — the top or the bottom?

kunikma: Know the speed of light in different media: greatest in a vacuum, lower in optically denser media
usul: Light travels fastest in a vacuum (about 300 000 km/s); almost as fast in air, slower in water, slower still in glass, and even slower in diamond.

variantlar.savol: In which of the following does light travel SLOWEST?

yechim.ovoz: Light travels fastest in empty space, a vacuum: about three hundred thousand kilometers per second.
In air it is almost as fast, in water about a quarter slower, and in diamond about two and a half times slower.
So, of the media listed, light travels slowest in diamond.
So the correct answer is option D.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought light has a hard time traveling with nothing to “lean on”; in fact, light travels fastest in a vacuum.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought of light like sound and assumed it is slow in a thin medium; in air, light is almost as fast as in a vacuum.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought a liquid is “thicker” than a solid; light travels much faster in water than in diamond.

variantlar.maslahat: Remember that sound and light “respond” to a medium differently: for light, is the medium an obstacle or a help?

variantlar.savol: In which row are the media arranged in order of DECREASING speed of light?

yechim.ovoz: Light travels at its greatest speed in a vacuum.
The speed in air differs very little from that in a vacuum, but it is still lower.
In water it is about two hundred twenty-five thousand, and in ordinary glass about two hundred thousand kilometers per second.
So the decreasing order is: vacuum, air, water, glass.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) vacuum → air → water → glass
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B confused light with sound: sound is fast in solids and does not travel in a vacuum at all; for light, the order is the reverse.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought light needs air to travel and slows down in a vacuum; in fact, the greatest speed is in a vacuum.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D linked speed to how clear the medium is; the speed decreases going from vacuum to air, water, and glass.

variantlar.maslahat: Recall where light travels fastest and arrange the rest starting from there.

kunikma: Apply the stages of the water cycle (evaporation, condensation and cloud formation, transport by wind, precipitation) to explain how seawater falls as rain on distant land
usul: Water vapor rises, cools, and condenses to form clouds; the wind carries the clouds over land; when the droplets grow larger and heavier, they fall as rain.

variantlar.savol: Water that evaporates from the surface of the sea can fall as rain on foothills hundreds of kilometers away. Which explanation describes this correctly?
javoblar: Water vapor rises, cools, and condenses to form clouds; the wind carries the clouds over land; when the droplets grow larger and heavier, it rains
Water vapor sinks into the seabed, flows to land with groundwater, and comes out there as rain
Water vapor heats up over land, turns back into liquid, and falls as rain
Clouds form only over the sea and rain there; rain over land forms only from water that evaporates from rivers and lakes

yechim.ovoz: Seawater warmed by the Sun evaporates, and the vapor rises with the warm air.

yechim.doska: 2) Condensation: vapor cools → tiny droplets → cloud
yechim.ovoz: The air higher up is cold; the vapor cools and turns into tiny droplets, forming a cloud.

yechim.doska: 3) The wind carries the cloud over land
yechim.ovoz: The wind moves the cloud hundreds of kilometers away, over land.
The droplets merge and grow larger; once they are heavy enough, the air can no longer hold them, and they fall as rain.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) Water vapor rises, cools, and condenses to form clouds; the wind carries the clouds over land; when the droplets grow larger and heavier, it rains
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B confused evaporation with the movement of groundwater; vapor rises into the air, and rain falls only from clouds.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought vapor turns into liquid when it heats up; in fact, condensation happens only when vapor cools.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought clouds stay in one place; the wind can carry clouds over long distances.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about when vapor turns into liquid and what makes clouds move.

variantlar.savol:
Nilufar used the following diagram to explain how water evaporated from the sea falls as rain on distant land:
1) The Sun warms the seawater, and the water evaporates.
2) ?
3) The wind carries the cloud over land.
4) The droplets in the cloud grow larger and fall as rain.
What should be written in step 2?
javoblar: The water vapor heats up again high in the air, becomes lighter, and disappears from view
The water vapor freezes at once and falls into the sea as hail
The water vapor rises, cools, and turns into tiny droplets (condenses), forming a cloud
The water vapor soaks into the ground and joins the groundwater

yechim.doska: Step 3 has a cloud → a cloud must form in step 2
yechim.ovoz: In step three, the wind is moving the cloud, so the cloud must appear in step two.

yechim.doska: The air higher up is cold → the vapor cools
yechim.ovoz: As the vapor rises, the air gets colder, and the vapor cools.
The cooled vapor turns into tiny water droplets — this is condensation — and a mass of droplets is a cloud.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) The water vapor rises, cools, and turns into tiny droplets (condenses), forming a cloud
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought clouds form through heating; in fact, the air higher up is colder, and the vapor turns into droplets when it cools.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B linked the cooling of vapor directly to precipitation; then the cloud in step 3 would never form.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D confused evaporation with water soaking into the ground; vapor rises into the air and does not soak into the ground.

variantlar.maslahat: What is the wind moving in step 3? How does that thing appear in step 2?

kunikma: Know the function of leukocytes (white blood cells), the blood cells that protect the body from bacteria
usul: Recall the functions of blood cells: red blood cells carry oxygen, platelets make blood clot, and white blood cells engulf and destroy microbes and provide immunity.

variantlar.savol: Aziz scratched his hand, and microbes got into the wound. Which blood cells engulf and destroy the bacteria that got into the wound?

yechim.ovoz: Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to the tissues.
Platelets take part in blood clotting and stop bleeding from a wound.
White blood cells reach the wound, engulf the bacteria, and digest and destroy them.
So the correct answer is option C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought the most numerous blood cells also do the protecting; red blood cells carry oxygen and carbon dioxide.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B remembered that platelets gather at a wound and thought they also destroy microbes; their job is to make blood clot and stop bleeding.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought that because skin protects the body from the outside, it also destroys microbes inside; microbes that enter a wound are destroyed by white blood cells.

variantlar.maslahat: Which blood cells are called the body's “guards”?

variantlar.savol: Malika came down with the flu. Which blood cells fight the disease-causing agents that have entered the body and provide immunity?

yechim.doska: Immunity — the body's ability to defend itself
yechim.ovoz: Immunity is the body's ability to protect itself from foreign substances and microbes.

yechim.doska: White blood cells: engulf microbes, produce antibodies
yechim.ovoz: Some white blood cells engulf microbes, and others produce antibodies against them.

yechim.doska: Red blood cell — oxygen; platelet — clotting
yechim.ovoz: The other blood cells have different jobs: red blood cells carry oxygen, and platelets make blood clot.
So the correct answer is option B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought the cells that make blood red also do the protecting; the job of red blood cells is to carry oxygen.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C linked the word “protection” to protection from bleeding; platelets make blood clot and do not destroy microbes.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D confused sensing a disease with fighting it; nerve cells transmit signals, while immunity is provided by white blood cells.

variantlar.maslahat: Which blood cell is also called a “white blood cell,” and what does it do?

kunikma: Analyze a sharp drop in population size on a graph and identify its likely cause based on factors in the ecosystem
usul: Determine whether the change on the graph is sharp (over a short time) or gradual. A sharp drop is caused by an event that happened suddenly and destroyed the food supply or living conditions; factors that act gradually or that increase the number do not fit.

variantlar.savol:
The graph shows the number of gazelles in a nature reserve over several years.
Which of the following MOST LIKELY caused the sharp change in the number of gazelles between 2019 and 2020?
javoblar: gradual warming of the climate over decades
wolves disappearing completely from the area
a thick layer of snow and ice covering the grass for a long time in winter, so the gazelles could not find food

yechim.ovoz: Let's look at the graph: from 2016 to 2019 the number of gazelles stayed steady at about two hundred forty.
Within one year, the number fell to about seventy — a very fast, sharp drop.

yechim.doska: Sharp drop ← sudden loss of food
yechim.ovoz: Such a fast drop is caused by an event that happened suddenly and destroyed the food supply; gradual effects do not produce such a jump.

yechim.doska: Snow and ice covered the grass → no food
yechim.ovoz: Gazelles cannot reach grass under a thick layer of ice, and many die of starvation.

yechim.doska: Answer: D) a thick layer of snow and ice covering the grass for a long time in winter, so the gazelles could not find food
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option D.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A linked every change to climate warming; the climate changes gradually, but on the graph the number fell sharply within one year.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B thought about predators but got the direction of the effect wrong; if predators disappear, the number of gazelles does not drop — it may even rise.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C chose a well-known environmental problem; the ozone layer changes gradually and does not suddenly destroy the gazelles' food.

variantlar.maslahat: Look at how long the change took: one year or several decades?

variantlar.savol:
The graph shows the number of fish in a lake over several years.
Which of the following MOST LIKELY caused the sharp change in the number of fish between 2013 and 2014?
javoblar: toxic waste being discharged into the lake from a nearby factory
the absence of predatory fish in the lake
more algae and food getting into the lake

yechim.ovoz: On the graph, from 2010 to 2013 the number of fish stayed at about twelve thousand.
Within one year, the number fell to two thousand — six times fewer; this is a sharp drop.
Such a fast change is caused by an event that suddenly damaged the water environment.
Toxic waste pollutes the water and causes fish to die in large numbers.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) toxic waste being discharged into the lake from a nearby factory
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option A.

xatolar.1: A student who chose B got the effect of predators backward; without predators, the number of other fish does not drop — it may even rise.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C linked every change to climate warming; warming is slow, but on the graph the number fell sharply within one year.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D thought about a change in food but got the direction wrong; if there is more food, the number of fish does not drop — it rises.

variantlar.maslahat: Which factor reduces the number and also acts suddenly?

kunikma: Use an organism's response to a change in its surroundings (the pupil of the eye widening or narrowing) to identify the environmental condition and the direction of its change
usul: Recall that the pupil changes in response to light: in bright light it narrows, and in dim light it widens. Then compare in which case the pupil is small and in which it is large.

variantlar.savol:
Jasur is at an appointment with an eye doctor. The doctor changed one condition in the room and photographed Jasur's eyes twice (Picture 1 and Picture 2).
Which condition did the doctor change, and how did this condition differ in the two pictures?

javoblar: Room temperature: in Picture 1 the room was warm, and in Picture 2 it was cold
Light: in Picture 1 the room was dimly lit, and in Picture 2 it was brightly lit
Light: in Picture 1 the room was brightly lit, and in Picture 2 it was dimly lit
Humidity: in Picture 1 the air was dry, and in Picture 2 it was humid

yechim.doska: Picture 1: small pupil;  Picture 2: large pupil
yechim.ovoz: Let's compare the pictures: in the first picture the pupil is very small, and in the second it is much larger.
The size of the pupil is controlled by the amount of light; temperature or humidity does not change it like this.
When the light is bright, the pupil narrows and keeps too much light from entering the eye. So in the first picture the room is bright.
When there is little light, the pupil widens and more light enters the eye. So in the second picture the room is dim.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) bright in Picture 1, dim in Picture 2
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is option C.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A thought pupil size depends on temperature; in fact, the pupil changes in response to light.
xatolar.1: A student who chose B identified the right condition but got the direction backward: a large pupil means there is little light, not a lot.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D guessed that humidity affects the eye; the pupil responds to light, not to humidity.

variantlar.maslahat: Remember that the pupil is a “window” that controls the amount of light entering the eye.

variantlar.savol:
A doctor measured the diameter of Nilufar's pupil under two different conditions. These two conditions differed in only one way.
Case 1: pupil diameter 7 mm.
Case 2: pupil diameter 2 mm.
Which statement is correct?
javoblar: In case 1 the light was bright and in case 2 it was dim, because the pupil widens when there is a lot of light
In case 1 the light was dim and in case 2 it was bright, because the pupil narrows when there is a lot of light
In case 1 the air was cold and in case 2 it was warm, because the pupil widens in the cold
In case 1 the room was noisy and in case 2 it was quiet, because the pupil widens in noise

yechim.ovoz: First, let's compare the sizes: in the first case the pupil is much larger, and in the second it is small.

yechim.doska: The pupil controls the light entering the eye
yechim.ovoz: Pupil size changes mainly in response to the amount of light.
In a dim place, the eye needs to collect more light, so the pupil widens — this is the first case.

yechim.doska: A lot of light → narrow pupil (2 mm)
yechim.ovoz: In a bright place, the pupil narrows — this is the second case.
So the correct answer is option B.

xatolar.0: A student who chose A got the pupil's response backward: in bright light the pupil does not widen; it narrows.
xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought the pupil responds to temperature; pupil size depends on light.
xatolar.3: A student who chose D wrongly guessed that the pupil responds to sound.

variantlar.maslahat: Think about the fact that more light enters the eye when the pupil widens: when is that needed?

kunikma: Know the specific benefits of regular physical exercise for the body (heart and blood vessels, muscles, fat storage)
usul: Compare each option with what actually happens in the body: during exercise the heart beats faster, the muscles work, and energy is used.

variantlar.savol: Malika goes running and does exercises every morning. Which of the following correctly states a specific benefit of regular physical exercise for the body?
javoblar: After exercise, the body needs less water
During exercise, the heart beats more slowly and rests
Exercise relaxes the muscles and makes them smaller
The heart muscle gets stronger and blood circulation improves

yechim.doska: During exercise: the heart beats faster

The number of fish in the pond increased
Nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizers flowed from the field into the pond with the irrigation water
Smoke from tractors working in the field

yechim.ovoz: The irrigation water carries the fertilizer into the pond, and the algae multiply very quickly.

Nitrogen and phosphorus compounds from the farm's manure and waste flowed into the lake
Noise from the farm scared the fish in the lake
In autumn the air got colder, and the water temperature dropped

xatolar.2: A student who chose C thought noise has the main effect on the ecosystem; algae growth depends on nutrients.

kunikma: Interpreting statistical information about shares, percentages and probability
usul: Check each statement separately: calculate the share, remember that “on average” does not mean “exactly”, and convert the percentage into a probability.

variantlar.savol:
The three statements below are about the factory's daily production.
1) One quarter of the products made each day are refrigerators.
2) Exactly 4 out of every 100 refrigerators are faulty.
3) If one of the day's air conditioners is chosen at random, the probability that it will be sent for repair is 0.02.

Which row correctly shows whether the statements are true?

yechim.ovoz: Statement one: refrigerators are a quarter of the total number — Yes.
Statement two: 4% is an average value; there do not have to be exactly 4 in every 100 — No.
Statement three: the probability that a randomly chosen air conditioner is faulty is 0.02 — Yes.
So the correct row is B.

xatolar.0: Statement two contains the word “exactly”. 4% is an average figure; some batches of 100 may have 3 or 6 faulty ones.
xatolar.2: Statement one is true: 3 000 : 12 000 = 0.25, that is, one quarter. You probably divided 3 000 by 9 000 (1/3).
xatolar.3: Statement three is true: a 2% fault rate means a probability of 0.02 for a randomly chosen product.

variantlar.maslahat: Where you see the words “on average”, be careful with words such as “exactly” or “always”.

kunikma: Linking a percentage to a number and evaluating a claim by calculation
usul: Compare the numbers of faulty products, not the percentages themselves: number × percentage.

variantlar.savol:
One of the inspectors said: “More refrigerators than air conditioners are sent for repair each day, because refrigerators have a higher fault percentage.”

Which answer correctly evaluates this claim?
javoblar: The claim is correct: 4% is twice as large as 2%
The claim is incorrect: 120 refrigerators and 180 air conditioners are sent for repair each day
The claim is correct: 120 refrigerators and 18 air conditioners are sent for repair
The claim is incorrect: equal numbers of both products are sent for repair each day

yechim.ovoz: On average, 120 refrigerators are sent for repair each day.
And for air conditioners, it is 180 on average.
Even though the percentage is smaller, three times as many air conditioners are made, so more of them are faulty.
The correct evaluation is B.

xatolar.0: Comparing the percentages is not enough: the numbers of products are different. 3 000 · 4% = 120, 9 000 · 2% = 180.
xatolar.2: 2% of 9 000 is 180, not 18. A place-value mistake was made when calculating the percentage.
xatolar.3: The numbers are not equal: 120 and 180. Check your calculation again.

variantlar.maslahat: A percentage tells you “how often”; to find out “how many”, you need to multiply by the total number.

kunikma: Calculating and comparing an overall (weighted) percentage for two groups
usul: For each factory, find the total number of faulty products and the total number of products, then calculate the overall percentage. Do not take the simple average of the percentages.

variantlar.savol:
The “Shamol” factory (a fictional name) also makes refrigerators and air conditioners.

“Navruz” | 3 000 | 4%
“Shamol” | 8 000 | 3%

Factory | Air conditioners (per day) | Fault rate
“Navruz” | 9 000 | 2%
“Shamol” | 2 000 | 1%

Which factory has the lower overall fault percentage for all its products?
javoblar: “Shamol”: the average of its percentages is (3% + 1%) : 2 = 2%, while for “Navruz” it is 3%
“Shamol”: it has 260 faulty products a day in total, while “Navruz” has 300
“Navruz”: its overall fault rate is 300 : 12 000 = 2.5%, while for “Shamol” it is 260 : 10 000 = 2.6%
They are equal: each has an overall fault rate of 2.5%

yechim.ovoz: At “Navruz” there are 3 000·4% + 9 000·2% = 300 faulty products a day.
That is 300 out of 12 000 products in total — 2.5%.
That is 260 out of 10 000 in total — 2.6%.
The overall percentage is lower at “Navruz”.
The correct answer is C.

xatolar.0: Taking the simple average of the percentages is wrong because the numbers of products are different. Overall percentage = total faulty : total products.
xatolar.1: Comparing the numbers of faulty products is not enough: “Shamol” makes fewer products (10 000). Calculate the percentage: 2.6% > 2.5%.
xatolar.3: For “Shamol”, 260 : 10 000 = 2.6%, so the percentages are not equal.

variantlar.maslahat: When you combine two groups to find a percentage, first add the numbers, then divide.

kunikma: Identifying the minimum measurements needed to find the area of a composite shape

variantlar.savol: To find the total area of the apartment (including the balcony and the walls), you do not need to measure every room separately — it is enough to measure four segments on the plan. Knowing the lengths of which four segments lets us calculate the total area exactly?

c and b are the dimensions of the cut-out piece.
If e = 10 m, f = 8 m, c = 4 m and b = 3 m, the area is 68 m².

yechim.doska: Answer: C) e, f, b and c
yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is C.

xatolar.0: In this set a + c = e, so one segment is unnecessary. And the height of the cut-out piece (b or d) remains unknown.
xatolar.1: In this set b + d = f — unnecessary information. The width of the cut-out piece (a or c) remains unknown.
xatolar.3: Since a + c = e, one segment is unnecessary; neither f nor b is known, so the length cannot be fully determined.

variantlar.maslahat: It is convenient to find the area of a composite shape as “large rectangle minus the cut-out part”.

We add the horizontal, slanted and vertical parts.
Since each square is 0.5 m, the length is 5 meters.
The tape is 5 meters long.

xatolar.umumiy: Common mistakes: writing 10 without taking the scale into account; taking the slanted part as 3 + 4 = 7 squares; calculating only the slanted part (2.5 m).

The floor area is 32.5 m².
