kunikma: Calculating the central angle when a circle is divided into equal sectors
usul: A full turn is 360°. Divide by the number of equal sectors.

variantlar.savol: How many degrees is the angle between two neighboring wings?

yechim.ovoz: The wings divide the full circle around the center.
Four equal sectors — each is 90 degrees.
The angle between neighboring wings is 90°.

xatolar.umumiy: Common mistakes: dividing 360 by 3 (120°) or dividing 180 by 4 (45°). The wings come out of the center and divide the whole circle — 360° — equally.

variantlar.maslahat: All the angles around a center add up to 360°.

kunikma: Interpreting a geometric model and calculating an arc length
usul: To keep air from passing through, each wall must be able to fully close off at least one sector. The two walls and the two openings together make up 360°. Find the angle of an opening and calculate the arc length as a fraction of the circumference.

variantlar.savol: If the openings are too wide, the wings cannot form a closed space: some sector will be open to both the entrance and the exit sides at the same time, and air will flow freely from the street inside (heat is lost). For air never to flow freely from the entrance to the exit, what is the maximum length, in centimeters, of the arc of each opening? (Use π ≈ 3.14 and round your answer to the nearest whole number.)

yechim.ovoz: A wall must close off at least one sector; otherwise a sector touches both openings.
On the edge of the circle there are two openings and two walls.
So each opening is at most 90°.
90° is a quarter of the circle: 3.14 · 240 : 4.
The arc of each opening is at most about 188 cm.

xatolar.umumiy: Common mistakes: writing the sum of both openings (377 cm), mixing up the radius and the diameter (94 cm), or simply writing the radius (120 cm) as the answer. Each opening is a quarter of the circle — a 90° arc.

variantlar.maslahat: First find the angle, then the length: L = (α/360°) · π · d.

kunikma: Selecting data and building a hidden quantitative model (turns, sectors, time)
usul: Find how many sectors pass the entrance in one turn and how many people fit in each; then multiply by the turns per minute and by the time.

variantlar.savol: The door makes 3 full turns per minute. Each of the four sectors holds at most 2 people. What is the greatest number of people who can enter the building through the door in 20 minutes?

yechim.ovoz: In one turn, each of the four sectors passes the entrance once.
3 turns per minute.
We multiply by the time.
The correct answer is C.

xatolar.0: 60 is only the number of turns (3 · 20); it does not take into account that several people enter with each turn.
xatolar.1: 240 — it was forgotten that each sector holds 2 people (4 · 3 · 20).
xatolar.3: 960 — people were counted twice: each person enters only once, in one sector.

variantlar.maslahat: Ask yourself step by step: how many people in one turn? How many in one minute? How many in 20 minutes?

kunikma: Finding the row of an experiment table that matches given conditions and identifying a danger limit
usul: First find the row that matches the conditions, then compare each result with its danger limit.

variantlar.savol: Sardor ran for one hour without drinking water on a day when the air temperature was 30 °C and the humidity was 40 %. Which danger does he face, and in which column of the table can it be seen?
javoblar: Heatstroke — in the body temperature column
Dehydration — in the water loss column
Dehydration — in the sweat volume column
No danger — all results are normal

yechim.ovoz: We find the row in the table that matches exactly these three conditions — it is row 4.
The water lost is above the 2 % limit, so there is a risk of dehydration.
Body temperature did not reach 40 °C, so there is no heatstroke.

yechim.doska: Answer: B) Dehydration — in the water loss column
yechim.ovoz: The danger shows up in the value in the water loss column.

xatolar.0: In row 4 the body temperature is 38.6 °C, which is below 40 °C — there is no heatstroke.
xatolar.2: No danger limit is given for sweat volume; dehydration is judged by the percentage of water lost (%).
xatolar.3: Water loss is 2.3 % — that is above the 2 % limit, so there is a danger.

variantlar.maslahat: Always compare a result with the limit given in the conditions: the conclusion comes from whichever column the limit applies to.

kunikma: Comparing two experiments that differ in only one variable (drinking water) to find its effect
usul: Find two rows with the same temperature and humidity that differ only in the “Drank water?” column, and compare their results.

variantlar.savol: At a temperature of 40 °C and humidity of 40 %, how does drinking water change Sardor's risk of dehydration and heatstroke? Which rows show this?
javoblar: Drinking water removes both dangers (rows 10 and 12)
Drinking water removes the risk of heatstroke, but not dehydration (rows 11 and 12)
Drinking water removes the risk of dehydration, but not heatstroke (rows 11 and 12)
Drinking water does not reduce either danger (rows 12 and 13)

yechim.ovoz: The pair that differs only in drinking water is rows 11 and 12.
Without water, there is both dehydration and heatstroke.
With water, the water loss is less than 2 %, but the body temperature is still above 40 °C.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) dehydration goes away, heatstroke remains
yechim.ovoz: So drinking water protects against dehydration, but not against heatstroke.

xatolar.0: Row 10 has 20 % humidity and row 12 has 40 % — two conditions differ; also, in row 12 the body temperature is 40.6 °C, so heatstroke remains.
xatolar.1: This is the opposite conclusion: in row 12 the body temperature is 40.6 °C — heatstroke remains, while water loss has dropped to 1.5 %.
xatolar.3: Rows 12 and 13 differ in humidity, not in drinking water; they do not show the effect of drinking water.

variantlar.maslahat: To test the effect of one factor, choose two experiments that differ only in that factor, with all other conditions the same.

asl_id: Running in Hot Weather Q3A (item Q03)
kunikma: Selecting data that support a conclusion while controlling variables
usul: Check whether the conclusion is correct, then check that the two chosen rows have the same humidity and water drinking, and differ only in temperature.

variantlar.savol: At 60 % humidity, how does a rise in air temperature affect sweat volume? Choose the conclusion and the two rows that correctly support it.
javoblar: Sweat volume does not change — rows 8 and 9

yechim.ovoz: We pick out the rows where humidity and water drinking are the same.
Rows 3 and 5 differ only in temperature, and the sweat volume has increased.

yechim.doska: 2 and 9: both humidity and water differ
yechim.ovoz: A pair like this cannot show the effect of temperature on its own.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) Sweat increases — rows 3 and 5
yechim.ovoz: The correct conclusion with a correctly controlled pair is A.

xatolar.1: The conclusion is correct, but row 2 has 40 % humidity and no water, while row 9 has 60 % and water — several conditions changed at once.
xatolar.2: Row 1 has 0.9 L and row 13 has 2.4 L — sweat did not decrease, it increased.
xatolar.3: Rows 8 and 9 have the same temperature (35 °C), so they do not show the effect of temperature; they differ only in drinking water.

variantlar.maslahat: When choosing data, remember the “fair test” rule: only one factor changes, and the rest stay the same.

asl_id: Running in Hot Weather Q3B (item Q04)
kunikma: Explaining the biological function of sweating (thermoregulation)
usul: Recall what happens to sweat on the surface of the skin and where evaporation gets its heat from.

variantlar.savol: When running in hot weather, sweat volume increases. What is the biological reason for this?
javoblar: As sweat evaporates, it takes heat from the skin and cools the body, keeping its temperature normal
Sweat removes excess water from the body, which makes running easier
In hot weather the heart beats more slowly, so water leaks out onto the skin
Sweat shields the skin from sunlight and prevents heat from entering the body

yechim.doska: Sweat → evaporates on the skin surface
yechim.ovoz: Sweating produces liquid on the surface of the skin, and this liquid evaporates.
The heat needed for evaporation is taken from the skin and the blood.
Because of this, the body does not overheat — this is thermoregulation.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) evaporation cools the body
yechim.ovoz: The higher the temperature, the more the body sweats and the more it cools itself.

xatolar.1: Sweat is not for getting rid of “excess water”; on the contrary, heavy sweating leads to dehydration (look at water loss in the table).
xatolar.2: The heart beats faster during running; sweating does not happen because the heartbeat slows down.
xatolar.3: Sweat does not block sunlight; its benefit is cooling through evaporation.

variantlar.maslahat: In a biological “why?” question, find the function of the organ or process for the organism: sweating is a cooling mechanism.

asl_id: Running in Hot Weather Q4 (item Q05)
kunikma: Finding the point where a series of values of one factor crosses a danger limit and justifying it with evidence
usul: Arrange the rows with 60 % humidity and water drinking by temperature, and find where body temperature goes above 40 °C.

variantlar.savol: On a day with 60 % humidity, Sardor runs while drinking water. What is the highest air temperature (from the values in the table) at which he will not get heatstroke?
javoblar: 35 °C, because in row 9 the water loss is only 1.3 %
30 °C, because at 30 °C body temperature is 39.4 °C, but at 35 °C it is 40.2 °C
40 °C, because in row 13 the most sweat is produced and the body cools well
25 °C, because only at this temperature is body temperature below 39 °C

yechim.ovoz: We take only the rows that match these conditions.
In row 5 the body temperature is below 40 °C.
In row 9 it is over the limit, so 35 °C is already dangerous.
The highest safe value is 30 °C, because at the next value heatstroke begins.

xatolar.0: Water loss indicates dehydration; heatstroke is judged by body temperature, and in row 9 it is 40.2 °C.
xatolar.2: In row 13 the body temperature is 41.3 °C — heatstroke; heavy sweating could not cool the body enough.
xatolar.3: At 30 °C the body temperature is also 39.4 °C, which is below 40 °C — so 25 °C is not the highest safe value.

variantlar.maslahat: In an “at most” question, find the boundary between the safe and dangerous cases: the last safe value is the answer.

asl_id: Running in Hot Weather Q5 (item Q06)
kunikma: Making a reasoned prediction for a condition not in the table, based on neighboring data
usul: 50 % humidity lies between 40 % and 60 %. Compare the results of those two rows, which have the same temperature and water-drinking condition.

variantlar.savol: The coach wants to let Sardor run without drinking water on a day when the air is 35 °C and the humidity is 50 %. There is no 50 % humidity in the table. Is this run safe?
javoblar: Safe, because no experiment was done at 50 % humidity
Safe, because in row 6 the body temperature is below 40 °C
Dangerous: in rows 6 and 8 (40 % and 60 %) water loss is above 2 %, and 50 % lies between them
Dangerous, because in row 13 the body temperature is 41.3 °C

yechim.ovoz: We take the two rows with the same temperature and water condition whose humidity values surround 50 %.
In both cases the dehydration limit is exceeded.

yechim.doska: 50 % is in between → water loss is also ~3 %
yechim.ovoz: For a value in between, the result is expected to lie between these two values too.
So at 50 % humidity there is also a risk of dehydration.

xatolar.0: The fact that no experiment was done does not mean it is safe; a prediction can be made from the results under neighboring conditions.
xatolar.1: Only heatstroke was checked; in row 6 the water loss is 3.0 % — there is a risk of dehydration.
xatolar.3: Row 13 has a temperature of 40 °C, 60 % humidity, and water drinking — these are different conditions, so it is not evidence for this question.

variantlar.maslahat: When predicting for an in-between value, use data that surround that value on both sides and have all other conditions the same.

kunikma: Explaining animal behavior through natural selection (evolution)
usul: In an evolutionary explanation, look for the answer to the question “which individuals, with which trait, survived more and left more offspring?”

variantlar.savol: Most small songbirds fly at night during migration. This behavior developed through evolution. Which explanation is the most scientific?
javoblar: The birds learned that flying in the daytime is dangerous and taught this knowledge to their chicks
Birds that flew in the daytime were caught more often by birds of prey, so fewer of them survived and they left fewer offspring
There are many insects in the air at night, so the birds can feed well while they fly
Birds that flew at night called birds of other species to join them on the journey

yechim.doska: Behavior is an inherited trait, passed down generations
yechim.ovoz: In evolution, it is inherited traits that are selected, not learned ones.
Birds that flew in the daytime died more often.
That is why, after many generations, flying at night became widespread.

yechim.doska: Answer: B) survival and leaving offspring
yechim.ovoz: The natural selection explanation is option B.

xatolar.0: Knowledge learned during a lifetime is not passed to the next generation through genes — this is not an evolutionary explanation.
xatolar.2: According to the text, the birds feed during the day; also, this does not explain why the trait spread through the generations.
xatolar.3: Calling other species does not increase this species' survival or number of offspring — it cannot be a reason for selection.

variantlar.maslahat: Key words in evolution questions: “survived”, “left more offspring”, “the trait was passed on to the next generation”.

kunikma: Identifying limitations of a data collection method and their effect on the results
usul: Check two things in each option: does this factor really affect the count, and is its effect described correctly?

variantlar.savol: The volunteers count passing birds during the day. Which of the following correctly identifies a factor that affects the accuracy of the counts and its effect?
javoblar: Ringed birds become heavier and fly slowly, so they are counted twice
The volunteers write the results in a different notebook each year, so the numbers become too high
Many birds fly at night, so some of them are not counted and the number comes out lower than the real one
Cranes are large birds, so there are no errors at all in counting them

yechim.ovoz: The observers work only during the day.

yechim.doska: Text: many birds fly at night
yechim.ovoz: So birds that pass at night are not seen.
This error makes the count lower than the real number — both the factor and its effect are clear.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) flying at night → undercounted
yechim.ovoz: The limitation of the method and its effect on the result are shown correctly.

xatolar.0: A small ring does not noticeably change a bird's speed, and flying slowly does not cause double counting.
xatolar.1: Which notebook the results are written in does not change the number — this is not a factor affecting accuracy.
xatolar.3: Even for flocks of large birds the count is an estimate; they can fly behind clouds or very high — it is wrong to say there are no errors.

variantlar.maslahat: To find a limitation of a study, ask yourself: “Which birds might the observers miss?”

kunikma: Comparing information on two maps and choosing the conclusions the maps support
usul: Check each claim separately: is there evidence for it on the maps? Claims about information that is not on the maps at all (changes in numbers, shifts over the years) are not supported.

variantlar.savol:
Which of the following claims are supported by the maps?
I. In spring, some of the birds return by a different route from the autumn one.
II. The birds spend the winter in an area to the southeast of where they nest.
III. Over the last ten years the number of cranes flying south has decreased.
IV. Over the years the migration routes have moved away from the Aral Sea.

yechim.doska: I: in spring there is an eastern route (over the mountains)
yechim.ovoz: Map 2 shows a new route that was not there in autumn — I is supported.

yechim.doska: II: wintering area is to the southeast
yechim.ovoz: On both maps the wintering area is below and to the right of the nesting area.

yechim.doska: III, IV: no data over the years
yechim.ovoz: The maps do not show changes in numbers or routes over time.
Only claims I and II are based on the maps.

xatolar.0: II is also supported: the wintering area lies to the southeast of the nesting area.
xatolar.2: III is not on the maps — the arrows show flock size, but not changes over the years.
xatolar.3: Claim IV would need maps from different years; the maps given summarize ten years and do not show any shift.

variantlar.maslahat: In map questions, first read the key (arrow thickness, compass), then support each claim with a specific feature on the map.

kunikma: Explaining why an object speeds up as it approaches a celestial body using the force of gravity
usul: What changes an object's speed? Find the force acting on it.

variantlar.savol: A meteoroid falling toward the Moon moves faster and faster as it gets closer to the Moon's surface. What is the reason for this?
javoblar: The Moon spins on its axis and pushes the meteoroid toward itself
The Moon's atmosphere heats the meteoroid and increases its speed
The meteoroid is pulled by the Moon's mass
Sunlight pushes the meteoroid from behind and drives it toward the Moon

yechim.doska: Speed changes → a force is acting
yechim.ovoz: If an object is speeding up, a force is acting on it in the direction of motion.

yechim.doska: Objects with mass attract each other
yechim.ovoz: This is universal gravitation.
The Moon's mass pulls the meteoroid and speeds it up.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) the Moon's mass pulls it
yechim.ovoz: The reason for the speeding up is the force of gravity.

xatolar.0: Spinning on its axis does not create a force that pushes objects.
xatolar.1: According to the text, the Moon has almost no atmosphere; and heating does not increase speed.
xatolar.3: The pressure of sunlight is very small and is not necessarily directed toward the Moon — it does not explain the speeding up.

variantlar.maslahat: In a “why does it speed up?” question, look for the force acting on the object; for celestial bodies this is usually the force of gravity.

kunikma: Explaining the link between the thickness of an atmosphere, meteoroids burning up, and the number of craters
usul: In a denser atmosphere a meteoroid travels farther through air and experiences more friction. From this, work out how many reach the surface.

variantlar.savol: Venus's atmosphere is much denser than Earth's. How would the number of small craters on the surface of Venus be expected to compare with Earth, and why?
javoblar: Fewer, because more meteoroids burn up in the atmosphere
More, because more meteoroids burn up in the atmosphere
More, because fewer meteoroids burn up in the atmosphere
Fewer, because fewer meteoroids burn up in the atmosphere

yechim.ovoz: A meteoroid heats up more strongly in dense air.
Small meteoroids in particular do not reach the surface.

yechim.doska: Fewer reach the surface → fewer craters
yechim.ovoz: Only meteoroids that do not burn up in time form craters.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) Fewer, more burn up
yechim.ovoz: The denser the atmosphere, the fewer small craters there are.

xatolar.1: If more meteoroids burn up, fewer reach the surface — the number of craters cannot increase.
xatolar.2: In a dense atmosphere, the number of meteoroids that burn up does not decrease — it increases.
xatolar.3: The conclusion is correct, but the reason is wrong: in a dense atmosphere more meteoroids burn up, not fewer.

variantlar.maslahat: Write out the cause-and-effect chain step by step: atmosphere → burning up → reaching the surface → craters.

kunikma: Determining the size of a meteoroid from the size of its crater
usul: A larger meteoroid leaves a larger crater. Compare the craters in the picture by size.

variantlar.savol: Put the craters in order by the size of the meteoroids that made them, from largest to smallest.

yechim.ovoz: The size of a crater depends on the size of the meteoroid.

yechim.doska: In the picture: K largest, L medium, M small
yechim.ovoz: We compare the sizes of the circles.
The order by meteoroid size is K, L, M.

xatolar.1: This is the reverse order — from smallest to largest.
xatolar.2: Crater L lies inside K and is smaller than it — L is not the largest.
xatolar.3: Crater M is smaller than L, so it cannot be in second place.

variantlar.maslahat: Pay attention to the direction “from largest to smallest” — reversing the order is the most common mistake.

kunikma: Determining the order in which craters formed from how they overlap
usul: A crater that formed later lies on top of an earlier one and breaks its rim. Work out which crater lies on top of which.

variantlar.savol: Put the craters in order of when they formed, from oldest to newest.

yechim.doska: Rim of K cuts across M → M came first
yechim.ovoz: Part of crater M is covered by K, so M is older than K.

yechim.doska: L is entirely inside K → L came later
yechim.ovoz: If L had come first, K would have destroyed it; L is intact — so it formed after K.
The oldest is M, then K, and the newest is L.
That is the order according to the overlap rule.

xatolar.0: This is the order by size, not by age; K lies on top of M, so M is older than K.
xatolar.1: L sits intact inside K — it formed after K, not before.
xatolar.2: L lies inside K, so it cannot have formed before K.

variantlar.maslahat: A rule from geology: when marks overlap, the intact (undamaged) mark is the newest and the damaged one is older.

kunikma: Explaining the scientific advantage of repeated (multiple) measurements
usul: Even on one slope, shade, rocks, and steepness vary. What do the results of two instruments tell us about this?

variantlar.savol: Why did the students set up two instruments, rather than one, for each factor on each slope?
javoblar: So that one instrument measures during the day and the other at night
To take into account differences in conditions within a slope, make the measurements more accurate, and check whether the difference between the slopes is real
To add the results of the two instruments and double the total solar energy reaching the slope
Because the instruments were cheap, so the extra ones could be used up too

yechim.doska: Conditions vary even on one slope
yechim.ovoz: One spot may be in the shade and another in the open.
Several measurements make the mean more reliable and allow the uncertainty to be estimated.
Only then can we trust the difference between the slopes.

yechim.doska: Answer: B) accuracy and checking the difference
yechim.ovoz: That is the scientific purpose of repeated measurement.

xatolar.0: The text says the instruments all worked the same way for one month; nothing is said about splitting into day and night.
xatolar.2: The results are not added; their mean is taken — the energy received does not depend on the number of instruments.
xatolar.3: Price is not a scientific reason; the question asks about the scientific logic of the study design.

variantlar.maslahat: In questions about study design, think: “how does this step make the results more trustworthy?”

kunikma: Interpreting data while taking measurement uncertainty into account, and evaluating two claims
usul: For each factor, write the ranges for the two slopes (mean ± uncertainty) and check whether or not they overlap.

variantlar.savol:
Two students are arguing about the reason for the difference in soil moisture.
Student 1: “The reason for the difference is the difference in precipitation”.
Student 2: “The reason for the difference is the difference in solar radiation”.
According to the table, which student is right?
javoblar: Student 1, because more precipitation falls on the south slope (545 > 520)
Student 2, because the difference in radiation is much larger than the uncertainty, while the precipitation ranges overlap
Student 2, because less precipitation falls on the north slope
Both are right, because the mean values of both factors are different

yechim.ovoz: The ranges overlap — there is no real difference in precipitation.
The ranges do not overlap at all — the difference is real and large.
On the south slope there is more evaporation, so the moisture is lower.
The difference in radiation explains the difference in moisture.

xatolar.0: The 25 mm difference is within the uncertainty (±45 and ±50 mm) — this difference cannot be relied on; besides, the slope that got more precipitation turned out drier.
xatolar.2: The conclusion is correct, but the reason is wrong: there is no reliable difference in precipitation; Student 2's claim is based on radiation.
xatolar.3: It is not enough for the mean values to be different: the precipitation difference is within the uncertainty, so it is not a reliable difference.

variantlar.maslahat: Write results given with “±” as ranges: if the ranges overlap, the difference is not reliable.

kunikma: Understanding the roles of organisms in an ecosystem and placing them to fit the purpose of the system
usul: Write down the role of each pond (growing food, raising fish, cleaning water), then work out which role each organism performs.

variantlar.savol: How should the organisms be placed so that the carp have food and the water returns clean to the river?
javoblar: Pond 2: carp and daphnia; Pond 3: reeds and mussels
Pond 2: carp and reeds; Pond 3: daphnia and mussels
Pond 2: carp and mussels; Pond 3: daphnia and reeds
Pond 2: carp, daphnia, and mussels; Pond 3: reeds

yechim.ovoz: We work out the role of each pond from the diagram.

yechim.doska: Daphnia eat microalgae, carp eat daphnia
yechim.ovoz: Food chain: microalgae → daphnia → carp; they are together in Pond 2.
Both clean the water, so they go in Pond 3.
Then the fish are well fed and the water returns clean.

xatolar.1: If the daphnia are in Pond 3, the carp are left without food; and the reeds are needed in the final cleaning pond, not in Pond 2.
xatolar.2: Carp feed on daphnia; mussels in Pond 2 would compete with the daphnia for microalgae, and the carp would be left without food.
xatolar.3: The mussels would eat the daphnia's food, and in Pond 3 the job of cleaning particles from the water would not get done.

variantlar.maslahat: In a question about a system, first write down the goal (“the fish are fed, the water returns clean”), then link each part to that goal.

kunikma: Using descriptions of organisms to choose the organism that solves a problem
usul: From the list of organisms, find the one that absorbs nutrients from the water.

variantlar.savol: A check showed that a lot of nutrients are leaving the farm and going into the river. What should be added more of in Pond 3 to reduce the problem?

yechim.doska: Problem: too many nutrients in water
yechim.ovoz: We need an organism that takes nutrients out of the water.
In the list, only the reeds have this role.
If there are more reeds, fewer nutrients go into the river.

xatolar.0: More carp produce more waste — the nutrients would increase even more.
xatolar.1: Daphnia eat microalgae, not nutrients dissolved in the water.
xatolar.3: Mussels catch microalgae and particles; they do not absorb dissolved nutrients.

variantlar.maslahat: Compare the descriptions in the text word for word with the problem in the question: “absorb nutrients” is the key phrase.

kunikma: Applying the idea of sustainability to choose a way to improve a system
usul: A sustainable system takes few resources from outside and turns waste into something useful. Does each option fit this?

variantlar.savol: Which of the following changes would make the fish farm more sustainable?
javoblar: Making the water flow through the ponds faster
Replacing the filters between the ponds with ones that let large organisms through too
Producing biogas from the organisms' waste and using this fuel to run the water pumps

yechim.ovoz: A sustainable system uses its own waste and depends little on outside energy.
No outside energy is needed for the pumps, and there is also less waste.

yechim.doska: Others: use up resources or break the system
yechim.ovoz: Extra nutrients or a faster flow do not make the system more sustainable.
This brings the system closer to supplying itself.

xatolar.0: If the flow is faster, the pumps use more energy and the water does not have time to be cleaned.
xatolar.1: Adding more nutrients increases the use of outside resources and increases the waste going into the river.
xatolar.2: If large organisms mix between the ponds, the role of each pond is disrupted.

variantlar.maslahat: When you see the word “sustainable”, ask two questions: are outside resources reduced? is waste turned into something useful?

kunikma: Explaining the effect of an electricity shortage on community life with a cause-and-effect chain
usul: Check two things in each option: is this really a problem for the town, and is it clearly linked to the electricity shortage?

variantlar.savol: If the town does not have enough electricity, what problem will it face? Choose the answer that correctly links the problem to the electricity shortage.
javoblar: People will get food poisoning more often
Some families will not be able to watch TV in the evening
Refrigerators will stop working, food will spoil, and the risk of food poisoning will increase
Because there is little electricity, carbon dioxide in the air will increase

yechim.doska: Need a problem + a link to electricity
yechim.ovoz: The answer must include both the problem and how it results from the lack of electricity.
The reason: refrigerators run on electricity.
This is a serious problem for the whole town.
Only in C is the problem linked to the electricity shortage through a chain.

xatolar.0: A problem is stated, but it does not show how it results from the electricity shortage.
xatolar.1: Not being able to watch TV is not a serious problem for the town — it does not affect safety or health.
xatolar.3: A lack of electricity does not in itself increase CO₂; this link is wrong.

variantlar.maslahat: In an “explain the problem” question, build your answer on the pattern “because there is no …, … does not work, and as a result …”.

kunikma: Comparing several graphs/tables to identify a source that always covers demand
usul: Find the highest value of demand and compare it with the lowest amount each source supplies during the day.

variantlar.savol: Which single source can always cover the town's demand throughout the day?

yechim.ovoz: The source must be enough even at the busiest time.
These sources supply less than the demand at some times.
Only gas supplies more than the demand at every hour.
Only gas is enough as the single source.

xatolar.0: From 10:00 to 14:00 wind supplies only 8 MW, while demand is 24 MW — not enough.
xatolar.1: Solar supplies no energy at all at night.
xatolar.2: Hydro is constant, but only 22 MW; after 10:00 demand rises to 24–34 MW.

variantlar.maslahat: The word “always” means you must check the worst time: find the hour when demand is highest and the source is lowest.

kunikma: Combining information from several sources to choose the best solution by cost and reliability, and evaluating its risk
usul: For each pair, first use the first source fully and make up the shortfall with the second. Check whether it is enough at every hour, then compare the cost.

variantlar.savol: The town wants to use two sources: the first source's power is used fully, and the second is switched on only when the first is not enough. Which pair always supplies the town at the lowest cost, with its risk stated correctly?
javoblar: Hydro | gas — gas is expensive, but this pair has no risk at all
Wind | solar — both are clean sources, so they are safe
Hydro | wind — wind cannot be predicted; if the wind drops in the evening, there may not be enough power
Hydro | wind — wind turbines use a lot of river water and will stop the hydro station

yechim.ovoz: For example, at 20:00, 22 + 26 = 48 MW ≥ 34 MW.
This pair does not cover demand in the evening.
If the rest is covered by wind at 420 thousand soums, it is cheaper than gas at 850.
On an evening when the wind is weak, there may not be enough power.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) Hydro | wind + wind risk
yechim.ovoz: The cheapest reliable pair, and the real risk that comes with it.

xatolar.0: Hydro | gas works, but the shortfall is covered by expensive gas (850 thousand soums) — it is not the cheapest; gas also carries risks of price and pollution.
xatolar.1: Wind and solar together do not cover demand from 18:00 to 24:00 (for example, at 22:00, 22 < 26).
xatolar.3: The pair is correct, but the risk is wrong: wind turbines do not use water.

variantlar.maslahat: Choosing a combination takes two steps: (1) is it enough at every hour? (2) of those that are enough, which is cheapest? Then think about the weak point of your choice.

kunikma: Calculating surplus and missing energy to evaluate a battery solution
usul: Calculate the surplus energy in the periods when demand is below the hydro power, and the shortfall in the periods when demand is higher (MW × 2 hours), and compare them.

variantlar.savol: The town wants to use only hydro, storing surplus energy in a battery and then using it when demand is high. Will this solution always supply the town?
javoblar: Yes, because hydro supplies the same power day and night
Yes, because there is surplus energy at night and it is stored in the battery
No, because the surplus energy at night (56 MWh) is less than the shortfall during the day and evening (72 MWh)
No, because a battery cannot be charged with hydro energy

yechim.ovoz: From 00:00 to 08:00 demand is below 22 MW — we multiply the difference by two hours.
From 10:00 to 24:00 demand is above 22 MW.
The stored energy does not fully cover the shortfall.
Hydro and a battery alone are not enough.

xatolar.0: A constant power of 22 MW is not enough when demand rises to 34 MW; being constant does not mean being sufficient.
xatolar.1: Having surplus energy is not enough — its amount (56 MWh) is less than the shortfall (72 MWh).
xatolar.3: A battery can be charged by any electricity source, including hydro.

variantlar.maslahat: Energy = power × time. In an “is it enough?” question, calculate the amounts and compare them; do not stop at “there is / there isn't”.

kunikma: Explaining which source a carbon tax affects and the government's goals
usul: Work out which source emits CO₂ when generating electricity. Then think about how the purpose of the tax relates to the environment and the economy.

variantlar.savol: The government introduced a “carbon tax” for every tonne of carbon dioxide emitted in generating electricity. Which source's price will rise the most, and for what purposes might the government introduce this tax?
javoblar: Gas; the purpose is to raise money for clean energy research and to encourage sources that do less harm to the environment
Gas; the purpose is to supply the town with constant power and to increase the total power produced
Solar; the purpose is to raise money for clean energy research and to reduce polluting sources
Hydro; the purpose is to use river water efficiently and to increase the total power

yechim.ovoz: Wind, solar, and hydro do not emit CO₂ when they operate.

yechim.doska: Tax → gas electricity becomes more expensive
yechim.ovoz: That is why the price of gas rises the most.
Expensive gas encourages people to switch to clean sources.
The tax collected can be directed to clean energy inventions.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) Gas; two environmental goals
yechim.ovoz: Both the source and the goals are correct.

xatolar.1: The source is correct, but the tax does not increase power or guarantee a constant supply — that is not the purpose of the tax.
xatolar.2: Solar panels do not emit CO₂ when they operate, so their price hardly rises because of the tax.
xatolar.3: Hydro does not emit CO₂ either; saving water and increasing power are not the purposes of a carbon tax.

variantlar.maslahat: Find “what” the tax is placed on (here, CO₂) — the tax affects the source that emits it.

kunikma: Explaining the relationship between predator and prey populations
usul: Who eats whom? Think about what happens to the number of those being eaten if the eaters increase.

variantlar.savol: If the number of ladybugs in a cotton field increases, what happens to the number of aphids in that field, and why?
javoblar: It increases, because ladybugs leave more food for the aphids
It decreases, because ladybugs feed on aphids
It does not change, because ladybugs and aphids eat different food
It decreases, because ladybugs eat the cotton leaves and leave the aphids without food

yechim.ovoz: According to the text, ladybugs and their larvae eat aphids.
Each ladybug destroys hundreds of aphids.
That is why ladybugs are considered useful.

yechim.doska: Answer: B) It decreases — predator and prey
yechim.ovoz: The correct reason: ladybugs eat aphids.

xatolar.0: Ladybugs do not leave food for aphids; on the contrary, they eat them.
xatolar.2: The text says ladybugs feed on aphids — they are directly linked.
xatolar.3: The result is correct, but the reason is wrong: ladybugs do not eat plant leaves; they are predatory insects.

variantlar.maslahat: In a question about populations, first draw the food chain: cotton → aphid → ladybug.

kunikma: Explaining the reason for molting in insects (exoskeleton and growth)
usul: An exoskeleton does not stretch. What happens to the old covering as the larva grows?

variantlar.savol: Why do ladybug larvae molt several times?
javoblar: They grow quickly and no longer fit inside their outer covering
They eat their old skin to get extra food
They replace their skin because aphids have damaged it
Their internal backbone grows and breaks through the skin

yechim.doska: The exoskeleton is hard and does not stretch
yechim.ovoz: It protects the body, but it does not grow.
After a while, the body no longer fits inside the old covering.

yechim.doska: The old skin is shed and a larger one forms
yechim.ovoz: This process is repeated at each stage of growth.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) grows quickly, no longer fits its covering
yechim.ovoz: Molting is for growth.

xatolar.1: The main reason for molting is growth, not feeding.
xatolar.2: The skin is replaced because it has become too small, not because it is damaged.
xatolar.3: Insects have no backbone — they are invertebrates.

variantlar.maslahat: Insects and crustaceans have their skeleton on the outside — that is why they molt in order to grow.

kunikma: Applying the life cycle and the principle of maintaining a population to a real production situation
usul: Follow the life cycle: larvae released into the fields do not come back to the biofactory. Where do new larvae come from?

variantlar.savol: At the biofactory, most larvae are released into the fields, but some are deliberately kept in the laboratory. What is the reason for this?
javoblar: The larvae that are kept grow into adults and lay eggs, so that new larvae keep appearing at the biofactory
The extra larvae are kept because there is not enough room for them in the fields
The larvae that are kept eat the aphids in the biofactory and clean the room
Some of the larvae are sick, so they are not released into the fields

yechim.doska: Life cycle: egg → larva → pupa → beetle
yechim.ovoz: Only an adult female lays new eggs.

yechim.doska: If all are released → the cycle is broken
yechim.ovoz: There would be no ladybugs left at the biofactory to lay eggs.

yechim.doska: Those kept → grow into adults and reproduce
yechim.ovoz: Because of this, production continues without a break.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) to keep the cycle going
yechim.ovoz: Maintaining the population is the main reason for keeping some.

xatolar.1: The fields are large, and the text says nothing about lack of space; this is not a biological reason.
xatolar.2: At the biofactory the larvae are fed on aphids, but that is not the reason for keeping them — the main goal is breeding.
xatolar.3: The text gives no information about disease; keeping some on purpose is a planned process.

variantlar.maslahat: Sustainable production follows the rule of keeping a “seed” portion — seed grain for wheat, breeding individuals for insects.

kunikma: Applying the difference between the speeds of light and sound in air to an everyday event
usul: The flash and the sound are produced at the same moment. Which one reaches the observer faster?

variantlar.savol: Why is the flash of a firework seen before its sound is heard?
javoblar: The eyes work faster than the ears, and the brain senses sound later
Light travels through air much faster than sound
Light needs air to travel, while sound can travel without air
Sound is heavier than light, so it travels slowly

yechim.doska: Flash and sound are produced at the same time
yechim.ovoz: Both are produced at the moment of the explosion.
Light arrives almost instantly, while sound takes about 3 s to travel a kilometer.
The delay comes from the difference in speeds.

xatolar.0: The difference in reaction time between the eyes and ears is thousandths of a second — it does not explain a delay of seconds; the delay depends on distance.
xatolar.2: It is the other way around: light also travels through a vacuum, while sound needs a medium (air).
xatolar.3: Sound is a wave, not a substance; it has no “weight”.

variantlar.maslahat: Remember that the delay increases as the distance increases — this shows it depends on wave speed, not on the sense organs.

kunikma: Using table data to test the effect of one factor while another factor is kept constant
usul: Find rows with the same distance but different charges, and compare the delay times.

variantlar.savol: Does the size of the firework charge affect the delay between the flash and the sound? Answer with evidence from the table.
javoblar: Yes: in experiment 8, with a large charge, the delay is 11.7 s, but in experiment 1, with a small charge, it is 2.9 s
No: at a distance of 2 km the delay is always 5.8 s for small, medium, and large charges
Yes: a large charge is louder, so its sound arrives faster
No: because in experiment 6 there was only one measurement

yechim.doska: Rows with the same distance: 3, 4, 5 (2 km)
yechim.ovoz: In these rows only the charge size differs.
Even when the charge changed, the delay did not change.
At 1 km it is 2.9 s and at 4 km it is 11.7 s — whatever the charge.

yechim.doska: Answer: B) No — at 2 km always 5.8 s
yechim.ovoz: The delay depends only on distance.

xatolar.0: Experiments 1 and 8 also differ in distance (1 km and 4 km); the difference in delay comes from the distance.
xatolar.2: How loud a sound is does not change its speed — at 4 km the time is the same for small and large charges (11.7 s).
xatolar.3: The conclusion is correct, but the evidence is wrong: experiment 6 does not show the effect of the charge, because no other charge was tested at 3 km.

variantlar.maslahat: In a “does it affect…?” question, compare only rows where just that factor changed — a pair in which another factor also changed is not evidence.

kunikma: Choosing and applying a method to calculate the speed of sound from experimental data
usul: Speed = distance ÷ time. Convert the distance to meters and calculate using one row.

variantlar.savol: How can the speed of sound in air be found from the data in the table, and approximately what is it?
javoblar: Divide the time by the distance: 11.7 ÷ 4000 ≈ 0.003 m/s
Multiply the distance by the time: 4000 · 11.7 ≈ 46 800 m/s
Divide the distance by the time: 4000 m ÷ 11.7 s ≈ 342 m/s
Divide the distance by the number of charge sizes: 4000 ÷ 3 ≈ 1333 m/s

yechim.ovoz: The sound travels the distance to the observer during the delay time.
Since light arrives almost instantly, the delay is the travel time of the sound.
The other rows also give about 340–345 m/s (2000 ÷ 5.8 ≈ 345).
The method and the result are correct.

xatolar.0: Dividing time by distance does not give speed but “the time taken per meter”; the unit is not m/s either.
xatolar.1: The product of distance and time does not give speed; the result is a hundred times greater than the real speed of sound.
xatolar.3: The charge size does not affect the delay, so including it in the calculation makes no sense.

variantlar.maslahat: Check your result against what you know: the speed of sound in air is about 340 m/s. A number that is far too large or far too small points to a mistake in the method.

kunikma: Extending a pattern in a table to make a prediction for a distance that was not tested
usul: The delay is proportional to distance: when the distance increases by some factor, the time increases by the same factor. Use the time for 1 km.

variantlar.savol: An observer is standing 10 km from where a firework explodes. How many seconds after seeing the flash will he hear the sound? (Write a whole number or round to the nearest tenth.)

yechim.ovoz: When the distance doubles, the time also doubles.
So the time is also 10 times the time for 1 km.
The sound will be heard after about 29 seconds.

xatolar.umumiy: Common mistakes: adding up distances (11.7 + 6 · 2.9), changing the time depending on the charge size, or multiplying, as in 343 · 10.

variantlar.maslahat: In a proportional relationship, find one “unit” value (the time for 1 km), then multiply by the number you need.

kunikma: Identifying science-based measures that reduce the environmental harm of growing cotton
usul: Evaluate each measure separately: does it really reduce water use, chemical pollution, or harm to living organisms, or does it just move the problem somewhere else?

variantlar.savol:
Which of the following measures reduce the environmental harm of producing cotton fabric?
I. Switching to drip irrigation and using water efficiently.
II. Lowering the quality of the fabric produced.
III. Increasing the number of workers on the farm.
IV. Using pesticides or biological methods that affect only the pest species.
V. Taking chemical waste far away from the fields and burying it.

yechim.doska: I: less water taken → good for the rivers and the Aral
yechim.ovoz: Efficient irrigation reduces the amount of water taken.

yechim.doska: IV: targeted products → useful species survive
yechim.ovoz: Other insects, birds, and soil animals are not harmed.

yechim.doska: V: the waste does not disappear, it just moves
yechim.ovoz: Burying it far away moves the pollution to another area.

yechim.doska: II, III: nothing to do with the environment
yechim.ovoz: Poor-quality fabric is thrown away sooner; the number of workers does not reduce harm.
You need to choose both correct measures and rule out the wrong ones.

xatolar.0: IV is also correct: products that affect only the pest protect other living organisms.
xatolar.2: V does not solve the problem — chemical waste pollutes soil and water even far away.
xatolar.3: Lowering fabric quality makes “fast fashion” worse, and the number of workers does not change the environmental impact.

variantlar.maslahat: In a “select all that apply” question, evaluate each statement separately with “yes/no”, and only then choose an option.

kunikma: Distinguishing evidence that supports a claim (with its mechanism) from other statements
usul: A statement that just repeats the claim in other words is not evidence. Look for a statement that compares organic and conventional cotton and shows the reason.

variantlar.savol: A researcher made this claim: “Growing organic cotton is safer for bodies of water, because fewer harmful substances run off organic fields into irrigation ditches and drainage channels”. Which of the following statements supports this claim?
javoblar: Growing organic cotton does less harm to bodies of water
Because no synthetic fertilizers or pesticides are used on organic fields, much lower levels of nitrate and pesticide residues were found in their drainage water
The water running off organic cotton fields and organic wheat fields has the same composition
The drainage channels of cotton fields eventually flow into large bodies of water

yechim.doska: Need: organic vs. conventional comparison + reason
yechim.ovoz: Evidence must show that the claim is true.

yechim.doska: B: has a measured result and a mechanism
yechim.ovoz: No synthetic substances are used → fewer residues in the drainage water.

yechim.doska: A — repetition, C and D — answer a different question
yechim.ovoz: They do not compare organic and conventional cotton.

yechim.doska: Answer: B) fewer residues in drainage water
yechim.ovoz: Only B supports the claim.

xatolar.0: This just repeats the claim itself in other words — no evidence is given.
xatolar.2: Two organic crops are compared; there is no information about the difference between organic and conventional cotton.
xatolar.3: This is a general fact about all cotton fields; it does not show any advantage of the organic method.

variantlar.maslahat: When choosing evidence, ask: “Does this statement compare the organic and conventional methods, and does it show the reason for the difference?”

kunikma: Applying criteria to judge the reliability of sources of scientific information
usul: Compare who the author of each source is, whether they have an interest in the outcome, whether the work was checked by other experts, and over how many years the data were collected.

variantlar.savol:
There are three sources about organic cotton:
A — The website of an online store that sells organic cotton clothing: “Organic cotton protects nature and is good for the earth”.
B — The blog of a business journalist who spoke at a nonprofit conference: “Organic cotton gives lower yields, so it needs more land and water”.
C — An article in an international journal, peer-reviewed by agricultural scientists (the author is a data analysis specialist): “From 2019 to 2023 the yields of organic and conventional cotton were compared every year; the average difference is not significant: in 2023, organic 28 centners/ha, conventional 29 centners/ha”.
Which source is the most reliable, and why?
javoblar: C — it was checked by other experts, the results were compared over several years, and the author is a data analysis specialist
C — the text is nicely written and it gives a definition of organic cotton
A — the store works with organic cotton, so it knows it better than anyone
B — the journalist reaches many people and spoke at a conference

yechim.doska: A: seller — has an interest, no evidence
yechim.ovoz: The store benefits from praising its own product.

yechim.doska: B: not an expert, no numbers
yechim.ovoz: A business journalist is not an agricultural scientist.

yechim.doska: C: peer review + 5 years of data + expert
yechim.ovoz: It has three signs of reliability at once.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) source C, with three reasons
yechim.ovoz: Both the source and the reasons are correct.

xatolar.1: The source is chosen correctly, but the reasons are not criteria of reliability: being nicely written and including a definition do not indicate scientific quality.
xatolar.2: The seller is an interested party — what it says may be advertising, and no data are given.
xatolar.3: The size of the audience does not make a source more reliable; the journalist is not an expert in this field and gave no evidence.

variantlar.maslahat: To evaluate a source, remember “WRIT”: Who wrote it? Was it Reviewed (peer review)? Does the author have an Interest? Is there enough data over Time?

kunikma: Explaining the environmental advantage of renewable energy over fossil fuels
usul: Compare what is produced when coal and gas are burned with what happens when a wind turbine operates.

variantlar.savol: What benefit does getting electricity from wind instead of coal and gas bring to the environment?
javoblar: No carbon dioxide is released when generating electricity, so greenhouse gases and air pollution are reduced
Wind turbines absorb carbon dioxide from the air and turn it into oxygen
Wind turbines cool the air and stop global warming
Wind energy is always cheaper than coal, so nature is not harmed

yechim.doska: Coal and gas burn → CO₂ and smoke
yechim.ovoz: Burning releases carbon dioxide and harmful gases.
Nothing burns, and no CO₂ is released.
This helps slow down climate change.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) no CO₂ is released
yechim.ovoz: The main environmental benefit is a reduction in waste gases.

xatolar.1: Turbines do not absorb CO₂ — that is photosynthesis, a process carried out by plants.
xatolar.2: Turbines do not cool the air; their benefit is that they do not release CO₂.
xatolar.3: Price is an economic measure, not an environmental benefit; also, the claim that it is “always cheaper” has no basis.

variantlar.maslahat: When asked for an environmental benefit, show how the burden on nature is reduced: waste, gases, pollution.

kunikma: Explaining the negative effect of a wind farm on the local ecosystem
usul: The answer must concern the living things in this particular place, and the effect must really be negative.

variantlar.savol: What negative effect might a wind farm have on the local natural environment in the area where it is built?
javoblar: The turbines will stop the wind across the whole region and cause it to stop raining
The price of electricity will go up
Birds may be killed by flying into the turning blades, and during construction the plant cover and animal burrows may be destroyed
The turbines release a lot of carbon dioxide when they operate

yechim.ovoz: The effect must be on the living organisms right around the wind farm.
This is a big danger, especially on a migration route.
Roads and foundations destroy plants and burrows.
A real negative effect on the local ecosystem.

xatolar.0: Turbines only slow the wind slightly; they cannot change the climate of a whole region — this is an exaggerated claim.
xatolar.1: Price is an economic issue, not an effect on the local natural environment.
xatolar.3: An operating turbine burns nothing and does not release CO₂.

variantlar.maslahat: When asked about “effects on the local natural environment”, name specific living organisms and their habitats.

kunikma: Considering economic and environmental factors together to choose and justify a compromise solution
usul: Make two columns for each zone: cost (distance) and harm to nature. Find the zone that is acceptable in both.

variantlar.savol: In which zone would building the wind farm be the best compromise between cost and environmental impact?
javoblar: Zone A — closest to the grid, so it is the cheapest option
Zone B — plants do not move around, so the turbines will not disturb them
Zone C — more expensive than A and B, but the animals here can move to neighboring areas; and it is much cheaper than zone D
Zone D — the farthest away, so there will be no effect on nature at all

yechim.doska: A: cheap, but on the birds' route
yechim.ovoz: The turbines would cause many birds to die.
They do not grow anywhere else — they could become extinct.

yechim.doska: C and D: little impact, and C is cheaper
yechim.ovoz: 30 km of cable is much cheaper than 70 km, and the animals can move away.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) both cost and nature are considered
yechim.ovoz: A compromise is a solution that is acceptable on both factors.

xatolar.0: Only cost is considered; in zone A large flocks of birds fly low — the environmental harm is great.
xatolar.1: Precisely because they cannot move away, the rare plants could be wiped out completely by construction.
xatolar.3: There are animals in zone D too, so the impact is not zero; on top of that, it is the most expensive option.

variantlar.maslahat: In a compromise question, your answer must mention both sides, for example: “even though it is more expensive, … it does less harm to nature”.

kunikma: Reading and comparing values from a bar chart
usul: Read the length of each bar using the scale and compare it with the claim in the option.

variantlar.savol: Which of the following claims is supported by the data in the graph?
javoblar: The percentage of threatened species is the same for mammals and birds
The percentage of threatened species is higher for birds than for the other groups
The percentage of threatened species is higher for fish than for the other groups
The percentage of threatened species is higher for vascular plants than for reptiles

yechim.ovoz: The other groups are between 8 and 20 %.
They are not equal.
Claim D is the other way around.
The graph supports only C.

xatolar.1: The percentage for birds (12 %) is one of the lowest.
xatolar.3: The percentage for vascular plants is 8 % and for reptiles 16 % — the opposite is true.

variantlar.maslahat: On a chart, read the ends of the bars against the scale lines; comparing roughly by eye leads to mistakes.

kunikma: Judging the reliability of a source of scientific information using the criteria of expertise and peer review
usul: A reliable source is one that has been checked by experts on the topic and has no interest in the outcome.

variantlar.savol: Which information best shows that the article containing the graph is reliable?

The article is based on sources checked by scientists who are experts in biodiversity
The article was written by a famous athlete
The article was published by a company that sells ecotourism trips

This guarantees the quality of the information.
They do not indicate scientific reliability.
The most reliable sign is expert review.

xatolar.2: An athlete is not a biodiversity expert.
xatolar.3: An ecotourism company has an interest — it makes money from nature topics.

variantlar.maslahat: Ask about the source: “Who checked it, and are they an expert in this field?”

kunikma: Judging whether data can or cannot serve as evidence for a claim (epistemic knowledge)
usul: Compare what the claim in the headline is about (the cause) with what the graph actually shows.

Yes, because fish live in water, and the Aral Sea is a body of water
No, because the graph only shows the percentage of threatened species; there is no information about any link with the Aral Sea or its drying
No, because in the graph the percentage for fish is lower than for the other groups

yechim.doska: Claim: the cause is the drying of the Aral Sea
yechim.ovoz: The headline claims a cause-and-effect relationship.
It has nothing about the Aral Sea, water level, or change over time.

yechim.doska: No information about the cause → not evidence
yechim.ovoz: The graph neither supports nor rejects the claim.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) No — no link is shown
yechim.ovoz: The data are not sufficient or relevant for the claim.

xatolar.0: A high percentage does not show the cause; the threat may come from other factors too — the graph has no evidence for this.
xatolar.1: The fact that fish live in water does not prove that the drying of the Aral Sea is wiping them out.
xatolar.3: The graph has been misread: the percentage for fish (36 %) is the highest.

variantlar.maslahat: When evaluating a claim, ask: “Was the cause in the claim measured in the data at all?” If it was not measured, it is not evidence.

kunikma: Find specific information about time in a blog text (where other dates and periods are mixed in)
usul: Identify what the question asks: when the fieldwork BEGAN. Mark all the time expressions in the text and check which one refers to exactly this event.

yechim.ovoz: First we find all the words in the text that refer to time — there are three of them.

yechim.doska: “the rusting ships I have studied for the past nine months”
yechim.ovoz: The professor writes that she studied the ships for the past nine months, so the fieldwork lasted that long.

yechim.doska: The 1990s — when the mystery of the ships was solved
yechim.ovoz: The 1990s refer not to the fieldwork but to the time when the mystery of the ships was solved; May 23 is the date of the post.
So the correct answer is option B.

xatolar.2: The text does not say “one year” — avoid estimates and rely on the exact “nine months” in the text.
xatolar.3: May 23 is the date of the post. It was written when the fieldwork was ending, not when it began.

variantlar.maslahat: If a text contains several dates, write down next to each one what it refers to.

kunikma: Understand exactly what a sentence in the text refers to (literal meaning)
usul: Find the given sentence in the text and read the sentences that follow it: the question that comes after the word “mystery” is the answer.

variantlar.savol: Based on Source 1 (the blog). In the last part of the blog, the professor writes, “However, another mystery still remains.” Which mystery does she mean?
javoblar: How the ships ended up sitting on the sand
When the cannery in Moynaq closed
Why the sea dried up almost completely in only half a century
When the professor will return to Tashkent

yechim.ovoz: The word “however” shows that this is a new mystery, different from the first one.

yechim.doska: Next sentence: “Why did the sea … dry up almost completely?”
yechim.ovoz: The question that comes right after this sentence is exactly the mystery the professor means.

yechim.doska: The mystery of the ships — described as “solved”
yechim.ovoz: The mystery of the ships was already solved in the previous paragraph, so it cannot be “another mystery.”

yechim.doska: Answer: C) Why the sea dried up almost completely in only half…
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option C.

xatolar.0: This is the first mystery, and it was solved in the 1990s. “Another mystery” means a new, unsolved one.
xatolar.1: The blog says nothing about the cannery closing; it only says that it operated in the 1960s.
xatolar.3: The time of her return is no mystery — the professor openly writes that she will “soon return.”

variantlar.maslahat: After words such as “however” or “but,” the author usually moves on to a new idea — read that part carefully.

kunikma: Sort the sentences in a review into facts (information that can be checked) and opinions (the author's judgments)
usul: Ask of each sentence: “Can this be checked and proven?” If it contains judgment words (tragic, skillfully, should), it is an opinion.

variantlar.savol:
Based on Source 2 (the review). Decide whether each of the following sentences from the review is a fact or an opinion.
1) The book describes several lakes and rivers that have changed dramatically because of human activity.
2) One of the most tragic examples in the book is the Aral Sea.
3) Starting in the 1960s, a large part of the water of the two rivers was diverted to irrigate fields.
4) In 1960, the Aral was the fourth-largest lake in the world.
5) The book is skillfully written, and everyone who loves nature should read it.
Which row gives the correct answers?

yechim.doska: 1) the content of the book — can be checked → fact
yechim.ovoz: You can open the book and see which lakes it describes — so this is a fact.
Each person judges for themselves which example is the most tragic; this is the reviewer's opinion.
The diversion of water for irrigation and the size of the lake can be checked with documents and measurements.
This is the reviewer's judgment and recommendation; it cannot be proven.

yechim.doska: Answer: A) fact, opinion, fact, fact, opinion
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option A.

xatolar.1: The words “most tragic” in sentence 2 are a judgment — this is an opinion. It is a mistake to think it is a fact just because the topic is serious.
xatolar.2: Sentence 1 describes the content of the book and can be checked by reading it — it is a fact, not an opinion.
xatolar.3: “The fourth-largest lake” in sentence 4 is the result of a measurement (area), not a judgment — it is a fact.

variantlar.maslahat: When separating facts from opinions, pay attention to judgment and recommendation words such as “most,” “remarkable,” “should” and “skillfully.”

kunikma: Find the point on which two sides agree in an article (separating it from distracting information nearby)
usul: Find the paragraph in the article that mentions the scientists and Nurmatov. Look at where the words “agree” and “disagree” appear: the idea that follows “agree” is the answer.

variantlar.savol: Based on Source 3 (the article). On what do the scientists mentioned in the article and Akmal Nurmatov agree?

yechim.doska: The cannery is mentioned only to show the time
yechim.ovoz: The cannery is not what they agree on; it is only a marker showing when the water decreased.

yechim.doska: Answer: D) That the amount of river water reaching the Aral fell sharply
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option D.

xatolar.1: This is Karimova and Yoldoshev's new theory; Nurmatov does not agree with this cause.
xatolar.2: The cannery is given only as a time marker (“after the period…”); what they agree on is the decrease in water.

variantlar.maslahat: In a text about a debate, mark the words “agree,” “admit,” “however” and “disagree” — they show who agrees on what.

kunikma: Distinguish the evidence supporting a theory from the theory itself and from general information
usul: First identify the theory (the climate is to blame; the sea also became shallower in the past). Then ask of each option: “Is this the theory itself, general information, or a finding that proves it?”

variantlar.savol: Based on Source 3 (the article). What evidence do Karimova and Yoldoshev give to support their theory?
javoblar: The Aral became shallower naturally several times in the past
In dry years, rivers carry little water to the sea

The remains of a 14th-century mausoleum were found on the dried-up seabed

yechim.ovoz: The article contains the phrase “to support their theory” — the evidence comes right after it.

yechim.doska: A and B — the theory itself; C — general information
yechim.ovoz: Repeating a claim does not prove it, and evaporation in hot weather is a general phenomenon that happens everywhere.

yechim.doska: Answer: D) The remains of a 14th-century mausoleum were fo…
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option D.

xatolar.1: This is also the theory's explanation (its mechanism), not a finding that supports it.
xatolar.2: This is general information: more evaporation in hot weather does not prove that the Aral became shallower in the past.

variantlar.maslahat: Evidence is something observed, found or measured. Do not confuse a claim or an explanation with evidence.

kunikma: Place two theories from several sources into a cause-and-effect table (finding the common effect)
usul: For each theory, ask separately: “What happened?” (effect) and “Why?” (cause). What both sides agree on is the common effect.

variantlar.savol: Based on all three sources. We placed the two theories in a table: “Nurmatov's cause — Karimova and Yoldoshev's cause — common effect for both.” Which row is filled in correctly?
javoblar: River water was diverted for irrigation — the climate became drier — ships were left stranded in the port

River water was diverted for irrigation — the climate became drier — too little water reached the sea
River water was diverted for irrigation — people dug canals — too little water reached the sea

yechim.doska: Common effect: too little river water reached the Aral
yechim.ovoz: Both sides agree that the amount of river water fell sharply — this is the common effect.

yechim.doska: The ships are a different mystery from the blog, not the effect
yechim.ovoz: The ships left on the sand are a separate matter; the theories do not explain it.

yechim.doska: Answer: C) River water was diverted for irrigation — the climate became…
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option C.

xatolar.0: The causes are correct, but the effect is wrong: the information about the ships comes from the blog and is not what the theories are about.
xatolar.1: The causes are swapped: the climate is Karimova and Yoldoshev's cause, and irrigation is Nurmatov's.
xatolar.3: Both causes are about irrigation. But Karimova and Yoldoshev see the main cause in the climate.

variantlar.maslahat: In a multi-source text, write each author's view on a separate line, then look for what they have in common.

kunikma: Read conflicting sources and choose a well-founded conclusion based on evidence in the text
usul: Check two things in each conclusion: 1) Is the evidence really in the sources? 2) Are the sources quoted correctly, without distortion?

variantlar.savol: Based on all three sources. Four students wrote answers to the question “What caused the Aral to dry up?” Which conclusion is CORRECTLY supported by the information in the sources?
javoblar: Only the climate is to blame: the scientists in the article say people played no role at all.
People are to blame: according to the review, a large part of the river water was diverted to the fields, and the scientists in the article also admit that irrigation played a role.
Storms are to blame: according to the blog, storms threw the ships onto land.
No conclusion can be drawn: all three sources say the sea did not dry up.

yechim.doska: Review: a large part of the water was diverted for irrigation
yechim.ovoz: The first piece of evidence in option B is written exactly like this in the review.

yechim.doska: Article: “they admit that irrigation also played a role”
yechim.ovoz: Even the authors of the rival theory do not deny the role of irrigation — this makes the conclusion even stronger.

yechim.doska: A, C, D — distort the sources
yechim.ovoz: In A, the scientists' words are distorted; in C, a rejected guess is used as evidence; in D, the text is understood the opposite way.

yechim.doska: Answer: B) People are to blame: according to the review, a large part…
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option B.

xatolar.0: The article clearly states that the scientists admit irrigation also played a role; “no role at all” is a distortion.
xatolar.2: In the blog, the storm idea is presented as a rejected guess: the water retreated from the ships.
xatolar.3: All three sources say that the sea dried up or that the water fell sharply — this option understands the text the opposite way.

variantlar.maslahat: When choosing a conclusion, look not only at the opinion but at the evidence behind it: is the evidence in the text, and is it quoted correctly?

kunikma: Recognize the main question of a forum post in an option that expresses it in different words
usul: Find the question in Dilfuza_88's post. Then choose the option that gives exactly the same meaning in other words.

yechim.ovoz: The main question in Dilfuza's post is whether she can give her own antibiotic to the chicks.

yechim.ovoz: The correct option expresses the same meaning in other words.

kunikma: Connect several sentences in a post to infer the author's intention
usul: Find out why Dilfuza could not get help in another way and what she is worried about — from this, infer why she posted on the forum.

Because she wanted to buy medicine for the chicks through the forum

Because she wanted to warn other poultry keepers about the disease

yechim.ovoz: Dilfuza cannot get quick help in the usual way — through a vet.

yechim.doska: “I'm afraid the other chicks will catch it … I need to do something”
yechim.ovoz: She does not want to wait; she wants to act right now.

yechim.doska: Conclusion: she posted on the forum to get help faster
yechim.ovoz: If we connect the two ideas, her goal is to help her chicks as quickly as possible.

yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option C.

xatolar.1: The post says nothing about buying medicine — she already has the medicine at home.
xatolar.3: She is asking for advice, not giving a warning; the post ends with a question.

variantlar.maslahat: To find the author's purpose, also ask: “Why didn't she choose another way?”

kunikma: Judge whether each post in a forum is relevant to the main topic
usul: First recall the topic: giving medicine to chicks. Then read each post separately and mark whether it answers this question or is about something else.

variantlar.savol: Which posts in the forum are relevant to Dilfuza_88's problem?

yechim.ovoz: Based on her own experience, Nilufar advises not giving medicine without a vet.

yechim.ovoz: Even if Mohira's advice is not right, she wrote about exactly this topic.

kunikma: Identify which of several posts matches a given description (literal meaning)
usul: Briefly summarize each post: who said what? Then choose the one that matches “gave medicine and got a good result.”

xatolar.3: Farhod_vet gave advice but did not write about giving medicine to his own birds and getting a result.

variantlar.maslahat: Compare each part of the description in the question (who? what did they do? what was the result?) with the text separately.

kunikma: Infer an author's purpose that is not stated openly in a post
usul: See what the post is about and whether it answers the question. If it does not, think about what the author is trying to achieve.

variantlar.savol: Why did Poultry_Bazaar post in Dilfuza_88's topic?
javoblar: To advertise the products of its business
To show off its knowledge about poultry

yechim.ovoz: The username and the content show that it is a seller.
Even though it is not stated openly, the purpose of the post is to advertise products.

yechim.doska: Answer: B) To advertise the products of its business
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option B.

xatolar.0: Dilfuza asked about medicine, but Poultry_Bazaar wrote about discounts — that is not an answer.
xatolar.2: The post does not mention Mohira and does not continue her idea.
xatolar.3: The post gives no knowledge at all about poultry health; it only mentions prices.

variantlar.maslahat: On forums and social media, off-topic posts with words like “discount” and “cheap” are often ads.

kunikma: Judge the reliability of several sources (forum posts) based on the author's expertise and evidence
usul: Find out who wrote each answer and what they based their opinion on: professional knowledge and a handbook, personal experience, or a commercial interest.

variantlar.savol: Which answer to Dilfuza_88's question is the most reliable, and why?

Mohira — she wrote very confidently, with exclamation marks

yechim.ovoz: The advice is based on an official source, not on a personal impression.

yechim.doska: Mohira — one chance experience; Bazaar — a commercial interest
yechim.ovoz: A single success is not a rule, and a seller may not be impartial.

yechim.doska: Answer: D) Farhod_vet — he is a poultry vet and relies on…
yechim.ovoz: So the correct answer is option D.

xatolar.1: Writing confidently is not evidence. One successful case does not guarantee the same result with other chicks.
xatolar.2: Bobur_T did not answer Dilfuza's question at all; he wrote about a different topic.

variantlar.maslahat: When judging the reliability of a source, ask: who is the author, what do they rely on, and do they have something to gain?

kunikma: Compare two posts and infer what is missing in an answer
usul: Find what the vet says the dose should be calculated from, then check whether Dilfuza's post contains that information.

Dilfuza did not give her chicks' age
The vet believes advice should not be given on a forum
The handbook does not give the dose of the medicine

variantlar.maslahat: When comparing two texts, find what was asked in the first one and what the second one says is needed — and find the gap between them.

kunikma: Recognize the content of a quotation in an option that expresses it in different words (literal meaning)

kunikma: Determine the main purpose of a text from its content and form (who wrote it and how)

variantlar.savol: Based on Source 1. What is the main purpose of the “Oqsoy Dairy Farm” page?

To warn people about the harmful effects of milk
To introduce readers to pediatrician Rano Aliyeva

kunikma: Evaluate the possible purposes of an article's author based on the content and form of the text
usul: Compare each statement with the article: is the author doing this? Rule out any statement that contradicts the text.

variantlar.savol:

We move all terms to one side.

The peach trees, because they are inside the orchard, and the inside is always bigger than the edge.

For the poplars the second factor is always 12, while for the peach trees 2n keeps growing.

yechim.ovoz: So in the long run, the number of peach trees grows faster.

kunikma: Using the rule about opposite faces of a cube to work out a hidden face

variantlar.savol: How many dots are on the face of each die that is touching the table (the bottom face)? Order of the dice: (a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (f).

yechim.ovoz: The top and bottom faces are opposite, and their total is 7.
We calculate for the first three dice.
We do the same for the other three.
The correct answer is A.

xatolar.2: The total was taken as 6 instead of 7: a die has no face with 0 dots.
xatolar.3: Dice (e) and (f) were mixed up: (e) shows 2 on top, so its bottom is 5.

variantlar.maslahat: Always check: the top and bottom numbers must add up to 7.

kunikma: Estimating the area of an irregular shape using a scale
usul: Replace the shape with a rectangle close to it (or with several simple figures), convert its dimensions to km using the scale, and multiply.

kunikma: Finding the starting value when the amount of change is known (subtracting decimals)
usul: The word “increased” means the new value is greater than the old one; to find the old value, subtract the increase from the new value.

So to find last year's value, we subtract.
We calculate: 130.4.

xatolar.umumiy: If you got 138, you added instead of subtracting; if you got 130.6 or 131.4, you made a place-value error when subtracting decimals.

variantlar.maslahat: Check your answer: $130.4 + 3.8$ must equal 134.2 again.

kunikma: Interpreting a change in the steepness of a graph in terms of rate of growth
usul: The rate of growth shows up as the steepness (slope) of the line on the graph: a steep line means fast growth, a flat line means slow growth.

After week 5 the sunflower line becomes less steep: the growth per week gets smaller.
After week 5 the sunflower line still keeps going up.
In week 5 the sunflowers are taller than the corn.

yechim.ovoz: How much a plant grew in a week shows in how steeply the line rises.
Up to week 5, the sunflowers grew 20 to 24 cm per week.

xatolar.2: Rising shows that growth continues, but it does not show the slowdown.

variantlar.maslahat: If a question asks “how does the graph show…”, refer in your answer to the shape of the graph (steep or flat).

kunikma: Determining an interval from the relative position of two graphs
usul: Find the points where the two lines cross; see which line is on top between them.
