yechim.ovoz: Before week 4 and after week 7, the corn line is on top.
The correct answer is C.

xatolar.0: During this period the sunflower line is below: the corn is taller.
xatolar.1: The sunflowers are taller in week 5, but they are also taller in week 6; the whole interval is not given.
xatolar.3: After week 7 the sunflowers' growth slows down and the corn overtakes them.

variantlar.maslahat: In a “which one is taller” question, finding the points where the lines cross is the most reliable way to find the ends of the interval.

kunikma: Finding a long section of acceleration on a graph
usul: On a straight section the car speeds up, and before a curve it slows down. The longest straight section is where the speed keeps increasing over the longest interval.

variantlar.savol: Approximately how far is it from the starting line to the beginning of the longest straight section of the track?

yechim.doska: Curve: low speed; straight: speed increases
yechim.ovoz: We look for the sections of the graph where the speed keeps increasing.

yechim.doska: From 0.5 km to 1.3 km the speed goes 40 → 170
yechim.ovoz: This is the longest rise: it lasts 0.8 km.
The other rises are much shorter.
The longest straight section begins at about 0.5 km.

xatolar.2: The top speed ends at 1.4 km: this is the end of the longest straight section.

variantlar.maslahat: Read the speed graph as a “map of the track”: deep dips are sharp curves, a long rise is a long straight section.

kunikma: Finding the smallest value on a graph
usul: Find the lowest point of the graph and read its coordinate on the horizontal axis.

xatolar.1: There is also a curve at 1.55 km, but the speed there is 70 km/h.
xatolar.3: Halfway around the track the car is speeding up (about 150 km/h).

variantlar.maslahat: When the smallest value is asked for, read the vertical axis; when its location is asked for, read the horizontal axis.

kunikma: Determining how a quantity changes over a section of a graph
usul: Look at whether the line goes up, goes down, or stays horizontal over the given interval.

yechim.ovoz: We read the speed at 2.2 km from the graph.

yechim.ovoz: The line goes up from left to right.

yechim.ovoz: The correct answer is B.

variantlar.maslahat: If a graph rises from left to right, the quantity increases; if it falls, the quantity decreases; if it is horizontal, the quantity does not change.

kunikma: Comparing a geometric description with drawings and choosing the one that meets all conditions
usul: Check the conditions one by one: where the right angle is, which side is longer, which sides the midpoints are on, and where P is.

yechim.ovoz: In drawing B, side AB is shorter than BC, so B is ruled out.

yechim.doska: Condition 3: N is the midpoint of AB — in A, N is on BC
yechim.ovoz: In drawing A, point N lies on side BC.

yechim.doska: Condition 4: BP < BM — in D, P is close to A
yechim.ovoz: In drawing D, point P is farther from B than M is.
Only drawing C meets all the conditions.

xatolar.1: In B, side AB is shorter than BC, but in the description AB is longer.

kunikma: Critically evaluating a chart whose vertical axis does not start at zero
usul: First look at which number the vertical axis starts from, then read the actual values and calculate the increase as a number and as a percentage.

kunikma: Comparing the perimeters of different shapes with the perimeter of a rectangle
usul: For a stepped shape, check that the horizontal pieces add up to the width and the vertical pieces add up to the height; a notch and slanted sides increase the perimeter.

yechim.doska: B: the step pieces add up to 11+7 — Yes

kunikma: Finding the difference between time zones and calculating local time
usul: Use the table to find the difference between the two cities (compare the times at the same moment) and subtract it.

variantlar.savol: When it is 20:00 in Tashkent, what time is it in New York? (Write your answer in 24-hour format, for example 09:00.)

yechim.ovoz: Times at the same moment: from 5:00 back to 19:00 is 10 hours.
So New York is 10 hours behind Tashkent.
We subtract 10 hours from 20:00 in Tashkent.
In New York it will be 10 o'clock in the morning.

xatolar.umumiy: If you got 06:00, you added 10 hours (wrong direction); if you got 15:00, you confused the difference with Greenwich (5 hours).

variantlar.maslahat: To find a time difference, take two times for the same moment and take “previous day” into account.

kunikma: Finding a convenient time for both while taking into account the restrictions in two time zones

variantlar.savol: Aziz and Jasur are at school from 8:30 to 16:00 local time and sleep from 23:00 to 7:00. Which of the following is a convenient time for them to talk?

Subtracting 10 hours from 17:30 gives 7:30; both are free times.
The correct answer is B.

xatolar.2: At 12:00 in New York, Jasur is at school.
xatolar.3: At 6:30 in New York, Jasur is still asleep.

variantlar.maslahat: When there are several conditions, check each option against all of them: fitting just one condition is not enough.

kunikma: Calculating an amount of money using an exchange rate (multiplication)
usul: Use the rate to see how many tenge you get for 1 000 soums, and split the sum into 1 000-soum pieces.

variantlar.savol: The bank's rate is 1 000 soums = 41 tenge. Malika exchanged 2 500 000 soums for tenge at this rate. How many tenge did she get?

yechim.ovoz: We find how many 1 000 soums there are in the sum.
You get 41 tenge for every 1 000 soums.
We multiply.
Malika got 102 500 tenge.

xatolar.umumiy: If you got 102 500 000, you forgot to divide by 1 000; if you got 60 976, you divided by 41 instead of multiplying.

variantlar.maslahat: Check your answer for sense: the number of tenge must be much smaller than the number of soums, because 1 tenge is worth more than 1 soum.

kunikma: Calculating a reverse currency exchange (division)
usul: When exchanging tenge for soums, divide the amount of tenge by 40 to find how many 1 000-soum “pieces” you get.

variantlar.savol: After two months, Malika had 18 000 tenge left. On her return the rate had changed: 1 000 soums = 40 tenge. Malika exchanged the 18 000 tenge for soums. How many soums did she get?

yechim.ovoz: You get 1 000 soums for every 40 tenge.
18 000 tenge contains 450 pieces of 40 tenge.
Each piece is 1 000 soums.
Malika got 450 000 soums.

xatolar.umumiy: If you got 720, you multiplied 18 000 by 40 and divided by 1 000 (the wrong direction); 450 means you forgot to multiply by 1 000.

variantlar.maslahat: Write down which currency you are converting from and to: for tenge → soums, you divide by the rate, not into the number of tenge.

kunikma: Evaluating, with reasons, how a change in the exchange rate affects the result

xatolar.2: The conclusion is right, but the reasoning is wrong: for someone exchanging soums for tenge, this change is actually a loss.

variantlar.maslahat: “The rate went down”: always check with a calculation who benefits; the result is opposite for the person selling the currency and the person buying it.

kunikma: Calculating classical probability from a bar chart
usul: First find the total number of balls (the sum of all the bars), then divide the number of blue balls by this number.

kunikma: Recovering the total from an average and calculating a new average
usul: Multiply the average by the number of tests to find the total score; add the new score and divide by the new number of tests.

kunikma: Justifying the choice of chart type based on the type of data

kunikma: Correctly interpreting the meaning of a statement about probability
usul: A probability does not mean “it will definitely happen” or “when it will happen”. Compare 2/3 with 1/3 (the probability that it does not happen).

javoblar: $\frac{2}{3}\cdot 30 = 20$, so there will be an earthquake in Yangiobod in exactly 20 years.
$\frac{2}{3}$ is greater than $\frac{1}{2}$, so there will definitely be an earthquake in Yangiobod in the next 30 years.

Nothing can be said, because no one knows exactly when an earthquake will happen.

variantlar.maslahat: An event is certain only if its probability equals 1. Any probability less than 1 only tells “how likely” the event is.

yechim.ovoz: We write down the number of pomegranates at each stage.
Each time, a row one longer than the previous one is added at the bottom.
The next difference will be +4.
Counting by rows also gives 10.
There are 10 pomegranates at stage 4.

xatolar.umumiy: The answer 9 comes from taking the difference as +3 again, and 8 from thinking the numbers double.

kunikma: Substituting a value into a formula and evaluating an expression with a square root
usul: Substitute 21 for t, first work out the expression in parentheses (under the root), then take the square root and multiply by 12.

variantlar.savol: Use the formula to find the diameter of a shrub, in centimeters, 21 years after the water retreated.

yechim.ovoz: We substitute t = 21 into the formula.
16 is left under the root, and its square root is 4.
We multiply four by 12.
The diameter of the shrub is about 48 cm.

xatolar.umumiy: Common mistakes: not subtracting 5 (12·√21 ≈ 55), not taking the root (12·16 = 192), or forgetting to multiply by 12 (4).

variantlar.maslahat: Order of operations: expression under the root → root → multiplication.

kunikma: The inverse problem: finding an unknown from under a square root
usul: Substitute d = 60 to form an equation: first divide by 12, then square both sides and add 5.

variantlar.savol: Madina measured a shrub with a diameter of 60 cm. How many years ago did the water retreat from this place?

yechim.ovoz: We substitute the known diameter into the formula.
We divide both sides by 12.
To get rid of the root, we square both sides.
We add five.
We check the answer by substituting it into the formula.
The water retreated 30 years ago.

xatolar.umumiy: The answer 10 comes from forgetting to square (5 + 5), and 25 from not adding 5 at the end.

variantlar.maslahat: In an inverse problem, do the operations in reverse order: divide → square → add.

kunikma: Building the longest sequence that meets the conditions, using percentage increase and rounding up to a whole number
usul: Start at 18 and multiply by 1.25 each time; if the result is not a whole number, round it UP (if you round down, the 25% condition is broken).

variantlar.savol: The set must start with an 18 mm coin and contain as many coins as possible. Which set meets all the requirements and has the most coins?

yechim.ovoz: The next coin must be at least 22.5 mm; to make it a whole number, we take 23 mm.
Each time, we choose the smallest possible whole-number diameter.
If we round down to 36, the increase is less than 25%.
The next coin would be 58.75 mm, which is outside the limit.
Five coins is the largest possible number.

xatolar.0: 22.5 was rounded down: 22 : 18 ≈ 1.22, so the increase is less than 25%.
xatolar.2: This set meets the requirements, but it has only 4 coins, and a set of 5 is possible.
xatolar.3: 36.25 was rounded down: 36 : 29 ≈ 1.24, which breaks the 25% condition.

variantlar.maslahat: With an “at least” condition, always round up; otherwise the condition is broken.

kunikma: Comparing the fact that the area of a circle is proportional to the square of its diameter with price
usul: The price is directly proportional to the diameter, while the amount of cake depends on the area, that is, on the square of the diameter. Compare how much cake you get per soum.

variantlar.savol: Which cake is the better buy (more cake for the same money)? Choose the answer with the best reasoning.
javoblar: Both are equal, because the diameter is 1.5 times larger and the price is also 1.5 times higher.
The large cake, because the amount of cake is proportional to the square of the diameter: it has 2.25 times as much, but costs only 1.5 times as much.
The small cake, because it is cheaper.
The large cake, because its diameter is 10 cm larger, while it costs only 60 000 soums more.

yechim.ovoz: The price increased by the same factor as the diameter.
For the same height, the amount of cake is proportional to the area, and the area is proportional to the square of the diameter.
For the small cake, you get about 2.62 cm² for every 1000 soums.
For the large cake, about 3.93 cm².

yechim.doska: Answer: B) the large cake is the better buy
yechim.ovoz: The amount increased 2.25 times, the price 1.5 times.

xatolar.0: The amount of cake is proportional to the area (the square of the diameter), not to the diameter; the amount increases 2.25 times.
xatolar.2: Being cheaper does not mean being a better buy: what matters is how much cake you get per soum.
xatolar.3: The conclusion is right, but the reasoning is wrong: comparing the difference in diameters with the difference in prices proves nothing.

variantlar.maslahat: If a shape is enlarged k times, its area is enlarged k² times.

kunikma: Comparing the areas of shapes by imagining them placed on top of each other
usul: Imagine placing each shape on top of another: which one completely covers the others?

variantlar.savol: Which flower bed has the largest area? Choose the answer with the best reasoning.
javoblar: B, because A and C can be placed inside B: their borders have parts that cut inward.
C, because its border is the longest.
A, because its border has the most curves.
All three have the same area, because their widths are almost the same.

yechim.doska: All three shapes are about the same width
yechim.ovoz: According to the picture, the flower beds fit inside the same circle.

yechim.doska: A and C have parts that cut inward
yechim.ovoz: These inward cuts reduce the area compared with the circle.
If we place A and C on top of B, they stay inside B.
So B has the largest area.

xatolar.1: The length of the perimeter does not tell you the area: a wavy border can be long while the area is small.
xatolar.2: Having more curves does not increase the area; on the contrary, inward cuts reduce it.
xatolar.3: Having the same width does not mean having the same area.

variantlar.maslahat: To compare areas, imagining the shapes placed on top of each other is a simple and reliable method.

kunikma: Choosing a method to estimate the area of an irregular shape
usul: Area is the part of the plane that a shape covers. It can be found by filling the shape with square units and counting them.

variantlar.savol: Which method is correct for estimating the area of flower bed C?
javoblar: Lay a string along the border of shape C and measure the length of the string.
Measure the greatest width of shape C and calculate with the formula for the area of a circle.
Copy the drawing onto grid paper and count the squares inside the shape (counting squares more than half filled as whole ones and ignoring the rest).
Count the number of parts sticking out of shape C and multiply it by the width of the flower bed.

yechim.ovoz: Measuring area means covering the shape with unit squares.
Each square on the grid paper represents a known area.
The errors in the border squares almost cancel each other out.
The smaller the squares, the more accurate the result.

xatolar.0: A string measures the perimeter (the length of the border), not the area.
xatolar.1: C is not a circle: the circle formula ignores the inward cuts and greatly overestimates the area.
xatolar.3: This product has nothing to do with area; even the unit of measurement comes out wrong.

variantlar.maslahat: Estimating the area of an irregular shape with grid paper is the most universal method.

kunikma: Choosing a method to measure the length of a curved line (the perimeter)
usul: The perimeter is the length of the border. A curved line cannot be straightened, but a string or small straight pieces can help.

variantlar.savol: To put a fence around the border of flower bed C, we need to estimate its perimeter. Which method is correct?
javoblar: Copy the drawing onto grid paper and count the squares inside the shape.
Lay a string along the border, following all its curves, then straighten the string, measure its length, and convert using the scale.
Draw a rectangle around shape C and measure its perimeter.
Measure the greatest width of shape C and multiply it by 3.14.

yechim.ovoz: We need the full length of the border.

yechim.doska: We lay the string along the border
yechim.ovoz: The string follows all the curves.

yechim.doska: We straighten the string and measure it with a ruler
yechim.ovoz: Then we convert it to the actual length using the scale.
Dividing the border into small straight pieces and adding them up is a similar method.

xatolar.0: Counting squares gives the area, not the perimeter.
xatolar.2: The perimeter of a rectangle ignores the inward cuts and the sides of the parts that stick out; the actual border is much longer.
xatolar.3: πd works only for a circle; the border of C is much longer than that of a circle.

variantlar.maslahat: The length of a curved line can be measured with a string or by dividing it into small, nearly straight pieces.

kunikma: Finding a value in a table
usul: Find the 100 km/h row and read the value in the “Reaction distance” column.

variantlar.savol: A car is traveling at 100 km/h. How many meters does it travel during the driver's reaction time?

yechim.ovoz: We find the row in the table where the speed is 100 km/h.
The second column gives the reaction distance.
During the reaction time, the car travels 27.8 m.

xatolar.umumiy: 82.9 is the total stopping distance and 4.97 is the time (in seconds); do not mix up the columns.

variantlar.maslahat: In a table, first find the row, then the column.

kunikma: Finding a value in a table
usul: Read the “Total stopping distance” column in the 100 km/h row.

variantlar.savol: How many meters in total does a car traveling at 100 km/h travel before it comes to a complete stop?

yechim.ovoz: Again we look at the 100 km/h row.
This column is the sum of the reaction and braking distances.
The car travels 82.9 m in total before it stops.

xatolar.umumiy: 27.8 is only the reaction distance; the question is about the total stopping distance.

variantlar.maslahat: The words “in total” mean the sum of both parts.

kunikma: Finding a time value in a table
usul: The question asks for a time, not a distance: look at the last column.

variantlar.savol: How many seconds does it take to bring a car traveling at 100 km/h to a complete stop?

yechim.ovoz: We find the row we need.
The last column is given in seconds.
It takes about 5 seconds to stop completely.

xatolar.umumiy: Values in meters (27.8 or 82.9) are not times; pay attention to the unit.

variantlar.maslahat: The unit of the answer must match the quantity in the question: time is in seconds.

kunikma: Finding a value not given in a table by subtracting from a total
usul: Total distance = reaction distance + braking distance. The braking distance is not in the table; find it by subtracting.

variantlar.savol: At 100 km/h, how many meters does the car travel from the moment the brake is pressed until it stops (the braking distance)?

yechim.ovoz: From the definition in the text, we know the total distance has two parts.
We subtract the two values in the table.
We calculate.
The braking distance is 55.1 m.

xatolar.umumiy: The answer 110.7 comes from adding the values; the braking distance must be smaller than the total distance.

variantlar.maslahat: A quantity that is not in the table can be calculated from other columns using its definition.

kunikma: Searching a table in reverse: finding the input value from the result
usul: This time, find 46.5 m in the “Total stopping distance” column and read the speed in that row.

variantlar.savol: Another driver, in good conditions, stopped the car within a total distance of 46.5 m. What speed was the car traveling at before the brake was pressed (in km/h)?

yechim.ovoz: This time the value is known and the speed is unknown, so we search the table in reverse.
46.5 m is in the 70 km/h row.
The car was traveling at 70 km/h.

xatolar.umumiy: Looking for 46.5 in the reaction distance column, or reading a neighboring row (60 or 80), leads to a mistake.

variantlar.maslahat: In an inverse problem, first find the value in the right column, then look left along the row.

kunikma: Calculating the area of a rectangle with decimals and multiplying by a rate
usul: First find the area (m²), then multiply it by the number of tiles per 1 m². Do not round the area.

variantlar.savol: How many tiles does Akmal need for the whole porch? (If the result is not a whole number, round it up.)

yechim.ovoz: The area of the porch is the length times the width.
We calculate: 4.75 · 3.2 = 15.2.
There are 64 tiles per square meter.
Since tiles come only as whole pieces, we round up.
Akmal needs 973 tiles.

xatolar.umumiy: Rounding the area to 15 m² gives 960 tiles; adding 64 to 15.2 instead of multiplying, or using the perimeter, are also common mistakes.

variantlar.maslahat: Multiply decimal measurements exactly all the way through, and round only at the last step.

kunikma: Calculating a decrease by the same percentage at each step (a geometric sequence)
usul: Each hour, multiply the amount by 0.75: 8:00 → 9:00 → 10:00 → 11:00, three times.

variantlar.savol: The patient was given 400 mg of antibiotic at 8:00. How many mg of active medicine will remain in the blood at 11:00?

yechim.ovoz: After the first hour, 75% remains.
Each hour, we take 75% of the previous amount.
After the third hour.
The same multiplier is applied three times.
At 11:00, about 168.75 mg of active medicine remains.

xatolar.umumiy: The answer 100 comes from thinking the amount decreases by the same 100 mg (25% of 400) every hour; the percentage is taken of the new amount each time.

variantlar.maslahat: “X percent of the previous amount” means multiplying by the same number at each step.

kunikma: Reading the value of a point on a graph
usul: Find day 1 on the horizontal axis, go straight up to the graph, and read the value on the vertical axis.

variantlar.savol: How much active medicine is left in Bahodir aka's blood at the end of the first day?

yechim.ovoz: We find 1 on the horizontal axis.
The point is on the 90 mg line.
At the end of the first day, 90 mg of active medicine remains.

xatolar.0: 60 mg is the amount broken down in one day (150 − 90), not the amount remaining.
xatolar.2: 54 mg is the value at the end of the second day.
xatolar.3: 100 mg does not match any point on the graph.

variantlar.maslahat: When reading a value from a graph, look along a straight line from the point to the axis.

kunikma: Finding a constant ratio (percentage) from graph data
usul: Divide the values for two consecutive days: 90 : 150, 54 : 90. Convert the ratio to a percentage.

variantlar.savol: The graph shows that each day about the same fraction of the previous day's active medicine stays in the blood. About what percentage is this?

yechim.ovoz: We divide the day 1 value by the initial amount.
Dividing the day 2 value by the day 1 value also gives 0.6.
Each day, 60% of the previous amount remains.
Each day 40% is broken down and 60% remains.

xatolar.0: 40% is the part broken down each day; the question is about the part that remains.
xatolar.1: If it were 50%, 150 would be followed by 75, but the graph shows 90.
xatolar.3: 90 is in milligrams (the day 1 value), not a percentage.

variantlar.maslahat: To check for a decrease by the same percentage, calculate the ratios of neighboring values.

kunikma: Finding the volume of a rectangular box by counting unit cubes
usul: Count the cubes in one layer (length × width), then multiply by the number of layers.

variantlar.savol: How many cubes does Kamola need to make block B?

yechim.ovoz: The bottom layer has 4 rows of 2 cubes.
The block is 2 cubes high.
We multiply by the number of layers.
Block B needs 16 cubes.

xatolar.umumiy: Counting only the visible cubes (for example, 12 or 14) leads to a mistake: there are also cubes at the back and inside.

variantlar.maslahat: Volume = length × width × height (in cubes).

kunikma: Finding the volume of a cube using unit cubes
usul: Find how many cubes there are along each edge of block C, and multiply the three dimensions.

variantlar.savol: How many cubes does Kamola need to make the solid block C?

yechim.ovoz: One layer of the cube has 16 small cubes.
The height is also 4 cubes.
Block C needs 64 cubes.

xatolar.umumiy: The answers 48 (only the three visible faces) or 96 (six faces: 6·16) come from counting the squares on the faces, not the cubes.

variantlar.maslahat: The volume of a cube is a³: multiply the edge by itself three times.

kunikma: Finding the number of cubes needed for a hollow block (the outer shell)
usul: For the outside to look the same, all the outer cubes must stay. To find the size of the inside, subtract 2 from each dimension.

variantlar.savol: Kamola realized she could save cubes by making a block like C but hollow inside. What is the smallest number of cubes needed for a hollow block that looks like block C from the outside?

yechim.ovoz: The solid block has 64 cubes.
One outer layer stays on each side, leaving a 2×2×2 space inside.
We remove the inner cubes.
At least 56 cubes are needed.

xatolar.umumiy: The answer 63 comes from thinking only one central cube is removed, and 37 from taking the inner space as 3×3×3 = 27 (64 − 27).

variantlar.maslahat: The inner part is 2 smaller in each direction: (a−2)·(b−2)·(c−2).

kunikma: Generalizing the count of shell cubes for a hollow rectangular box
usul: Subtract the volume of the inner space from the volume of the solid block; each dimension of the space is 2 less than the outer dimension.

variantlar.savol: Now Kamola wants to make a block that looks from the outside like a solid block 7 cubes long, 6 cubes wide and 5 cubes high, but with as large a space inside as possible. What is the smallest number of cubes she needs?

yechim.ovoz: First, the number of cubes in the solid block.
We subtract the two end cubes from each dimension.
The number of cubes in the shell.
At least 150 cubes are needed.

xatolar.umumiy: Taking 6·5·4 = 120 as the space (subtracting 1 from each dimension) or adding up the face areas (2·(42+35+30) = 214) are common mistakes.

variantlar.maslahat: Shell = outer volume − inner volume; the inner dimensions are 2 smaller because one layer is removed from each side.

kunikma: Comparing decimals from a table and ordering the smallest final times
usul: The winner is the athlete with the smallest final time. Look only at the “Final time” column and leave out the runner who did not finish.

variantlar.savol: The athletes in which lanes won the gold, silver and bronze medals? (order: gold, silver, bronze)

yechim.ovoz: The medal is decided by the final time, not the reaction time — and it must be as small as possible.

yechim.doska: Lane 4 did not finish — not counted
yechim.ovoz: The athlete in lane 4 did not finish the race, so we leave them out.
Let’s write the final times in increasing order: 10.12 (lane 5), 10.22 (lane 2), 10.27 (lane 6).
So gold goes to lane 5, silver to lane 2, and bronze to lane 6.

xatolar.0: These are the fastest reaction times (0.141; 0.152; 0.164). An athlete can react quickly and still run slowly.
xatolar.1: You subtracted the reaction time and compared the pure running times. But medals are awarded by final time.
xatolar.2: These are the largest final times — that is, the last places. The smaller the time, the better the result.

variantlar.maslahat: Work out what is being measured in the race: the winner is decided by the final time.

kunikma: Recalculating a time in a hypothetical situation and justifying the result by comparison
usul: Subtract the actual reaction time from the final time to find the running time, then add the smallest possible reaction time to it.

variantlar.savol: So far, no human has been able to respond to the starting signal faster than 0.110 seconds. If the bronze medalist had reacted faster, could he have won the silver medal? Which answer is correct and correctly justified?
javoblar: No: his final time is 10.27 s, which is greater than the silver medalist’s 10.22 s, and the reaction time does not change that.
Yes, he would even have won gold, because 10.154 s < 10.12 s.
Yes: in the best case it would be 10.27 − 0.226 + 0.110 = 10.154 s, which is less than 10.22 s.
No: 10.27 − 0.110 = 10.16 s, which is still more than the winner’s 10.12 s.

yechim.ovoz: The bronze medalist is in lane 6: final time 10.27 s, reaction time 0.226 s.
His pure running time is 10.044 seconds.
We add the fastest possible reaction time, 0.110 s.
That is less than the silver medalist’s 10.22 s, but more than the gold medalist’s 10.12 s.
So he could have won silver, but not gold.

xatolar.0: The final time includes the reaction time. If the reaction time gets shorter, the final time gets shorter too.
xatolar.1: The comparison is wrong: 10.154 seconds is greater than 10.12 seconds, so it would not be gold.
xatolar.3: Two mistakes: you removed the reaction time completely instead of replacing it with 0.110, and you compared with gold instead of silver.

variantlar.maslahat: First ask “what changes and what stays the same?”: the reaction time changes, but the running time stays the same.

kunikma: Choosing the graph of water level against time based on the shape of the tank
usul: For each part, think “how much does the level rise in 1 second?”: where the tank is wide, slowly; where it is narrow, quickly.

variantlar.savol: Which graph correctly shows how the height of the water level changes over time?
javoblar: Graph A: one straight line from start to finish
Graph B: first a straight line, then a curve that gets steeper and steeper
Graph C: first a steeply rising curve, then a straight line
Graph D: first a straight line, then a horizontal line

yechim.ovoz: The same amount of water flows into the tank every second.
In the lower cylinder the width does not change, so the level rises steadily — the graph is a straight line.
The upper part keeps narrowing, so 2 liters of water make a taller and taller layer — the graph gets steeper and steeper.

yechim.doska: Answer: B) straight line, then a steeper curve
yechim.ovoz: That graph is B.

xatolar.0: This is true only if the whole tank has the same width. The upper part narrows, so the level rises faster.
xatolar.2: This fits a tank that is narrow at the bottom and then widens (for example, a cylinder on top of a cone with its tip at the bottom).
xatolar.3: A horizontal line means the level has stopped rising, but water is still being pumped in.

variantlar.maslahat: Where the shape is wide, the level rises slowly; where it is narrow, it rises quickly — connect this to the slope of the graph.

kunikma: Estimating the probability of a two-stage random event
usul: Find the probability of each stage separately and multiply them, then describe the result in words.

variantlar.savol: How likely is it that Malika wins a prize?

yechim.ovoz: Of the 6 numbers on the spinner, 5 are even; only 3 is odd.
So the probability of getting to take a ball from the bag is 5/6 — quite high.
Of the 16 balls in the bag, 4 are black.
Both conditions must happen, so the probabilities are multiplied: about 21%.
21% is not impossible, but it is much less than 50%, so it is unlikely.

xatolar.0: There are black balls and an even number can come up, so winning is possible.
xatolar.2: You also need to look at the second stage: the probability of a black ball is only 1/4, and the overall probability is about 21%.
xatolar.3: You looked only at the spinner (5/6). To win the prize, a black ball must also come out.

variantlar.maslahat: In a multi-stage game, each stage has a probability less than 1, so the overall probability gets smaller.

kunikma: Connecting real motion to a graph: decreasing amplitude of oscillation
usul: Check two things: how the highest points change, and where the lowest points stay.

variantlar.savol: Which graph best shows how the height of Zarina’s feet above the ground changes over time?

yechim.ovoz: The swing moves back and forth, so the graph is wave-shaped.
Since nobody pushes it, it rises lower each time — the peaks get lower.
The lowest point is always at the same height — the dips are all at one level.

yechim.doska: Answer: B) peaks decrease, bottom level stays the same
yechim.ovoz: Only graph B fits both conditions.

xatolar.0: In A the peaks keep increasing — that is a child pumping and swinging higher and higher.
xatolar.2: In C the swinging does not change, but the swing is slowing down and rising lower.
xatolar.3: In D the lowest points keep rising. But the lowest point of the swing is always at the same height.

variantlar.maslahat: Before choosing a graph, write down the most important features of the motion in words.

kunikma: Using properties of the arithmetic mean to decide which conclusion must be true
usul: Look for a counterexample to each conclusion. If the conclusion fails in at least one possible case, it is not necessarily true.

variantlar.savol: Which of the following conclusions must follow from the given information?
javoblar: One of the new members is a boy and the other is a girl.
The overall mean height of all club members did not change.
Malika is still the shortest member of the club.
If both new members are boys, their mean height is 165 cm.

yechim.doska: If the mean doesn’t change: new value = mean
yechim.ovoz: If you add a value equal to the mean to a group, the mean does not change.

yechim.doska: A: they could also be 2 girls (155 and 155)
yechim.ovoz: The condition still holds if both are girls, so A is not necessarily true.

yechim.doska: B: adding 165 + 155 may change the overall mean
yechim.ovoz: The overall mean depends on the numbers of boys and girls, so it can change.

yechim.doska: C: a new member could be 135 cm
yechim.ovoz: If one new girl is 135 cm and the other is 175 cm, the mean stays 155, and Malika is no longer the shortest.
If two boys join and the mean stays 165, their heights add up to 330, so their mean is 165.
So only conclusion D is true in every case.

xatolar.0: Both could be girls (for example, 150 and 160 cm) or both could be boys — the condition would still hold.
xatolar.1: For example, if two people of 165 cm and 155 cm join a group of 3 boys and 7 girls, the overall mean changes.
xatolar.2: Even if one new girl is shorter than 138 cm and the other is tall, the girls’ mean can stay at 155.

variantlar.maslahat: Pay attention to the word “must”: one counterexample is enough to reject a conclusion.

kunikma: Evaluating properties of direct proportion in a real situation
usul: “In proportion to the area” means everyone pays the same amount per 1 m². Check each statement against this rule.

variantlar.savol: Which of the following statements is correct?
javoblar: The owner of the largest apartment pays more per 1 m² than the owner of the smallest apartment.
If we know the total cost and how much each family pays, we can calculate the total floor area of the apartments.
If the price of the repair goes up by 20%, each family’s payment also goes up by 20%.
If the price of the repair goes up by 20%, each family’s payment goes up by the same amount of money.

yechim.ovoz: Proportional sharing: the price per 1 m² is the same for everyone.

yechim.doska: A: same price per 1 m² → A is wrong
yechim.ovoz: The owner of a large apartment pays more in total, but the same per 1 m².

yechim.doska: B: only amounts of money → area unknown
yechim.ovoz: Amounts of money do not tell us the area, so the total area cannot be found.
If the total amount goes up by 20%, each share also goes up by 20%.
D is wrong: the payments go up by the same percentage, not by the same amount.

xatolar.0: With proportional sharing, the price per 1 m² is the same for everyone; only the total payment differs.
xatolar.1: From the amounts of money we only know the shares, not the square meters.
xatolar.3: The owner of a large apartment sees a bigger increase: payments do not all go up by the same amount, but by the same percentage.

variantlar.maslahat: With proportional sharing, a percentage change affects everyone by the same percentage.

kunikma: Dividing a total amount in proportion to areas
usul: First find the total area, then calculate the amount per 1 m².

variantlar.savol: There are three apartments in the entrance: apartment 1 is 72 m², apartment 2 is 64 m², and apartment 3 is 54 m². The roof repair costs 47 500 000 soums in total. How many soums should the owner of apartment 2 pay?

yechim.ovoz: First, we add up the areas of all the apartments.
Each square meter costs 250 thousand soums.
Apartment 2 is 64 m², so we multiply 250 thousand soums by 64.
The owner of apartment 2 pays 16 million soums.

xatolar.umumiy: A common mistake is to divide the amount equally by 3 (15 833 333) or to divide 64 by 72 instead of by the total area. The payment equals the 64/190 share.

variantlar.maslahat: Check your result: the three payments must add up to the total cost.

kunikma: Finding the needed value in a table of intervals
usul: Find which interval (between “from” and “to”) the height falls into, and read the size in that row.

variantlar.savol: Dilnoza is 137 cm tall. According to the chart, what clothing size fits her?

yechim.ovoz: We look for the row in the table that contains the number 137.
137 is in the interval from 135 to 140.
The last column of this row says 38.
Size 38 fits Dilnoza.

xatolar.umumiy: Students often take the neighboring row (36 or 40) or confuse the height with the size. 137 is exactly in the 135–140 interval.

variantlar.maslahat: In interval tables, always check both boundaries.

kunikma: Combinatorics: distributing all pairs into rounds without repetition
usul: First count all the pairs (4 people give 6 pairs), cross out the ones from round 1, and arrange the rest so that everyone plays once in each round.

variantlar.savol: Which schedule for rounds 2 and 3 is correct?
javoblar: Round 2: Aziz – Dilshod, Bekzod – Sardor; Round 3: Aziz – Bekzod, Dilshod – Sardor
Round 2: Aziz – Dilshod, Aziz – Sardor; Round 3: Bekzod – Dilshod, Bekzod – Sardor
Round 2: Aziz – Dilshod, Bekzod – Sardor; Round 3: Aziz – Sardor, Bekzod – Dilshod
Round 2: Aziz – Dilshod, Bekzod – Sardor; Round 3: Aziz – Sardor, Dilshod – Sardor

yechim.ovoz: Four people make 6 different pairs.
These have already been played. Remaining: Aziz–Dilshod, Aziz–Sardor, Bekzod–Dilshod, Bekzod–Sardor.
In one round, a student cannot play on two boards.

yechim.doska: Round 2: Az–Dil, Bek–Sar; Round 3: Az–Sar, Bek–Dil
yechim.ovoz: If we arrange them like this, every pair meets exactly once.
This is option C.

xatolar.0: Round 3 repeats the games from round 1, and Aziz – Sardor and Bekzod – Dilshod are never played.
xatolar.1: In one round, Aziz cannot play on two boards at the same time.
xatolar.3: In round 3 Sardor plays twice, and the Bekzod – Dilshod game is left out.

variantlar.maslahat: When checking a schedule, ask two questions: is any game repeated? Does anyone play twice in one round?

kunikma: Finding the period from the graph of a periodic process
usul: On the graph, find the point after which exactly the same sequence repeats from the start of the pattern.

variantlar.savol: Which of the following could be the period of this light’s pattern?

yechim.ovoz: We read the segments of the graph one after another.
From the 6th second on, the same sequence repeats.
So one complete cycle is 6 seconds.
The correct answer is C.

xatolar.0: 2 seconds is only the first light segment. After 2 seconds the pattern continues differently.
xatolar.1: From 0 to 3 seconds it is “2 s light, 1 s dark”, but from 3 to 6 it is “1 s light, 2 s dark” — these are not the same.
xatolar.3: At 4 seconds it is dark, but at 0 seconds it was light — the pattern does not repeat after 4 s.

variantlar.maslahat: Once you have found the period, check the next cycle too — the pattern must match completely.

kunikma: Using a value over one period to calculate a value over a longer time interval
usul: Find how many seconds the light is on during one period, then calculate how many periods there are in 1 minute.

variantlar.savol: In total, how many seconds is the light on during 1 minute?

yechim.doska: One period (6 s): light 2 s + 1 s = 3 s
yechim.ovoz: In every 6 seconds, the light is on for 3 seconds in total.
There are 10 complete periods in one minute.
In 10 periods, it is light for 30 seconds.
The correct answer is D.

xatolar.0: 20 is the number of flashes in one minute (2 per period). But the question asks about the seconds the light is on.
xatolar.1: You took both flashes as 2 seconds each. In fact, the second one is 1 second.
xatolar.2: 10 is the number of periods in one minute, not the time the light is on.

variantlar.maslahat: Be clear about what the question asks: not the number of flashes, but the time the light is on.

kunikma: Choosing a periodic pattern that meets given conditions (period and total time on)
usul: For each pattern, check two things: is the period 5 seconds, and is the light on for 2 seconds in each period (60 : 5 · 2 = 24)?

kunikma: Calculating the percentage change between two values
usul: Find the change (new − old), divide it by the starting (old) value, and then multiply by 100.

variantlar.savol: The table does not show the percentage change for Navoi region. By what percentage did the amount of waste in Navoi region increase from 2015 to 2023?

yechim.ovoz: First we find the change: it increased by 39 thousand tonnes.
We divide the change by the value for the starting year, 2015.
We convert to a percentage.
Waste in Navoi region increased by 26%.

xatolar.umumiy: A common mistake is to divide 39 by the 2023 value (189), which gives 21%. The divisor is the starting value, 150.

variantlar.maslahat: For a percentage change, the divisor is always the starting value.

kunikma: Comparing percentage changes of a part and the whole to evaluate a claim
usul: Remember that the change in the whole is the result of the changes in all its parts: some parts may increase while others decrease.

variantlar.savol: Malika looked at the table and said: “In Fergana region waste decreased by 15%, but in the whole valley by only 2%. That is impossible, because Fergana region is part of the valley.” Which statement is correct?
javoblar: Malika is right: if a part decreases, the whole must decrease by at least the same percentage.
Malika is right: −15% + 8% + 2% = −5%, so the valley should show −5%.
Malika is right, because in 2023 the waste in the valley was more than 1500 thousand tonnes.
Malika is wrong: waste increased in Andijan and Namangan, so the decrease for the valley as a whole is smaller.

yechim.ovoz: The valley as a whole is made up of three regions.
It decreased in one region and increased in two.
The increases make up for part of the decrease: 30 : 1500 = 2%.
So a part can decrease by more than the whole.

xatolar.0: The whole is not made up of only one part: if other parts grow, the overall decrease is smaller.
xatolar.1: You cannot simply add the percentages — each region has a different amount.
xatolar.2: According to the table, the valley had 1470 thousand tonnes in 2023 — less than 1500.

variantlar.maslahat: To check a claim that something is “impossible”, calculate with the numbers in the table.

kunikma: Distinguishing absolute and relative (percentage) growth and justifying two different correct conclusions
usul: “The greatest increase” can be measured in two ways: in thousand tonnes (absolute) and in percent (relative). Find the largest in each.

variantlar.savol: Nodir: “Waste increased the most in Tashkent city.” Zarina: “No, it increased the most in Navoi region.” Which conclusion is correct?
javoblar: Both are right: Tashkent had the largest increase in thousand tonnes (+180), and Navoi had the largest increase in percent (+26%).
Only Nodir is right: percentages are misleading, so only the tonnes should be compared.
Only Zarina is right: the regions are of different sizes, so only the percentages can be compared.
Both are wrong: the greatest increase was in Samarkand, because it is high on both measures.

yechim.ovoz: The largest increase in thousand tonnes is in Tashkent: 1380 − 1200 = 180.
In the other regions the increase is much smaller.
The largest increase in percent is in Navoi, 26%.
Nodir meant absolute growth, and Zarina meant relative growth.

xatolar.1: Measuring in tonnes is a valid method, but comparing by percentage is also valid — it shows relative growth.
xatolar.2: Comparing by percentage is valid, but the absolute increase (in tonnes) is also a meaningful measure.
xatolar.3: Samarkand is not first on either measure: Tashkent leads in tonnes, and Navoi leads in percent.

variantlar.maslahat: When there is a debate about data, first work out which measure each side is using.

kunikma: Estimating real measurements: estimating the height of a building from the number of floors and the height of one floor
usul: Count the floors correctly (ground floor + residential floors) and use a realistic height for one floor (3–4 m).

variantlar.savol: Which range is the most realistic for the total height of the building?

yechim.ovoz: We must not forget to include the ground floor — 25 floors in total.
A residential floor is about 3 meters high, and up to 4 meters including the slab between floors.
So the height is roughly 75 to 100 meters.
We choose the option that matches this range.

xatolar.0: This assumes one floor is only 1–1.5 m high — a person could not stand up straight in such a room.
xatolar.1: That is the height of a house with only 3–4 floors; the 25 floors were not taken into account.
xatolar.2: This assumes one floor is 6–8 m high — far too tall for an ordinary residential building.

variantlar.maslahat: For an estimate, use your everyday experience: how many meters high is the ceiling in your room?

kunikma: Finding an observer’s position from a plan and compass directions
usul: Put yourself in the observer’s place: when you face the building, which compass direction is on your left?

variantlar.savol: An observer looks at the ground floor from ground level. They see only a narrow (20 m) wall of the building, and the elevator cylinder appears on the left side of that wall. From which direction is the observer looking at the building?

yechim.ovoz: The long sides run from west to east, so the 20 m walls are on the west and east.
The elevator cylinder is in the middle of the south wall.

yechim.doska: Looking from the east: facing west, south is on the left
yechim.ovoz: When you face west, your left hand points south.
For the cylinder to appear on the left, the observer must be standing on the east side.

xatolar.0: From the north, you would see the long (40 m) north wall, and the cylinder would be hidden behind the building.
xatolar.1: Looking from the west, the observer faces east — south is on their right, so the cylinder appears on the right.
xatolar.3: From the south, you would see the long south wall with the cylinder in the middle of it.

variantlar.maslahat: In spatial problems, check by rotating the drawing or by facing that direction yourself.

kunikma: Working out which faces are visible when viewed from a corner
usul: When viewed from a corner direction (for example, from the southwest), you see the walls that face those two directions.

variantlar.savol: Another observer looks at the ground floor from the southwest. Which two walls do they see, and is the elevator cylinder visible?
javoblar: The south and west walls; the cylinder is visible
The north and east walls; the cylinder is not visible
The south and east walls; the cylinder is visible
The north and west walls; the cylinder is not visible

yechim.ovoz: The observer is on the south side and the west side at the same time.
They see the walls that face those two directions.

yechim.doska: Cylinder on the south wall → visible
yechim.ovoz: The elevator cylinder is on the south wall, so it is visible too.
The correct answer is A.

xatolar.1: This is the view from the northeast — the opposite side from the observer.
xatolar.2: The east wall is on the far side from the observer — it is visible from the southeast.
xatolar.3: The north wall is on the back side of the building and cannot be seen from the southwest.

variantlar.maslahat: First name the directions where the observer is standing, then find the walls that face those directions.

kunikma: Finding the rotation angle of an intermediate floor in a uniform twist
usul: Find the rotation angle per floor (total rotation : number of floors), then multiply it by the number of the floor you need.

variantlar.savol: The top floor, floor 24, is rotated by 90° relative to the ground floor. By how many degrees is floor 16 rotated relative to the ground floor?

yechim.ovoz: From the ground floor to floor 24 there is a total rotation of 90°.
Each floor is rotated by 3.75 degrees relative to the one below it.
Up to floor 16, there have been 16 rotations.
Floor 16 is rotated by 60° relative to the ground floor.

xatolar.umumiy: A common mistake is to assume floor 16 is in the middle and write 45°, or to divide 90° by 25 (the number of floors including the ground floor). There are 24 rotations.

variantlar.maslahat: Check your result: 16 is 2/3 of 24, so the angle is also 2/3 of 90° — 60°.

kunikma: Setting two linear formulas equal to find the value beyond which one is smaller
usul: Set the two formulas equal and find x; then check which fare is cheaper for distances greater than that point.

variantlar.savol: For trips longer than how many kilometers is the new fare cheaper than the old fare?

yechim.ovoz: We find the distance at which the prices are equal.
We move the x terms to one side and the numbers to the other side.
At 20 km both fares are the same: 38 000 soums.
Let’s check: at 30 km the new fare is cheaper.
For trips longer than 20 km, the new fare is cheaper.

xatolar.umumiy: A common mistake is to divide 4 000 by 1 500 or by 1 300 (2.7 or 3.1 km). In the equation, the difference between the coefficients of x is 200.

variantlar.maslahat: Always check the answer you get from an equation by substituting one number — which fare is cheaper on which side?

kunikma: Applying a percentage discount to a formula to write a new formula
usul: The discount applies to the whole price: multiply the whole expression by 0.85 and expand the brackets.

variantlar.savol: The taxi service gives students a 15% discount on the new fare. Which is the correct formula for calculating a student’s price in terms of the distance x?

yechim.ovoz: The student pays 100% − 15% = 85% of the price.
We multiply the whole formula by 0.85.
We expand the brackets and multiply each term by 0.85.
The correct formula is A.

xatolar.1: The discount was applied only to the starting charge; it must also be applied to the price per km.
xatolar.2: The discount was applied only to the price per km; it must also be applied to the 12 000.
xatolar.3: This is the amount of the discount itself, not the price the student pays.

variantlar.maslahat: When expanding brackets, you must multiply each term inside the brackets by the factor.

kunikma: Estimating using proportion and rounding
usul: First find how many orbits there are in one day, then multiply by the number of days. You may round the numbers to calculate.

variantlar.savol: About how many times did the astronaut orbit the Earth during this mission?

yechim.ovoz: The station orbits the Earth about 15–16 times a day.
For 355 days, we multiply 15.5 by 355.
One twentieth of 113 000 is also about 5 650 — the same order of magnitude.
The closest answer is 5 500.

xatolar.0: This corresponds to about 35 days — a zero was lost in the calculation.
xatolar.1: This is the answer for about 3 500 days (nearly 10 years) — the order of magnitude is wrong.
xatolar.3: This is the station’s total number of orbits in 20 years, not one astronaut’s.

variantlar.maslahat: When estimating, first work out the order of magnitude of the answer (tens, hundreds, thousands).

kunikma: Estimating a number from area and realistic density (people per 1 m²)
usul: Find the area, then think about how many people fit in 1 m² in a dense standing crowd (about 3–4 people).

variantlar.savol: Which of the following is the best estimate of the number of people at the concert?

yechim.ovoz: First we calculate the area.
In a dense standing crowd, 3–4 people fit in one square meter.
So there are about 30 thousand people.
The most realistic estimate is 30 000.

xatolar.0: This gives each person more than 2 m² of space — the area would not be packed.
xatolar.1: This means only 1 person per 1 m² — far too sparse for a “packed” area.
xatolar.3: This would need 14 people per 1 m² — that is physically impossible.

variantlar.maslahat: Use your sense of real life: imagine how many people could stand in a 1 m × 1 m square.

kunikma: Finding speeds from a distance–time graph and adding speeds
usul: Find each person’s speed from the graph. A person walking on the walkway moves at their own speed plus the speed of the walkway.

variantlar.savol: A third passenger walks on the moving walkway at the same speed as the person on the floor. How many seconds does it take them to cover the 60-meter walkway?

yechim.ovoz: From the graph: the person on the floor covers 60 meters in 48 seconds.
The walkway carries the standing person along in 80 seconds — this gives the speed of the walkway.
When you walk on the walkway, the two speeds add up.
At 2 m/s, 60 meters takes 30 seconds.
Answer: 30 seconds — this would be the steepest line on the graph.

xatolar.umumiy: A common mistake is to add the times (128 s), subtract them (32 s) or take their mean (64 s). When walking on the walkway, the speeds add up: 1.25 + 0.75 = 2 m/s.

variantlar.maslahat: Add speeds, not times: 48 + 80 or their mean has no meaning here.

kunikma: Recognizing a piecewise-constant (step) relationship on a graph
usul: Within one interval, the price does not change even if the mass changes. Think about what this looks like on a graph.
